This paper introduces Hopper, a multi-hop transformer designed for the spatiotemporal reasoning required in multi-step prediction tasks. To handle the temporal dimension, Hopper executes multiple transformer instances in a serial manner, where the output sequence of one becomes the input sequence for the next. To address the spatial dimension, each hop utilizes the attention mechanism to establish multi-hop dependencies between the input and output sequences. We validate Hopper's efficacy through simulation-based evaluation on a simulated driving task and experimental analysis. The simulation results demonstrate that Hopper significantly outperforms both single-hop transformer baselines and recurrent neural network (RNN) baselines. Furthermore, experimental analysis confirms that Hopper's performance stems from its ability to effectively model spatiotemporal dependencies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwinb/hopper. Our findings indicate that Hopper holds promise for various multi-step inference tasks involving the joint modeling of spatial and temporal dependencies. Additionally, Hopper's attention visualization reveals the ability to capture long-range dependencies, making it a valuable tool for interpretability. Finally, the source code is available at https://github.com/ashwinb/hopper. We conclude that Hopper is valuable for various multi-step inference tasks that require the joint modeling of spatial and temporal dependencies. The attention-based design of Hopper also aids in interpreting the learned dependencies, enhancing its utility for model interpretability. The provided source code includes attention visualizations, which can be accessed via the link to assist in understanding how Hopper captures long-range dependencies. Recurrent models are well-suited for temporal inference but fail to account for spatial dependencies. Conversely, convolutional models can capture both spatial and temporal dependencies but are limited to single-hop inference. Transformer models, characterized by their attention mechanism, are capable of jointly modeling dependencies across both spatial and temporal dimensions. However, current transformer architectures are restricted to single-hop inference. This work explores the possibility of extending multi-hop recurrent models and multi-hop convolutions to the transformer framework. We demonstrate that a multi-hop recurrent network can be unrolled into a multi-hop transformer, and that both multi-hop recurrent and convolutional networks can be converted into single-hop multi-attention networks. This suggests that the proposed multi-hop transformer architecture can achieve comparable performance to its recurrent and convolutional counterparts. Furthermore, the attention mechanism enables the visualization of multi-hop dependencies, enhancing the interpretability of the model. Telepresence robots (TPRs) serve as effective solutions for remote human-robot interaction, allowing users to navigate environments, observe surroundings, engage in conversations, and perform various tasks. A key feature of these systems is their shared control interface, which is increasingly being enhanced with advanced features. However, this integration often creates a conflict between usability and the system's performance. This study evaluates the Quality of Experience (QoE) of users interacting with the environment via shared control, specifically analyzing the trade-off between the controller's quality and its usability. By simulating a user with a cognitive disability, the research demonstrates that a control interface can be both high-performing and usable. The paper outlines the methodology used to assess QoE and usability, comparing these metrics to identify the optimal balance. Results indicate that a task-specific mode, which activates when a user feels the user-mode controller is insufficient, effectively improves the overall experience by leveraging the user's unique abilities. Ultimately, this approach offers users greater control over their simulation environment. The paper concludes by discussing the experimental outcomes and their relevance to future research. Keywords: Quality of Experience (QoE), Telepresence Robots (TPR), Shared Control, Cognitive Impairment.

This paper offers a concise introduction to Bayesian hierarchical linear models (BLMs) designed for forecasting. It outlines the fundamental components of BLMs and demonstrates how to apply them using the R programming language and the R package `rstan`. The study presents several models for time series data, incorporating autoregressive structures and providing cases where traditional ARIMA models are inadequate. Additionally, several time series datasets are included to facilitate practical application. The approach is also extended to panel data via structural time series models. A key benefit of this method is its ability to forecast multiple related series simultaneously, allowing for the sharing of information across them. Furthermore, the Bayesian framework enables the modeling of uncertainty at various levels, and the hierarchical structure permits the analysis of a large number of series even when individual samples are small. The second part of this tutorial is structured to serve as an entry point for researchers new to Bayesian analysis. The accompanying R package, `multilevelforecast`, was developed to support this work and is also introduced. Finally, the paper concludes with potential extensions of the models discussed. Mafia is a well-known party game where participants are divided into two factions: the "Mafia," who collaborate to eliminate civilians, and the "Civilians," who work together to expose them. This paper introduces a numerical model of the game to simulate gameplay and determine victory conditions for both sides. Our findings indicate that civilian success is highly dependent on the specific starting ratio of mafia to civilian agents. Additionally, we observe that neither faction always holds an advantage; certain scenarios favor the mafia, while others benefit the civilians. The mass distribution of gas between Jupiter and Saturn is a critical factor in determining their final sizes and the structural evolution of their protoplanetary disk. Jupiter and Saturn formed within the same H2O-ice-rich region of the disk, separated by approximately 0.5 AU. During their concurrent accretion, the migration of this ice-rich zone influenced both planets' growth. We developed a model to trace the migration of this region and how it affected the accretion of Jupiter, Saturn, and core objects situated between them. Our findings indicate that the ice-rich region moved inward from Jupiter's location toward Saturn's during their simultaneous formation, causing the mass ratio of gas accreted by Jupiter versus Saturn to shift from 3 to 1.5. Consequently, Jupiter accreted a total of 20 M_E of gas, while Saturn accumulated 100 M_E. This model also predicts a mass ratio of 2.5 for core objects forming between the two giants, a result that aligns well with the actual mass ratio of ice giant cores observed in the Kepler-456 system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the evolution of the disk's midplane density profile around Jupiter and Saturn can be explained by the migration of the ice-rich region. Specifically, the midplane density relative to the disk surface mass increased by a factor of 10 between 10 and 100 M_E for Jupiter, and by a factor of 100 between 20 and 100 M_E for Saturn. These results provide a viable explanation for the evolution of the disk structure surrounding the two primary planets of our solar system. Additionally, we show that the H2O-rich region's evolution can be modeled using a similar approach, though the specific mass ratios differ. Finally, our model successfully reproduces the mass ratio of H2O-ice cores found in ice giants, such as Uranus and Neptune, which formed within this H2O-ice-rich region. This supports the hypothesis that the H2O-ice-rich region was an intrinsic component of the protoplanetary disk. Overall, the evolution of the midplane density profile in the inner disk, caused by the migration of the H2O-ice-rich region, appears to be a common phenomenon in protoplanetary disks. This process may have played a significant role in the formation of the solar system and the subsequent evolution of the solar system. This study introduces a novel fuzzy clustering technique designed for high-dimensional data. In this approach, data points are grouped into clusters based on their distance from cluster centers, while the degree of fuzziness is managed through variable feature weights. To optimize these weights, an entropy-based evaluation function is employed. The proposed method was validated using both synthetic datasets and the California Institute of Technology (Caltech) dataset. The results demonstrate that this algorithm surpasses conventional fuzzy clustering models in handling high-dimensional information. Furthermore, numerical analysis confirms that the method effectively avoids local optima and produces more precise cluster centers. Finally, the entropy-driven feature weighting mechanism identified the most critical features within the data. A comprehensive comparison with existing methods reveals that the proposed approach not only enhances clustering performance but also facilitates feature selection. Consequently, this technique is particularly well-suited for applications in bioinformatics and pattern recognition. Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have recently gained significant attention for their enhanced predictive accuracy and reduced inference costs. However, training MoE remains difficult due to the "cold-start" issue, where the system struggles to identify the most effective expert subsets during early training, and the "steady" issue, where the training process plateaus prematurely. This study introduces a series of new algorithms designed to address these stagnant phases. First, we propose a novel algorithm called "Expert-Matching" (EM-MoE), which eliminates the cold-start problem by utilizing a matching mechanism to ensure the model reaches the optimal global solution from any initial state. Subsequently, to tackle the steady-state issue, we integrate EM-MoE with existing methods to accelerate the search for the best expert subsets. Comprehensive experiments across various datasets confirm that these proposed algorithms significantly outperform state-of-the-art approaches. The source code is available at https://github.com/Chenchen-Zhang2020/EM-MoE. Furthermore, the implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenchen-Zhang2020/EM-MoE. Given a genus $g$ curve $C$ defined over a field $K$ with genus $d$ subcovers $C_1,\dots,C_n$ having genera $d_1,\dots,d_n$ respectively, we investigate the Jacobian $J_C$'s structure relative to the subcovers' Jacobians $J_{C_i}$'s structure over $K$. This is accomplished by analyzing token-firing games conducted on $C$ while restricting movement to the specific subcovers. As a result, we provide a concrete model for the Jacobian of any genus $g$ subcover $C'$—given the Jacobians of its subcovers $J_{C_i'}$—as a specific quotient of a torus formed by the product of the subcovers' Jacobians. Applying this framework to the case where $C$ is hyperelliptic and its subcovers are the ramification covers, we derive a description for the Prym-Jacobian $J_P$ of a ramification cover's ramification curve $P$, utilizing the Jacobians $J_{C_i}$ of the corresponding branch curves $C_i$. Furthermore, we offer descriptions for the Jacobians of certain superelliptic curves and bi-ramification curves. Finally, we present a novel proof for the classical result stating that the Jacobian of a ramification curve is an abelian subvariety of the product of the Jacobians of the corresponding branch curves. These findings hold for all $K$ and, whenever applicable, specifically for algebraically closed fields. Additionally, for the case of a hyperelliptic curve $C$ over an algebraically closed field, we construct a model for $J_{C}$ using the Jacobian $J_P$ of the ramification curve $P$ and the Jacobians $J_{C_i}$ of the non-ramification covers, thereby completing the previously mentioned description for this scenario. Finally, we extend these findings to the context of Riemann surfaces. Throughout this process, we also present a general framework for the Jacobian of a supercover based on the Jacobians of its subcovers. Specifically, we demonstrate that the Jacobian of a supercover is isomorphic to a specific quotient of the product of the subcovers' Jacobians, where "supercover" refers to a curve $C$ containing a subcover $C'$ such that the map $C \to C'$ is unramified and the map $C' \to C$ is surjective

We conducted a comprehensive UVIT survey of the globular cluster NGC 4147 to investigate the ultraviolet luminosity functions of both blue straggles and post-blue straggles. The study identified 13 blue straggles and 10 post-blue straggles, with the latter being fainter and more numerous than the former. The cluster's metallicity was determined to be [Fe/H] = -1.17 ± 0.04. Utilizing the theoretical isochrones from the PARSEC database, we derived an age of 11.55 ± 0.55 Gyr and a mass of 0.80 ± 0.02 M☉ for the blue straggles. The ultraviolet luminosity functions for these two stellar populations were analyzed and compared against various binary evolution models. Our results indicate that the post-blue straggles are best explained by the wind mass transfer scenario, whereas blue straggles likely result from a merger between two stars. Additionally, we examined the color-magnitude diagram and presented the findings. The analysis of UVIT photometry data revealed that the cluster's center is highly concentrated, with a core radius of 0.7 arcmin and a half-light radius of 2.5 arcmin. Furthermore, the cluster exhibits a low dynamical state, characterized by a mass-to-light ratio of 2.1 ± 0.1 M☉/L☉ and a velocity dispersion of 10.0 ± 0.5 km/s. Transferability is a core principle of generalization in deep learning, underpinned by two key agreements: the feature transfer agreement (FTA) and the task transfer agreement (TTA). This study challenges both agreements. Regarding FTA, we posit that transferability does not necessitate knowledge transfer; instead, it can arise from the generalization of specific learned patterns. To validate this, we introduce a novel ablation-based method called Ablation + Fine-tuning (A+), which, combined with a new metric termed the Ablation Consistency (AC), demonstrates this hypothesis. Furthermore, we introduce Task-Ablation (TA), a concept that reveals TTA is not universal. The performance of A+ and AC are robust, and the insights provided by TA offer a fresh perspective on deep learning. Our empirical findings indicate that the optimal strategy for transfer learning is to employ A+ within a multi-source framework, while selecting a specific source task based on the characteristics of the target task. Additionally, we propose a task clustering method to facilitate this selection process. This research presents a new viewpoint on transfer learning, potentially opening new avenues for its study. High modularity in social networks restricts the rapid dissemination of information. Our findings demonstrate that as a network's modularity increases, the speed of information spread decreases, even when the number of nodes and edges remains constant. This effect is particularly pronounced during the initial stages of dissemination. We validate this relationship across various model-based networks, including social and technological systems, as well as real-world data from a Twitter hashtag and a co-authorship network. Furthermore, we show that the velocity of information flow decreases linearly with network modularity. This linearity is attributed to the fact that the ratio of intra-community to inter-community edges is constant, regardless of the total edge count. Finally, we establish that this linearity holds true for both the parameter-free velocity and the parameter-dependent characteristic time required for information diffusion. These insights into network-driven information diffusion could inform the design of efficient dissemination strategies. Our framework offers potential applications in fields such as epidemiology, where understanding the impact of modularity on the rapid transmission of infectious diseases is crucial. Additionally, our approach can aid in designing efficient communication campaigns, such as those used in political campaigns. Utilizing the Conditional Calabi–Yau (CY) flow introduced by Chen and Tian, we establish the uniqueness and stability of the Complex Thomas–Yau (CTY) flow relative to mean curvature flow, with findings applicable to the Generalized Thomas–Yau (GTY) flow as well. This proof of distinctiveness not only offers a geometric demonstration of the Hilbert–Mumford criterion but also enables the resolution of algebraic stability issues concerning the closed canonical product-formation. Furthermore, our result provides additional insight into the long-time behavior and convergence of this technique. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any solution to the CY flow defined on a time interval $[0,T)$, if $T$ is finite, the solution exhibits blow-up behavior; conversely, if $T$ is infinite, the solution converges to a critical point of the CY functional. Additionally, we present a geometric interpretation of the gradient estimate and derive a novel Yang–Mills type curvature estimate for the holonomy connection associated with the CY flow. These estimates are instrumental in proving the distinctiveness and the main theorem. Finally, we illustrate how to apply this technique to analyze the stability of product-formation. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 provides a review of complex and generalized product-formation; Section 3 reviews the CY flow and its fundamental estimates; Section 4 proves the blow-up phenomenon and the Hilbert–Mumford criterion; Section 5 details the gradient estimate and its consequences; and Section 6 addresses the main theorem and the stability of product-formation. This study presents a discrete-time precision analysis of the time-domain standard perturbation model for unamplified link segments. We derive a novel precision analysis for amplified link sections, which will be addressed in our future research. Precision analysis offers substantial advantages in simulating time-domain models for long-haul transmission systems, as it enables the use of coarse time grids for narrowband signals, thereby significantly reducing computational demands. However, to the best of our knowledge, no prior work has explored the transition of this analysis from unamplified to amplified links. Our work addresses this gap by deriving the standard perturbation precision examination for amplified links. We validate the derived expressions using a two-node simulation within the long-haul transmission system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the standard perturbation model achieves a substantial computational reduction compared to the generalized fractional model. Finally, we show that our proposed amplified link precision examination remains effective in predicting the accuracy of the standard perturbation model. Additionally, we observe that the standard perturbation model remains highly accurate even at very small signal-to-noise ratios. These findings are particularly relevant for long-haul transmission systems, where simulations are typically conducted at moderate signal-to-noise ratios, potentially resulting in a significant underestimation of modeling errors. Building on the concept of a universal vessel, which offers a language for interactive computation, we propose a universal orchestration vessel designed to manage the synchronization and S4 streams of universal vessels. Ozy, our implementation of this concept, provides a unified interface for composing, synchronizing, and stream-processing with extensive libraries of vessels. It enables the modular assembly of sophisticated vessel networks and facilitates the stream-processing of large datasets using vessels from various libraries. We illustrate these capabilities through specific examples. Furthermore, we demonstrate that ozy vessels are equivalent to a specific type of Mealy machine, establishing a theoretical link to established computational models. Finally, we show that ozy vessels can be compiled into C++ and Python, thereby extending the ozy vessel ecosystem with established programming languages. This compilation capability allows for the integration of ozy vessels with existing programming and modeling frameworks. Additionally, we outline how ozy vessels and networks can be simulated, offering an alternative pathway to expand the ecosystem. The paper concludes with a summary and directions for future research. We obtained high-precision measurements of the quantized Hall resistance in a GaAs/AlGaAs two-dimensional electron system at high magnetic fields. Notably, a reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall stage was detected at filling factors ranging from 8.2 to 9.8. The persistence of this reentrant stage across magnetic field rates indicates a low level of disorder in our sample. Furthermore, this stage reemerges at magnetic field rates significantly higher than those required for the reentrant 3/2 and reentrant 2/3 stages, suggesting that the 5/2 state is more robust. Additionally, an extra 5/2 reentrant region was identified at filling factors between 12.6 and 13, accompanied by quantum Hall transitions at filling factors between 11 and 12. These findings imply the existence of reentrant multifluid quantum Hall states. The amplitude of the reentrant 5/2 stage is comparable to the amplitudes of the Reentrant Weak Integer Quantum Hall (RIQH) and Reentrant Composite Fermion Valence Bond Liquid (RCFVB) stages, supporting the multifluid scenario. However, the observed splitting of the reentrant 5/2 stage is smaller than the splitting between the RIQH and CFBVB stages, indicating that the 5/2 state is less fragile than the RIQH and CFBVB states. This suggests that the 5/2 state may be stabilized by a combination of 3/2 and 2/3 quantum Hall states. The moderate intensity of Landau level mixing in our experiment allowed for the observation of the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall stage, whereas such a phenomenon was previously detected only at very high magnetic field sweep rates. These results provide valuable insights into the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall state, which has been the subject of extensive theoretical and experimental investigation. The stability of the reentrant 5/2 quantum Hall stage offers a potential method for investigating the 5/2 state under varying experimental conditions. A fundamental tenet of statistical learning theory is that models should be neither excessively complex nor simple. However, the traditional complexity analysis of statistical learning methods often overlooks the computational resources required to train and infer them. This paper demonstrates that accounting for training and inference complexity can necessitate even greater overparameterization than what is driven by data issues like noise or sparsity. Specifically, we examine the training and inference costs for a broad class of sparse linear regression techniques, including Lasso, Bridge regression, and Least Angle Regression (LARS). We establish that while the minimum variance estimators in this category scale with data dimensionality, those achievable within practical computational limits depend solely on the effective rank of the data, a metric that is either polynomially bounded or, in many cases, constant. Furthermore, we support this finding with a lower bound indicating that overparameterization is indispensable for certain problems. Our results hold for both Gaussian and non-Gaussian settings. Finally, our findings align with the observation that large, overparameterized neural networks can be effectively trained via simple gradient descent. Additionally, we extend our results to scenarios where sparsity is not pre-assumed, revealing that sparsification can substantially lower the effective rank. This insight helps explain the success of pruning techniques in reducing the parameter count of overparameterized neural networks. Our paper includes supplementary materials with proofs and additional results. Supplementary code is available at https://github.com/Prathamesh1998O/Overparameterization. Urban dial-a-ride services are designed to enhance mobility for a broad spectrum of customers. This study examines the metropolitan dial-a-ride context, highlighting several specific challenges: heterogeneous customer needs, including both ride-sharing and non-ride-sharing requests; the necessity to determine whether a customer is served by a vehicle or by public transit; and the presence of public transit lines. We introduce a Branch-and-Bound algorithm designed to maximize the number of customers served while minimizing total vehicle kilometers. Computational results demonstrate that, within a five-minute limit, the algorithm identifies optimal solutions for instances involving up to 20 ride-sharing customers. Furthermore, the algorithm efficiently generates high-quality solutions, achieving an average gap of 1.2% from optimality. These findings indicate the algorithm's potential to significantly reduce vehicle kilometers in practical applications. Additionally, a real-world case study of the service reveals that the proposed approach can achieve a 10% reduction in vehicle kilometers compared to the current operational policy. Finally, we present a large-scale extension of the model, which is formulated as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) and solved using CPLEX. Finally, we demonstrate that this extended model yields a 12% reduction in vehicle kilometers relative to a simple first-come, first-served policy. Keywords: Dial-a-Ride, Ride-sharing, Public Transit, Vehicle Routing, Green Logistics.

We introduce the Insight Recognized Multi-modal Pretraining (IR-MP) framework, an end-to-end approach designed for product multilingual conversational dialog systems. This method integrates a pretraining phase with a posttraining phase. During pretraining, an RNN-based decoder is initially trained to facilitate multi-modal pretraining, which involves an attention mechanism that combines visual insights from images with linguistic insights derived from a vast corpus of product reviews across various e-commerce platforms in multiple e-commerce contexts (MICs). Subsequently, an e-commerce specific model is developed using this pre-trained RNN decoder, incorporating self-attention layers and transformer-based encoders to process product images and reviews. Finally, an RNN-based encoder-decoder based on the RNN decoder is trained on product dialog data to generate responses. Extensive experiments conducted on product dialog systems demonstrate the efficacy of our RNN decoder, achieving state-of-the-art (SOTA) results in both single-modal and multi-modal scenarios. Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a chronic, progressive condition that causes significant impairment in memory and cognitive functions. Early detection is crucial for initiating timely treatment to mitigate this progression. This study introduces a deep learning framework designed to predict AD onset from brain MRI scans. We developed a deep neural network utilizing the deep infoNLLB loss function, which was trained to classify images as either healthy controls or AD patients. The model was evaluated on the 2018 ADNI Challenge dataset, which included 3D MPRAGE and 3D PD MPRAGE modalities. The system achieved a 76% accuracy in identifying a binary classification of healthy controls versus AD patients and a 74% accuracy in predicting the advancement to AD. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/raja-singh/DeepInfoNLLB-ADNI. This approach demonstrates superior performance in classifying AD patients compared to existing methods. Furthermore, the findings indicate that 3D MPRAGE images yield better results than 3D PD MPRAGE images for the binary classification task. The results also highlight that deep infoNLLB loss functions are particularly effective for medical image classification. Finally, the study confirms that both 3D MPRAGE and 3D PD MPRAGE modalities are valuable for predicting the advancement to Alzheimer's disease. **Keywords:** Alzheimer's disease, deep infoNLLB loss, deep learning, MRI classification.

This paper introduces the semantics comprehension model for interactive recurrent neural networks. In this framework, semantic understanding is modeled as a sequence of interactions between a question and accumulated answers, where each step involves processing the previous answer, the original context, and a newly generated answer. To effectively capture the interdependence between contextual and query information, we employ an interaction-driven recurrent neural network. Furthermore, we incorporate a self-attention mechanism to identify the relevance between input instances, thereby enhancing semantic comprehension. The model's efficacy is validated using the SemEval dataset, with performance evaluated through precision, recall, and F1 scores. Experimental results confirm that the proposed model significantly outperforms baseline approaches. Additionally, the inclusion of the self-attention mechanism is shown to improve overall performance. Finally, we present a case study to illustrate how the interaction-driven neural network functions in practice. This study investigates the electronic and magnetic characteristics of a strongly spin-orbit-coupled, correlated paramagnetic alloy through a self-consistent analysis of the correlated band structure. Our findings indicate that the effective spin-orbit interaction (SOI) is amplified by the strong electronic correlations present in the system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this enhancement arises from the modulation of the Fermi level within the band structure. These results suggest that strongly correlated materials offer a promising platform for developing high-efficiency spin devices. Finally, our methodology is applicable to various materials exhibiting strong electronic correlations and spin-orbit coupling. Specifically, we outline a general approach for achieving paramagnetic states with strongly renormalized spin-orbit coupling, which is essential for creating materials suitable for spintronics and quantum computing. This involves tuning the Fermi level to occupy only states with significant SOI, a configuration that can be realized by adjusting the electronic correlation strength. Consequently, this strategy could enable the creation of paramagnets where spin-orbit coupling is orders of magnitude stronger than in conventional non-correlated paramagnetic metals. Such materials would be highly valuable for spintronic applications. Additionally, we propose that a similar material could be synthesized using a straightforward chemical substitution process. This involves replacing one element in a known paramagnetic alloy with another that has a similar atomic radius but possesses higher electronic correlations. This method would allow for the tuning of the Fermi level to align with regions of high SOI, thereby achieving the desired materials without necessitating extreme experimental conditions. Finally, we emphasize that the proposed methodology is general and can be applied to any material exhibiting strong electronic correlations and spin-orbit coupling. We examine a metastable dark matter candidate arising from a hidden conformal sector possessing a large anomalous dimension, $\Delta$. The characteristic mass scale of this sector, $m_\chi \sim \Lambda/m^{\Delta-1/2}_\pi$, serves as the dark matter mass, with the dark matter abundance established via the Metastable Shadow Matter (MSM) mechanism. In this framework, annihilation into visible states occurs through higher-dimensional operators of the form $\frac{1}{m_\pi^\Delta}\mathcal{O}_{\rm SM}\mathcal{O}_{\rm DM}$. The standard recombination redshift, $z_\mathrm{rec}$, is delayed to $z_\mathrm{rec} \sim (m_\pi/m_\chi)^{2(\Delta-1/2)}$, allowing the dark matter annihilation cross section to remain above the thermal freeze-out value for an extended period. This scenario accommodates both thermal and non-thermal dark matter production and remains consistent with current direct detection limits for dark fermions with masses up to approximately 10 PeV. Furthermore, we explore the potential for detecting dark matter produced in cosmic ray interactions at the proposed Proton Energy Enhancement Facility (PEF). Finally, we analyze the implications of non-observation of dark matter in the mass range $m_\chi \lesssim 100\,$TeV on the model's parameter space. We also address the production of dark matter within the Sun and its impact on neutrino flux predictions, noting that the PEF could offer a means to distinguish between different production mechanisms. Additionally, we investigate the production of dark matter within the Earth and the associated neutrino signals, which could be investigated using the proposed IceCube-Gen2 observatory. Finally, we discuss the implications of the non-observation of dark matter in the mass range $m_\chi \lesssim 10\,$TeV, as inferred from the absence of neutrino signals detected by IceCube. Developing artificial intelligence (AI) tools for clinical decision-making is a rapidly expanding field, yet these tools often face distributional shifts when moving from training environments to real-world healthcare settings. This discrepancy arises because historical data fails to capture the full complexity of actual clinical data, leading to inaccurate predictions and a lack of trust in AI-generated outputs. To address this, we introduce a novel evaluation framework designed to assess the reliability of AI predictions. Specifically, we develop a method to estimate the uncertainty surrounding each prediction, enabling the calculation of the probability that a specific outcome will occur. We validate this framework using exam performance data from a clinical decision support system intended for diagnosing diabetic foot ulcers. Our approach effectively accounts for distributional shifts and successfully identifies the most probable outcome for each clinical case. We anticipate that this framework will serve as a more robust evaluation metric for AI applications within healthcare. Additionally, the source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/NonParametricConformalPrediction. Finally, we plan to expand this methodology to evaluate other AI tools across diverse medical specialties in the future. Simulating the dynamics of biomolecules using atomistic molecular dynamics (MD) offers a fundamental understanding of their behavior, yet it often fails to capture rare events due to limited sampling. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective technique to enhance the sampling of DNA conformations. By applying a rigid (site-fixed) foundation biasing potential to specific phosphorus atoms, we successfully reproduce experimentally observed DNA bending. This approach is straightforward to implement in any MD simulation framework. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the method can replicate both the mean and variance of bending angles, as well as the distribution of twist angles, aligning closely with experimental data. The results indicate that even a single bending point is sufficient to generate conformations consistent with "oligonucleotide-sequencing-by-synthesis" protocols. Consequently, this simple strategy represents a significant advancement in the accurate sampling of DNA structures. The associated Python code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robertkoster/rf-potential. Finally, we illustrate the method's utility by reproducing the intrinsic bending profile of the $\lambda$-DNA molecule. This is achieved by calculating the probability density of the distances between the center-of-mass positions of the bend sites, which matches the bending profile reported in prior literature. The methodology is fully automated and can be easily adapted for specific sequence-dependent bending profiles. In summary, we present a highly effective, straightforward, and automated approach for sampling DNA conformations. This represents a significant step toward simulating DNA dynamics at the atomistic level. The technique is readily applicable to any DNA sequence and can be easily extended to other biomolecules. This study evaluates the ANS entropy compression and decompression algorithm, demonstrating its efficacy with lossless compression rates of up to 50% on certain file types. The research compares ANS performance against run-length encoding, LZ77, and entropy coding, while also assessing its impact alongside lossy compression techniques like H.264 video compression. Pore water is thought to be the primary driver of the dielectric response in cementitious materials. To investigate this relationship, we measured the dielectric properties of cement paste pore fluids across a frequency range of 10 Hz to 100 MHz, comparing these experimental results with a new electrostatic model. This theoretical approach accounts for the water's dielectric constant, ionic concentration, and specific surface area. The strong agreement between our results and the Poole-Frenkel theory indicates that the Poole-Frenkel dielectric relaxation of pore fluid is a key factor in the overall dielectric behavior of cementitious materials. Furthermore, our findings suggest that the Poole-Frenkel relaxation of pore water can be utilized to monitor the hydration process in cementitious materials. Additionally, the dielectric relaxation of hydroxyapatite has been modeled using the Debye equation, with the model's parameters determined by fitting the experimental data. This research holds significant potential for advancing the understanding of dielectric relaxation in cementitious materials. Ultimately, these results may aid in the development of dielectric sensors capable of detecting the degree of hydration in cementitious structures. Finally, the proposed theoretical framework could facilitate the design of dielectric devices for monitoring the hydration process in such materials. This doctoral thesis examines the design tools for building and managing military swarms of autonomous, remotely piloted drones. The study investigates the advantages of these swarm systems and their deployment in military contexts, with a specific emphasis on communication and control protocols. To achieve this, the research utilizes a multi-agent simulation environment to model the drones and their interactions. Furthermore, the thesis explores the application of Artificial Language Processing (ALP) to generate command language instructions for the autonomous drones. ALP serves as a framework for creating, analyzing, and evaluating languages through computational methods. The findings indicate that employing ALP to formulate building tools for swarm development is a promising approach for creating robotic systems. Additionally, the proposed ALP method was validated within the simulation environment, demonstrating its effectiveness in generating multi-agent behaviors. The thesis concludes by addressing the study's limitations and suggesting potential future research directions. The work is structured into six chapters, with the first chapter providing an overview of the investigation and an analysis of swarm robotics, while the second through fifth chapters detailing the specific research components. The fourth chapter specifically focuses on the ALP method and its validation in the simulated setting. The fifth chapter presents the conclusions of the research and outlines potential avenues for future inquiry. The fifth chapter also references related work, noting that ALP has been applied to various domains, including robotics and multi-agent systems. For instance, Shieber et al. demonstrated that ALP can generate commands for robot behaviors, while Shieber and Thomas showed its utility in modeling multi-agent systems. Other applications include the development of intelligent agents and the creation of new communication languages for robots. The Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serves as a valuable cosmological probe, offering insights into the thermal and ionization state of the intergalactic medium (IGM), as well as the growth of matter density fluctuations. This study introduces a straightforward cosmological deduction for the one-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum, expressed through the mean density and temperature of the IGM, the helium ionization fraction, the matter density parameter, and the amplitude of matter density fluctuations. These parameters are interconnected via the three-dimensional power spectrum of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, which is derived from the power spectrum of the thermal state of the IGM. By utilizing a Boltzmann code, we solve for the time evolution of these parameters. This fast and accurate approximation enables the analysis of the interplay among IGM properties, the thermal history of the IGM, and the growth of matter density fluctuations. We compare our approximation against full numerical simulations of the three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum, finding that the relative error remains below 10% for helium ionization fractions ($f_{\rm HeIII}$) ranging from 0 to 0.5. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the accuracy of our approximation can be further enhanced by incorporating the contribution from the thermal history of the IGM. Consequently, we provide a cosmological deduction for the mean density of Lyman limit systems, showing that the relative error is approximately 10% for $f_{\rm HeIII}$ values between 0 and 0.5. Our fast approximation proves particularly effective for scenarios involving reionization of helium. Finally, we apply this deduction to analyze the evolution of the IGM temperature and helium ionization, as well as the evolution of the three-dimensional Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum. This analysis yields the evolution of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum, which aligns well with results from full numerical simulations. The evolution of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest power spectrum is sensitive to the thermal and helium ionization history of the IGM, as well as to the amplitude of matter density fluctuations. We conclude that the accuracy of our cosmological deduction can be further improved by accounting for the contribution from the density power spectrum of the thermal state of the IGM. This further enhanced approximation is especially effective for cases involving the thermal and helium ionization history of the IGM. We present the first experimental confirmation of transverse-emittance dilution during the mixing process and offer a comprehensive modeling approach to explain these findings. Furthermore, we demonstrate the transfer of longitudinal emittances from a 1.6 GeV beam to a 1.2 GeV beam, achieving a final longitudinal emittances ratio of 1.1. This result surpasses the theoretical emittances ratio of 0.8 predicted by adiabatic invariance, thereby validating the non-adiabatic emittances matching theory. The successful transfer of both transverse and longitudinal emittances holds significant potential for beam-halo extraction in colliders and beam cooling in accelerators. Human trajectory prediction is a critical research area with extensive applications in robotics and autonomous systems. Experimental results demonstrate that SSCVAE outperforms other leading methods in predicting trajectories for both pedestrians and vehicles. This study introduces a methodology for quantifying complexity within Boltzmann networks, utilizing information-theoretic concepts of entropy, surprise, and complexity. These metrics are calculated based on the probability distributions of inputs, outputs, and weights. We establish a theoretical relationship between the complexity of the weights and both input and output complexities, demonstrating that the model's capacity is directly proportional to these information-theoretic measures. Furthermore, we analyze complexity trends across various architectures, including perceptrons, MUX units, and Hopfield networks. Our results indicate that perceptrons and MUX units exhibit a linear relationship between input and output complexity, whereas Hopfield networks display a non-linear, many-to-one mapping where multiple complexities can converge to a single output complexity. Finally, we illustrate how these metrics evolve during the training of a Hopfield network designed to store the Ising model. This approach offers a novel perspective on learning dynamics, effectively complementing traditional analyses that rely on weight evolution. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python library to facilitate the application of these tools to other neural network types. This paper introduces a novel, high-performance deep learning approach designed for the real-time recognition of sequential hand gestures involving multiple hands. Our method builds upon Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) and incorporates a newly developed preprocessing technique for hand images. We demonstrate that this preprocessing strategy and our neural network architecture are effective for recognizing human sequential hand gestures. Furthermore, our approach is not limited to this specific task; it yields substantial improvements in recent real-time hand gesture recognition models, achieving state-of-the-art accuracy with reduced complexity and enhanced speed. This advantage is particularly significant in edge computing scenarios, such as the human-machine interaction framework detailed later in the study. The model was trained and validated using the Charades dataset, a widely used benchmark in the field. Following these results, we outline a proof-of-concept system that integrates our model with the Microsoft HoloLens. This system allows users to collaborate with the HoloLens and manipulate its mixed reality interface using sequential hand gestures. The proposed solution facilitates a new form of human-machine interaction, enabling individuals to engage with HoloLens devices and Mixed Reality applications without requiring any device-specific training. This is crucial given that only a small fraction of the global population has used HoloLens devices. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this new interaction paradigm, highlighting its relevance in both civilian and military contexts. Specifically, in HEMS (Helicopter Emergency Medical Service) operations, our solution enables medical personnel to interact with HoloLens devices using intuitive hand gestures, thereby allowing them to maintain direct contact with patients. This capability is essential for ensuring patient safety and preventing exposure to viral agents. Additionally, the proposed solution offers military personnel a means of interacting with HoloLens devices, which could be valuable in various scenarios, including search and rescue operations. The method can be easily adapted to other military use cases by simply retraining the model with gesture sets relevant to the specific task at hand. To facilitate such retraining, we have made the model and the HoloLens interface accessible to the research community. This interface supports a set of 12 hand gestures and was utilized to develop a proof-of-concept system for controlling the HoloLens interface. The code is available at: https://github.com/sergio-oliveira-dias/distributed-hand-gesture-recognition. Additionally, we have made the model accessible for integration with other HoloLens interfaces that support different gesture sets. Counterdiabatic (CD) adiabatic evolution enables rapid ground-state preparation by suppressing non-adiabatic excitations through carefully designed auxiliary fields. However, implementing these CD fields exactly is generally impossible. In this study, we apply a generalized variational counterdiabatic (vCD) strategy to the well-known two-dimensional Hubbard model. By utilizing a CD field constructed from the exact analytic expression of the instantaneous adiabatic gauge potential, we demonstrate the successful preparation of the Hubbard model's ground state. Furthermore, we examine several distinct ansatz forms for the variational term Hamiltonian. Our results show that the vCD strategy outperforms the conventional CD approach when restricted to the same number of variational parameters, and it achieves rapid ground-state preparation even under severe constraints on the complexity of the variational term Hamiltonian. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this efficient vCD strategy in the context of quantum computing. Additionally, our methodology for analyzing vCD strategies and their performance is broadly applicable to other quantum many-body systems. This approach is expected to facilitate the study of quantum state preparation and adiabatic evolution using variational techniques on quantum computers. Our code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenLi1992/vCD_Hubbard. Our computational code is also available upon request. Furthermore, the supplementary material includes a detailed description of the vCD strategy and performance analysis for the transverse-field Ising model. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for photo tint mapping that maintains a specific hue temperature. Designed for creative photo editing, the method is grounded in high-velocity human color perception, specifically targeting decoloration processes. The study demonstrates that human hue temperature remains stable during decoloration, provided the process is slowed to a pace within acceptable perception limits. The proposed algorithm is formulated as a non-linear least squares optimization problem, utilizing least squares estimation for its solution. Additionally, experimental results are compared against an existing method to validate the approach's effectiveness. Keywords: Photo editing, photo tint mapping, photo decoloration, photo perception, photo chromaticity, photo optimization.

This paper introduces formulas for exponential Taylor expansions that retain the simplicity and utility of standard Taylor series, but with exponentiated coefficients. For instance, the series for $\exp(\alpha x)$ takes the form $\sum_{n=0}^\infty (\alpha^n x^n / n!)$, which converges for all real $x$ when $\alpha$ is real, and for $|x| < 1$ when $\alpha$ is complex. Additional results are provided for other functions of limited domain, such as $\exp(\alpha x^2)$, $\exp(\alpha x+x^3/3)$, $\exp(\alpha x+x^3/3+2\xi x^5/5!)$, $\exp(\alpha x^3/3)$, $\exp(\alpha x^4/4!)$$, and $\exp(\alpha x^5/5!)$. These expressions are intended for numerical evaluation where $|\alpha|$ is small, with specific bounds on $x$ depending on the function and the value of $\alpha$. The approach involves applying substitutions to well-established and frequently utilized functions like $\exp(\pm x)$, $\exp(-x^2/2)$, $\exp(-x^3/3)$, $\exp(-x^4/4!)$, and $\exp(-x^5/5!)$. The validity of these expansions relies on the convergence of the original standard Taylor series. The study concludes with numerical examples and a discussion on the advantages and disadvantages relative to the standard Taylor series. Furthermore, the appendix presents bounds for the remainder term of these expansions, which can be derived from the standard Lagrange remainder bound. Functions utilizing these expansions are available in the C++ header file expvn.h, which is part of the mvnlib library. This library also includes functions based on Chebyshev expansions for $\exp(\alpha x)$, $\exp(\alpha x^2/2)$, $\exp(\alpha x^3/3)$, $\exp(\alpha x^4/4!)$, and $\exp(\alpha x^5/5!)$. We demonstrate that harmonic maps from a compact surface with genus at least 2 to a compact metric space equipped with a CAT(-1) structure are precisely the homeomorphisms. This result extends to surfaces of genus 1 provided the boundary components map to disjoint points in the target space. The proof utilizes the minimal current approach to harmonic maps pioneered by J. Schoen and Y. Schoen. Furthermore, we establish that harmonic maps from genus 2 surfaces to tree metrics possess the unique extension property. These findings apply to branched harmonic maps where all branch points are totally ramified. We also present examples of harmonic maps exhibiting multiple minimal extensions and instances of non-uniqueness for harmonic maps defined on the universal cover. The paper concludes with a series of examples and questions concerning harmonic maps into CAT($k$) structures. A companion study will address the uniformization problem for surface groups via maximal maps. In that work, we will prove that harmonic maps from genus $g \geq 2$ surfaces to CAT(-1) structures are automatically injective and that the harmonic map is unique. Additionally, we will confirm the uniformization theorem for genus 1 surfaces with non-constant degree harmonic maps into tree metrics. The methodology for the genus 1 case relies on techniques developed by J. Cheeger and D. C. Johnson regarding minimal surfaces in negatively curved manifolds. Finally, the paper addresses the construction of harmonic maps from surfaces to simplicial complexes and the analysis of their harmonic differentials. These tools are essential for the theory of harmonic maps from surfaces to graphs, which forms the subject of our upcoming publication. We also explore the connection between harmonic maps and the Teichmüller space of harmonic differentials. One application involves characterizing the Teichmüller space of harmonic differentials on genus $g \geq 2$ surfaces as the space of homotopy classes of harmonic maps to a specific 4-valent tree. A second application involves characterizing the space of harmonic differentials on genus $g \geq 2$ surfaces as the space of harmonic maps from a surface to a simplicial complex with contractible universal cover. We introduce a theoretical framework for designing experiments involving photons generated by laser-plasma interactions. This approach is applicable to the photons arising from the intense electromagnetic fields of such plasmas, which can be harnessed to probe matter through non-linear quantum electro-dynamics. The framework is demonstrated using photon-photon scattering as a case study. Our findings indicate that laser intensity and plasma density are equally critical parameters in experimental design. Furthermore, we identify specific regions within the intensity-density parameter space where significant photon-photon interactions are expected. These target areas provide a strategic guide for optimizing future experiments. Additionally, we explore the potential for multi-peaked photon spectra, which could offer further opportunities to enhance photon interactions. This work establishes a foundation for the emerging field of photon-photon science. Optimized experimental conditions are poised to enable the creation of real, massive entities known as solitons, which have previously been observed only in controlled theoretical models. Moreover, the proposed framework is extensible to other relevant phenomena, including photon surfaces, photon crystals, and photon gases. Optimizing experiments based on this design approach will facilitate the investigation into the statistical mechanics governing these exotic systems. Ultimately, the outcomes of these studies are poised to have far-reaching implications across diverse areas of physics. Furthermore, the framework is not limited to laser-intensity-driven sources; it can also be applied to photon sources driven by plasma instabilities. This suggests that laser-plasma interactions could serve as a versatile platform for generating a wide variety of useful photon sources. Photon-photon science holds the promise of advancing both fundamental and applied research. This study examines the sensitivity of the lower mass bound for the lightest Higgs boson in the Two-Doublet Model to the soft-breaking $Z_2$ parameter, $m_{12}$. By analyzing the dependence on the model's free parameters, we determine the sensitivity coefficients regarding both tree-level and loop-level contributions. Although the $m_{12}$ parameter influences the lightest Higgs mass at loop level, its effects are marginal, and our results suggest a potential sensitivity enhancement. Furthermore, we identify a critical limitation: below certain values of $m_{12}$, the model becomes non-perturbative due to large loop couplings, which must be accounted for when setting lower mass bounds. This issue is particularly pronounced in mixed scenarios, where the sensitivity to $m_{12}$ far exceeds that of other loop parameters. Finally, we illustrate the sensitivity enhancement using the case of a light CP-even Higgs boson in the mixed scenario, where the CP-odd Higgs mass is set to half of the $W$ boson mass. In this context, we show that the sensitivity enhancement factor is approximately 2.5. Additionally, we discuss the implications of this sensitivity enhancement for future collider searches. We conclude that the proposed sensitivity coefficients serve as a valuable tool for setting lower mass bounds on additional Higgs bosons, as they allow researchers to rapidly and efficiently identify the most relevant parameters for the mass bound. This approach avoids unnecessary model scans, thereby optimizing the use of computational resources. This methodology is especially pertinent for establishing lower mass bounds on light charged and CP-odd Higgs bosons, which are often constrained by current experimental limits. We anticipate that this sensitivity-enhancement approach will be applicable to various other physics scenarios. A detailed examination of the sensitivity dependence on other model parameters will be presented in a forthcoming paper. Our findings suggest that the sensitivity dependence on the $\lambda_5$ parameter is relatively weak, whereas a significant enhancement is expected for the $\lambda_6$ and $\lambda_7$ parameters. This is because the $\lambda_6$ and $\lambda_7$ parameters appear in the mass eigenstate basis only at loop level, whereas $\lambda_5$ does. Consequently, the sensitivity-enhancement approach is particularly valuable for mixed scenarios, where the lightest Higgs mass is primarily determined by the $\lambda_6$ and $\lambda_7$ parameters. This paper introduces an algorithm for transferring information from Relational tables to RDF graphs that includes instance-level type information derived from Shape Expressions. The method employs materialization strategies for instance-level type information, generating this data from the Relational table's primary key to foreign key relationships. A test suite comprising various Relational schemas and corresponding type networks has been established to validate the algorithm. The transfer process is modeled using RDF mapping languages, and the resulting instance-level type information is utilized to enhance type information within the derived RDF graph. The study examines various materialization scenarios and their specific requirements for information transfer from Relational to RDF formats, analyzing how different approaches to materializing instance-level type information influence the accuracy of type inference in the target RDF graph. Finally, the paper addresses challenges related to modeling instance-level type information from Relational tables as Shape Expressions and explores methods for reconstructing Relational schemas from instance-level type-enriched RDF graphs. Through examples and test cases, the paper demonstrates the utility of instance-level type information in ensuring the accuracy of derived type information during the transfer process. Additionally, the paper explores methods for validating the correctness of the transfer process and assessing the correctness of type information in the target RDF graph based on Shape Expression constraints. The proposed approach is applicable to knowledge graph integration, semantic data migration, and data migration in general. The paper concludes by discussing potential future research directions and their potential impacts. This paper presents a new method for analyzing top-quark pair plus Higgs-like object events at the LHC to search for a Standard Model (SM)-like scalar boson $\phi$. The approach relies on the observation that the SM predicts a substantial number of events where a top quark decays leptonically, while the $\phi$ boson decays into bottom quarks. This technique is particularly effective for detecting a light $\phi$ boson, which is difficult to isolate in other channels due to overwhelming Standard Model backgrounds. We demonstrate that this strategy is sensitive to a $\phi$ boson with a mass as low as $10$ GeV, provided its production cross section relative to the SM Higgs (for a given mass) is at least $10^4$ times larger. Such high enhancements are feasible within beyond-Standard-Model frameworks, including those that address the muon $g-2$ anomaly. We illustrate the proposed analysis using a simplified model where a scalar leptoquark $S$ couples to both top quarks and bottom quarks. In this scenario, the dominant process is the associated production of top quark pairs via $t$-channel $S$ exchange, a mechanism that generates a scalar resonance decaying to $b\bar{b}$ when $\phi$ exists. The primary background for this search arises from $t\bar{t}$ events where the quarks decay semileptonically, with the leptonic decay products mimicking the $\phi$ signal. To mitigate this, we employ a novel method that utilizes the full kinematic information of the top quark decay products. Specifically, we construct a likelihood function based on the distributions of decay products in the $\phi$ mass range versus those outside it. This likelihood is sensitive to the presence of a scalar resonance within the mass range of the signal, even when the resonance is narrow. We show that the mass sensitivity can be significantly improved by incorporating additional information about the $\phi$ production mechanism, such as the Higgs boson associated production. Finally, we demonstrate that the proposed analysis can identify a light $\phi$ boson with a mass as low as $10$ GeV, assuming an integrated luminosity of $300$ fb$^{-1}$. We introduce a method to enable non-experts to effectively utilize state-of-the-art language models without access to advanced tools like attention visualizers. This approach leverages a novel class of prompts that allow users to interact with models using minimal domain knowledge and extremely limited examples. These prompts facilitate various examining tasks, including feature analysis, attention allocation, and error diagnosis. Empirical results demonstrate that our prompts yield significant improvements in feature analysis, guide the standard encoder to process inputs more effectively, and help the decoder generate more accurate responses. Furthermore, our prompts successfully direct the model's focus to the most critical input segments during the input processing stage and during the reconstruction of key keywords in the output stage. Additionally, our examining prompts assist the decoder in correcting errors, specifically by fixing incorrect keywords and ordering issues within the output. Overall, our findings indicate that our method successfully achieves the goal of providing a user-friendly interface for examining tasks, allowing access to current state-of-the-art models with just a few examples and basic domain knowledge. We present the findings of a spectroscopic survey of 20 Be-type stars within the 30 Doradus starburst region. Our analysis identifies 11 classical Be stars, three likely chemically peculiar Be-type stars, one likely Be/Bn hybrid star, one Be/B5 main-sequence binary, and four non-Be Be-type stars. Our investigation into the spectral characteristics of these stars reveals that the broadening of spectral lines in the broadest lineshapes is primarily caused by stellar rotation. Furthermore, the equivalent widths of absorption lines in the broadest-line profiles are comparable to those of the narrowest-line components, indicating that even the most broadened lines retain a significant narrow-line component. The equivalent width of the narrow-line component remains consistent across both the broadest and narrowest lineshapes, suggesting that the broadening mechanism in the broadest lineshapes does not obscure the intrinsic line strength. Additionally, we observe that the equivalent width of the narrow-line component is inversely proportional to the full width at half maximum (FWHM) of the broadest spectral lines, implying that as FWHM increases, the broadening mechanism diminishes. The prevalence of broad Be stars in this sample may be attributed to the cluster's age, which is approximately 4–5 Myr. We also determined the effective temperatures and surface gravities of the 20 stars, finding that the majority are Be subdwarfs. Finally, we calculated the masses and radii for these stars, noting that the most massive star is BD-51°2837, with a mass of 12.5 solar masses and a radius of 4.8 solar radii. This star is classified as Be9V, indicating it has not yet reached the main sequence. The second most massive star, BD-51°2835, has a mass of 10.1 solar masses and a radius of 4.0 solar radii, and it is classified as Be8V. The remaining stars are all classified as Be7V. We conclude that the 30 Doradus starburst region contains a high number of Be-type stars. This paper is the first of a series dedicated to the 30 Doradus Be-type star survey, with the second paper focusing on the analysis of radial velocities. The full series will be published in Chinese in the journal 天文学报. Keywords: Be-type stars, spectral analysis, radial velocity.

This paper outlines the strategy for generating speech that integrates both emotional and social characteristics. We merge neural text-to-speech models capable of producing speech with emotional traits with those capable of rendering speech with social traits. Our focus lies on societal dimensions within social language, which encompass factors like perceived age, gender, and accent. These traits are derived from reference utterances, utilizing a combination of acoustic analysis and machine learning to ensure the resulting synthetic speech sounds natural. We evaluated the speech generated by this approach against reference utterances using both objective metrics and listener studies. The experiments indicate that the speech generated under emotional conditions is well-aligned with the intended emotional context. Conversely, while listeners could identify the gender of the generated utterances, they struggled to perceive variations in age and societal accent. Furthermore, listeners found it difficult to rate the naturalness of the emotional-context speech based on its clarity. Finally, we discuss the limitations of this method and propose several avenues for future research. This work represents a step toward creating a speaker model that can accept an emotional context as input and generate speech appropriately matched to that context. To our knowledge, this is the first attempt to synthesize speech with social traits in an emotional context. Building upon the core principles of the geometric collective model, we introduce a straightforward extension designed to geometrically collective conceptually unify axial and triaxial nuclear shapes. This work aims to provide a basic framework for triaxiality that remains compatible with existing axial collective models and their experimental findings. Our approach is grounded in a new distance metric for nuclear shapes, recently introduced in a prior study, which is notably simpler than alternatives like the Williamson or Casten parameters. Distances derived from this metric align well with those calculated using more complex collection methods and effectively characterize the shape space of collective nuclei. Furthermore, we derive an analytical expression for the metric affinity, a quantity analogous to the casten parameter used to quantify nuclear shapes. Finally, incorporating the concept of triaxiality into an E(2) collective model, we develop a new Hamiltonian that accounts for the asymmetry parameter. By applying a simple cranking approximation, we demonstrate that this Hamiltonian can successfully describe the behavior of both axial and triaxial nuclei. Collectively, our findings indicate that the proposed framework for triaxiality is highly effective, simple, and consistent with current experimental data. Additionally, our results suggest that the new distance and the cranking approximation for the asymmetry parameter are valuable tools for further investigating nuclear shapes and dynamics. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for future research into the properties of triaxial nuclei. This paper introduces the concept of polyphase Golay complementary structures (PGCS) of degree $L$, extending both PGCs and PCS. The primary objective is to develop efficient, direct methods for constructing PGCS with minimal peak-to-average power ratio (PAPR). A necessary condition for PGCS of degree $L$ is established, followed by four construction methods based on this condition. These approaches generalize existing techniques for PGCs and PCS, as well as previously defined polyphase Golay complementary sequences of order 2. Additionally, a novel class of PGCS of degree 3 is defined, generated by a specific set of ternary sequences; this set is also utilized to construct prime-valued PGCS. Finally, the paper presents a method for building PGCS of arbitrary length and degree $L$ using a specific set of length-$N$ sequences, where $N = p^u(q)^v$ and $p, q$ are distinct primes. The conditions required for construction are examined for $L$ being a prime power. Furthermore, prime-length PGCS are constructed using a recursive method grounded in a condition on ternary auto-correlation balanced sequences. Numerical examples are provided to demonstrate the validity of the proposed methods. The study concludes by outlining open problems regarding PGCS. Notably, PGCS offer a versatile framework for addressing various design challenges, including polyphase complementary sequences of order greater than 2, polyphase low PAPR sequences, and the existence of PGCS of specific lengths. Future research will address these and other potential applications. This paper addresses the challenge of anomaly detection in hyperspectral images, which involves identifying alterations that differ from the background. We introduce a feature-level deep convolutional autoencoder architecture designed to integrate features across multiple image channels. To enhance the model's ability to extract relevant information, we implemented feature-level fusion by combining the outputs of individual channel autoencoders into a unified feature matrix. This matrix is subsequently fed into a classification layer. The proposed architecture was evaluated on the ROCS image dataset, comparing it against a single-channel deep autoencoder and a multi-channel deep convolutional neural network. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses both baseline approaches, achieving an anomaly detection accuracy of 96.11%. Furthermore, we provide a comparative analysis of the computational costs associated with the proposed model versus a standard multi-channel deep convolutional neural network. Finally, we illustrate the method's effectiveness through anomaly detection in a medical imaging context. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar12345/Deep-CarAutoEncoder. This study examines the link between normalized remaining entropy and transport viscosity using both molecular dynamics simulations and statistical integration methods. We analyzed 28 molecular fluids across a broad spectrum of temperatures and densities, alongside 10 Lennard-Jones and 30 non-Lennard-Jones one-component model potentials. Our results indicate that while the entropy-transport correlation holds for model potentials, it is significantly weaker for molecular fluids. To address this, we developed two distinct viscosity-prediction models for molecular fluids. The first is a machine learning approach utilizing the residual entropy-simulation data from our analysis, which demonstrates a mean squared error of 1.15. The second model is a physics-driven framework that incorporates the residual entropy-viscosity relationship alongside other structural and thermodynamic properties; this model was trained on 1,000 experimental viscosity data points and achieves a mean squared error of 1.05. These findings suggest that entropy alone is insufficient for accurately predicting the transport properties of molecular fluids. Furthermore, the successful application of our physics-driven model to experimental data underscores the critical role of structural and thermodynamic characteristics in transport behavior. Finally, the high accuracy of our models, particularly the physics-driven one, highlights the value of integrating machine learning with physical principles to enhance the prediction of molecular fluid transport characteristics. These results have significant implications for the design of molecular fluids with specific transport attributes. Additionally, we introduce a Python library, ResidualEntropyViscosity, which implements our analysis pipeline and models to facilitate the replication of this research and enable their application to other molecular fluids. The library is available at https://github.com/ResidualEntropyViscosity/ResidualEntropyViscosity. Our findings are expected to aid in the design of molecular fluids with desired transport attributes and support the development of machine learning models for predicting molecular fluid transport properties. The Python library, ResidualEntropyViscosity, is accessible at https://github.com/ResidualEntropyViscosity/ResidualEntropyViscosity. The analysis begins with a review of Bell's derivation of inequalities applicable to quantum entanglement. Subsequently, we construct a version of Bell's theorem that relies on the ISM's core tenet: the restriction of sampling to an invariant set. Following this formulation, we present a numerical simulation of Bell test experiments using this framework and compare its predictions against those of quantum mechanics. The results demonstrate that the ISM successfully replicates the statistical outcomes of quantum mechanics in entangled-particle experiments, thereby circumventing Bell's no-go theorem. Consequently, the ISM emerges as the first concrete model capable of doing so. We conclude that the ISM is the only model to date that can do this, as other models either incorrectly extend Bell's theorem or rely on statistical sampling from the entire sample space. Additionally, we address the free will assumption, which is essential to the ISM: the determinism inherent in the theory necessitates that the free will assumption is not required for its operation. Finally, we outline the implications of these findings for the broader scientific community. Furthermore, the ISM represents the first step toward a new scientific paradigm that could resolve the conflict between the Big Bang and Big Crunch theories and the Big Rip hypothesis. Keyphrase detection involves identifying relevant terms within a knowledge domain, a task typically approached by first training a state-of-the-art keyphrase scorer on a dataset of labeled phrases, then automatically generating concepts from scratch using unsupervised learning. This paper introduces Neural Networks for Keyphrase Detection on IoT gadgets (IoT2), a neural network dataset comprising IoT devices and their associated keyphrases. The dataset includes 1,000 IoT devices, each annotated with 10 to 20 keyphrases. We trained and evaluated three models—Bi-directional LSTM, Bi-directional CNN, and Bi-directional Transformer Encoder—on this new dataset. Our findings indicate that the Bi-directional Transformer Encoder outperforms the other two architectures, achieving an F1 score of 0.41. The literature on fermion models in classical statistical systems is extensive and established. This article aims to present recent findings within this domain. Initially, we examine the continuum model of two-dimensional Dirac fermions coupled to an abelian gauge field, analyzing the Wilson operator and the emergent entanglement entropy within this framework. Subsequently, we investigate the Ising dimer model on a square lattice, which can be formulated using fermion operators subject to a duality transformation. We explore the dimer model's connection to the Ising model, highlighting its duality under a background U(1) gauge field. Finally, we investigate dimer models featuring defects and dislocations, extending the analysis to include entanglement entropy. Our research demonstrates the significant interplay between statistical mechanics and field theory, offering fresh perspectives on the former. Additionally, we provide Python code for all calculations, which is publicly accessible. Our findings offer a novel approach to the Ising model, yielding fresh insights into dimer models and entanglement entropy. Furthermore, we elucidate the relationship between the entanglement entropy of dimer models and that of the Ising model. These results hold particular relevance for condensed matter physics, where dimer models effectively describe various systems, including spin liquids and dimers on honeycomb lattices. We anticipate that our findings will prove valuable in these specific physical contexts. Finally, we outline several directions for future investigation. Specifically, we propose extending the entanglement entropy analysis to the Potts model, as it too admits a description via dimer models. Additionally, we suggest exploring the entanglement entropy of the XY model, which can be formulated using fermion operators on a square lattice. These extensions would further illuminate the relationship between the Potts model and the Ising model. We conclude by emphasizing the necessity of developing new theoretical tools to address these and similar challenges. Our work establishes a foundation for the emerging field of statistical dimers, a discipline that will undoubtedly grow in the coming years. We anticipate that this research will inspire others to delve deeper into these fascinating areas.
