Group lasso methods are designed to induce sparsity in group-wise regression models, making them ideal for utilizing structured data; however, they struggle with sparse, high-dimensional binary or multi-indicator variables. This difficulty arises because group-structured data is inherently low-dimensional, causing many variables to have insufficient observations within their own groups. To address this, we introduce the concept of "effective group size," a metric that quantifies the observational strength of each variable. We subsequently develop the EGS (Effective Group Size) weight as a dimensionality reduction metric for very high-dimensional categorical data, demonstrating that EGS accurately identifies group-wise signals. Furthermore, we integrate EGS into the weighting scheme of group lasso methods to enhance their performance. This approach was validated across various datasets, including very high-dimensional ones, where it proved effective in identifying group-wise signals and significantly improved model performance. Additionally, the EGS framework was successfully applied to a real-world case study involving the classification of 10 distinct types of lung cancer. Embedded systems are increasingly vital in critical sectors like automotive, aerospace, and medical technology, where high availability and safety are non-negotiable. However, the growing complexity of running multiple real-time operating systems (RTOSs) on various hardware platforms makes manual configuration and scheduling increasingly difficult and error-prone. To address this, we introduce T-Visor, a novel hypervisor designed to integrate multiple RTOSs by abstracting hardware capabilities and providing a unified software interface. T-Visor supports both pure and mixed importance task scheduling, ensuring that higher-priority tasks complete before their deadlines while allowing lower-priority tasks to execute during hardware idle periods. Furthermore, the system has been validated on an FPGA-based hardware-in-the-loop testbed, demonstrating its practical feasibility. This approach enables the rapid, safe, and cost-effective development of complex embedded systems. Additionally, the paper details the implementation of RTOS abstraction layers, including kernel, device, and CPU components, and presents evaluation results derived from automotive and industrial use cases. Ultimately, T-Visor offers a promising solution for the efficient and safe execution of RTOSs, thereby facilitating the deployment of embedded systems across diverse industries. Keywords: Hypervisor, RTOS, Embedded System, FPGA, KVM.

This study presents three novel, minimal methods for stitching panoramic images. Our framework leverages the inherent vertical orientation of panoramic scenes, specifically the direction of gravity, as a prior. By modeling image warping through complex function representations, we establish solvable relationships between image warping and distortion based on gravity preference. These methods offer superior performance and execution speed compared to current state-of-the-art techniques. Furthermore, our approach is easily adaptable to other preferences, such as scene center preferences, requiring only the adjustment of an affine transformation. Extensive experiments validate the efficacy and speed of our methods across both indoor and outdoor environments. The implementation and demonstration code are accessible at https://github.

The entropy of an N-dimensional Ising spin glass scales linearly with N, whereas the mean square entropy grows quadratically with N. Consequently, the distribution of the entropy becomes Gaussian as N approaches infinity, rendering the ratio of the standard deviation to the mean independent of N in the thermodynamic limit. We demonstrate that this distribution is symmetrical, exhibiting mirror symmetry around the mean. Furthermore, we show that while a central limit theorem is applicable to the entropy of an N-dimensional Ising spin glass, an analogous limit does not hold for the entropy of a general N-dimensional ferromagnet under an external field. The distribution of the entropy for a ferromagnet displays significant asymmetry, with its symmetry breaking driven by the ratio of the magnetic field to the square root of the mean square interaction. Finally, we establish that the mirror symmetry observed in the entropy distribution of an Ising spin glass is a characteristic of random tensor networks. Additionally, we prove that a central limit theorem applies to the entropy of a N-dimensional ferromagnet only when the magnetic field exceeds the square root of the mean square interaction. When the magnetic field is smaller than this threshold, the entropy distribution becomes skewed, and its symmetry is broken due to the magnitude of the magnetic field relative to the mean square interaction. In this scenario, the standard deviation of the entropy scales with the absolute value of the magnetic field. These findings hold true in both the thermodynamic limit and for finite N. We also examine the behavior of higher-order moments of the entropy distribution. The skewness of the entropy distribution for a ferromagnet is proportional to the cube of the magnetic field, while kurtosis scales with the fourth power of the magnetic field. For the ferromagnet, we derive a lower bound for the kurtosis of the entropy distribution, which is independent of N and remains valid for all values of the magnetic field. Finally, we show that the skewness of the entropy distribution for a general ferromagnet exhibits mirror symmetry with respect to the mean. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to validate the theoretical findings. In this approach, a beam of spin-1/2 particles, each carrying spin $s$ along the direction perpendicular to their polarization, is prepared with zero polarization relative to the transverse direction. The beam then tunnels through a potential step or a potential barrier aligned with the propagation vector, with the polarization serving as the direction perpendicular to the barrier. Upon transmission, the spin component corresponding to the pre-barrier polarization is measured. The average change in the relative polarization of the polarization component is defined as the tunneling time. The BMS algebra, which extends the Poincaré group, is embedded within the infinite-dimensional Virasoro and $bc$-systems. This algebra is constructed using negative-frequency modes of holomorphic vector fields on the null sphere at light infinity. These vectors are defined by their angular dependence, which matches that of the corresponding soft graviton wavefunctions. Consequently, soft graviton insertions can be substituted with null sphere vector modes. This approach enables a reformulation of soft gravitational Ward identities that eliminates singularities. Furthermore, these identities can be expressed as a set of differential equations involving the non-local sphere integral of the null sphere vector mode associated with the soft pion insertion. Finally, a soft double copy relation is derived between gravity and gauge theories. This relation relies on the parallel between soft pion and soft photon insertions and on the use of null sphere vector modes to define the Poincaré subgroup within the BMS algebra. The resulting expressions for soft gravitational Ward identities feature singularities of reduced order compared to standard formulations. Additionally, these findings align with recent findings by Cachazo, Nguyen, and Wen. (arXiv:2106.02006). Mastering a vast array of skills is a core challenge for general artificial intelligence. While continual learning has traditionally concentrated on single agents, real-world learning processes often involve multiple learners collaborating to acquire a diverse range of skills. This paper introduces a fully neural framework designed for online collective continual learning. In this model, a learner can acquire a new skill without forgetting previously learned ones by incorporating a novel mechanism called the replayor, which enables the reuse of data from other learners. We provide both theoretical analysis and experimental validation to support this approach. Our framework and theoretical findings suggest that a network capable of collective continual learning could hold significant potential for creating more energy-efficient artificial general intelligence. Specifically, the compatibility of the replayor with sparse weights and structures indicates that the sparsity of connections within a collectively learning network could increase exponentially. This characteristic offers the potential for substantially reducing the energy required to train such a network. We have made our code public at https://github.com/kenji-1214/KCL. Furthermore, we plan to explore the possibility of sparsity-induced energy efficiency in energy-efficient neural chips as a future research direction. Our code will be utilized in this endeavor. Additionally, the concept of the replayor is expected to inspire applications in other domains, including multi-robot collective learning and online multi-agent reinforcement learning. We intend to investigate these applications in the future. We introduce the notion of a Ricci flat four-measure. When applied to smooth tensor fields, this concept translates into a system of four non-linear, non-holonomic differential equations. We demonstrate that any closed four-measure satisfies the non-holonomic conditions, allowing the associated tensor fields to act on closed four-forms. Furthermore, in a Lorentzian spacetime, the closed four-momentum of an isolated system can be defined without relying on integration, provided the closed four-measure is available. We also present the concept of a generalized shape operator and establish the equivalence between a closed four-measure and a triple of generalized shape operator triples. The article concludes with a discussion of various examples. As an application, we demonstrate that in an asymptotically flat spacetime, the closed four-momentum of an isolated system corresponds to its linear momentum. Additionally, we prove that for an asymptotically flat spacetime, a closed four-measure exists if and only if the spacetime possesses vanishing linear momentum. The linear momentum can then be calculated using the closed four-measure. We also show that the trace of a generalized metric operator triple in an asymptotically flat spacetime represents the mass of an isolated system, and that the Cassini oval of an isolated system can be derived from the closed four-measure. The discussion also covers an alternative method for determining linear momentum from a closed four-measure.

Building upon the work of Li and Mesnager, who introduced a class of complete permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2}}$, this study investigates these functions in the context of $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. We examine the conditions under which specific polynomials act as complete permutation functions and further develop examples for the case where $q$ is odd, aiming to construct a larger quantity of such functions in this setting. Additionally, we present polynomial examples that are complete permutation functions for $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ when $q$ is even, though these do not constitute true multivariate complete permutation functions. We also analyze rational functions that serve as complete permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. Finally, we demonstrate that the number of polynomials that are complete permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ is significantly smaller than the count over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{2}}$, indicating that the concept of complete permutation functions is not effective for $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$. To address this limitation, we propose an alternative definition of complete permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and provide several examples under this revised framework. Furthermore, we establish that the number of such functions in the new sense is substantially greater than in the previous definition, with many exhibiting a high degree of nonlinearity. We also present examples of rational functions that are complete permutation functions under this new definition. Notably, we prove that rational functions that are complete permutation functions in the old sense are also valid under the new sense, whereas this equivalence does not hold for polynomials. Our findings suggest that while the old definition is unsuitable for $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$, the new definition is more appropriate. Additionally, we demonstrate that rational functions that are complete permutation functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ are not necessarily complete mapping functions, and we provide examples of rational functions that are complete mapping functions but fail to be complete permutation functions under either definition. Finally, we present examples of rational functions that are complete mapping functions over $\mathbb{F}_{q^{3}}$ and are almost perfect nonlinear functions. These examples are significant because they are neither polynomials nor complete permutation functions under either definition, yet they remain valuable due to their high degree of nonlinearity. Identifying intestinal worms is a critical component of medical diagnosis, which significantly influences treatment strategies. This identification is typically performed by specialists by observing worm images. The primary difficulty lies in the visual similarities among different worm species, a factor that often causes diagnostic errors. To address this, we introduce a deep belief network enhanced with a dropout layer and a cost-sensitive learning module. The dropout layer mitigates overfitting, while the cost-sensitive learning mechanism accounts for the higher cost of false negatives. Our proposed model was evaluated using a dataset of 1,000 worm images, and the experimental results demonstrate that the model is effective for this categorization task. Furthermore, the network achieves a reduced false negative rate, thereby lowering the likelihood of misdiagnosis. Finally, the network is shown to be robust against variations in image contrast. This study examines a class of non-zero-sum investment and reinsurance games featuring two economic regimes, where the underlying stock price dynamics are governed by a compound Poisson process with a drift component. The objective is to determine optimal investment and reinsurance strategies for an insurer and a competitor to maximize their respective profits. We derive the explicit form of the value function and prove its uniqueness. Furthermore, utilizing the verification theorem, we explicitly calculate the optimal strategies for both the insurer and the competitor. Finally, we validate our analytical findings through numerical simulations. Additionally, we compare our proposed model with existing literature to demonstrate the superiority of our approach. This research holds significant practical value for non-life insurers, particularly those operating in competitive markets. Our methodology enables the simultaneous optimization of profits for both the company and a competitor, thereby enhancing the company's competitive edge. The optimal strategies derived in this paper can be applied to various scenarios, including the formation of strategic alliances, joint ventures, or acquisitions. Consequently, this framework serves as a robust tool for maximizing the benefits of both parties involved in such partnerships. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the compound Poisson process with drift and defines the non-zero-sum game. Section 3 outlines the Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs (HJI) equations. Section 4 presents the solution to the HJI equations and the derivation of the value function. Section 5 details the numerical simulation. Finally, Section 6 offers a comparison with current literature and potential future applications.

We present findings from a dispersion relation analysis of the $\pi N$ scattering amplitude that are valid at low energies. This approach yields low-energy constants for chiral perturbation theory, which govern the behavior of these amplitudes, and establishes constraints on them. The study relies on empirical inputs from two sources: low-energy scattering data and high-energy data from the Totem experiment at the LHC. Furthermore, we examine the implications of these results for the existence of a Pseudo-Goldstone boson. The entire analysis was conducted using the open-source Python package `dispersion_python`. Source code and supplementary materials are accessible at \url{https://github.com/DispersiveAnalysis/PionNucleonAnalysis}. A tutorial on utilizing `dispersion_python` for pion-nucleon analyses is provided in Ref.~\cite{Borunda:2020qro}. This work was published in Phys. Rev. D 104, 056001 (2021).

This study employs machine learning to investigate the morphologies of active galactic nucleus (AGN) host galaxies at redshifts $z<1$, utilizing a dataset of 1,000 objects drawn from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Extensive Survey (HSC-ES). We determined that 60% of AGN hosts are disk-dominated, 20% are bulge-dominated, and 20% exhibit mixed characteristics. Our analysis reveals that bulge-dominated AGN hosts are typically more massive ($\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})>10.0$) and reside in higher stellar density environments compared to their disk and mixed counterparts. Furthermore, bulge-dominated AGN hosts show a greater prevalence of red color indices ($\log(M_{\star}/M_{\odot})>10.0$) and lower specific star formation rates ($\log(SFR_{\rm SFR}<-10.0$) than disks and mixed hosts. These findings suggest that bulge-dominated AGN hosts are more likely to reside in galaxy clusters. Additionally, we identified a significant correlation between bulge fraction and the redness of color indices, a relationship that strengthens at higher redshifts. These results align with the "downsizing" paradigm, indicating that bulge-dominated AGN hosts are more common in the distant universe. Finally, we observed that AGN host galaxies with a bulge fraction exceeding 0.5 exhibit a higher incidence of radio-loud AGN ($\log(L_{\rm 1.4GHz}>42.0$) compared to those with a bulge fraction below 0.5. This supports the theory that radio-loud AGN preferentially occupy dense stellar environments, such as galaxy clusters. Our conclusions are based on a sample of 1,000 AGN hosts, and we anticipate that these trends will become more pronounced as future surveys expand the available sample size. We investigate short-distance correlations among nucleons and mesons using a permutationally invariant polynomial framework defined in nuclear phase space, which is conditioned on energy, momentum, and particle number. This approach enables the analysis of nuclear structure through nuclear effective field theory. By examining low-order approximations of the correlation energy, we develop a model for nuclear short-distance three-body correlations. The resulting three-body correlation energy demonstrates significant stability across different momentum partitions and shows qualitative agreement with findings from variational Monte Carlo studies. Furthermore, we extend our calculations to the meson sector, providing the initial computations of meson short-distance correlations within this correlation energy formalism. These calculations reveal that the leading-order meson three-body correlation energy is comparable to that of nucleons, indicating a substantial probability for meson three-body short-distance correlations. Our methodology and findings establish a foundation for future research into long-range nuclear correlations. Additionally, the network techniques employed to compute the polynomial coefficients are versatile and can be applied to various computational problems in quantum physics. Our code is publicly accessible. This paper introduces Co-domain Equivalence (CDE), a metric designed to assess the similarity of student responses to different items within a test. By evaluating whether students in one item's response category also answer another item correctly, CDE offers a more interpretable and reliable measure compared to existing metrics like Item Discrimination (ID) and Differential Item Functioning (DIF). Furthermore, CDE facilitates the generation of diverse equivalents for each test item. We demonstrate that incorporating these alternative items into itemspecific neural network models enhances their ability to generalize to new items, thereby improving overall test performance. Additionally, we validate the effectiveness of CDE in creating co-domain equivalent items for assessing student responses. Finally, we outline several potential application areas for CDE, including educational content recommendation, test construction, and adaptive testing. Our source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/CDE. Source files required to replicate the experiments are provided in the supplementary materials. Additionally, we have established a new benchmark, CDE-EQ, which comprises 1,000 instances of CDE-equivalent items. This paper is a joint effort between Georgia Tech and Purdue University. When photon-nucleon collisions at high energies produce a hadronic fireball, the resulting transverse density of hadrons eventually reaches a saturation limit as the photon virtuality $Q^2$ increases. Near this asymptotic saturation threshold, the transverse density decreases with rising $Q^2$ following a geometric scaling law. This behavior is observed across various hadronic and nuclear targets, including quencheron-induced $J/\psi$ and open charm production, as well as vector and quarkonium-like dileptons. At the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC), this scaling extends to both nuclear and quarkonium-like dilepton production, as well as to $J/\psi$ and open charm in heavy ion collisions. Notably, vector dilepton spectral density exhibits saturation scaling in collisions involving all four nucleon species: $p$, $^{3}$He, $^3$Li, and $^6$Li. These findings support the conclusion that saturation scaling serves as a probe for the intrinsic quark density within nucleons and other small nuclei. Furthermore, when the collision system expands into a quark-gluon plasma, this saturation scaling transitions into a partonic geometric scaling law, a phenomenon verified in RHIC data. Consequently, vector dilepton spectral density may offer a new method for extracting the parton density function of the nucleon. Finally, utilizing vector dilepton spectral density as a probe for the quark-gluon plasma could enhance our understanding of the equation of state and the transport coefficients of this state of matter. This potential could lead to more precise determinations of the QGP's shear and bulk viscosity-to-entropy density ratios, thereby refining our knowledge of its near-perfect fluid characteristics. Additionally, vector dilepton spectral density could aid in investigating chiral symmetry restoration and the in-medium quark mass within the QGP. These insights could be achieved through future measurements of vector dilepton spectral density at RHIC. To achieve this, future studies should focus on measuring the transverse momentum distribution of vector dileptons in heavy ion collisions and conducting precision measurements of thermal dilepton spectra in small collision systems. Such efforts could significantly advance our understanding of the QGP and the fundamental properties of the nucleon. The paper concludes with a discussion of the future prospects for vector dilepton measurements in heavy ion collisions. We investigate the frequency of wealth generation among low-metallicity stars by analyzing the impact of close encounters with giant molecules. Utilizing the Monte Carlo code MC3B, we simulate these interactions across various initial mass and density conditions. Our simulations demonstrate that, regardless of the specific initial parameters, a power-law mass distribution consistently emerges in the final population. This confirms that the collisional dynamics governing the transfer of binding energy during close encounters with giant molecules are the primary driver of wealth generation in low-metallicity stars. This paper introduces a geometric approach to identifying network structures that are susceptible to outbreaks. We propose a method for grouping nodes based on their betweenness, a centrality metric that indicates how essential a node is for communication across the network. The outbreak probability of a node is fundamentally linked to its degree and the betweenness of itself and nodes in its immediate neighborhood. We validate this theory using both synthetic networks and real-world social networks. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a clustering algorithm utilizing betweenness can detect diverse community structures across various networks. This algorithm is particularly effective at identifying "star" patterns, where nodes within a community share identical degrees and betweenness values. Additionally, experimental results indicate that our method surpasses other algorithms in terms of clustering coefficient and modularity scores. Finally, we show that applying this method to networks with known community structures successfully recovers those communities. The betweenness concept is detailed in [1]. The Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) map derived from the Planck mission exhibits prominent X-shaped artifacts centered on the Galactic poles. This study investigates the origin of these X-shapes and evaluates their evolution across various maximum entropy (MaxEnt) versions of the full-sky CMB map, specifically the 2015 final release and the 2018 data release. Our analysis indicates that these X-shaped features are a direct consequence of the data cleaning process employed to remove Galactic foregrounds. Although the features are more pronounced in the 2018 final map compared to the 2013 final map, they remain visible in X-band and K-band Galactic-pole-aligned maps after the application of MaxEnt component separation. We demonstrate that the intensity of these X-shapes can be mitigated by selecting a more compact region around the Galactic poles as the non-linear region for MaxEnt component separation. Furthermore, we show that the Planck 2018 CMB final map is largely free from these X-shaped residuals, whereas such features persist in the 2013 final map. Finally, we confirm that these X-shaped residuals do not bias the estimation of primordial CMB parameters. This research is part of the Planck Legacy Survey. (Abridged)

Quantum channel tomography is the procedure of characterizing quantum channels through experimental data. The shadow method, an efficient recent approach, employs classical shadow techniques to derive estimators for various channel properties from experimental outcomes. This study introduces the shadow method tomography (SMT) protocol, an efficient technique for quantum channel tomography that utilizes the distance between channel outputs and reference states as a figure of merit. We provide a theoretical analysis and numerical simulations demonstrating that, for the depolarizing, dephasing, and amplitude damping channels, the average fidelity of the reconstructed channels via SMT exhibits superior performance compared to the direct method. Furthermore, we apply SMT to reconstruct the ground state of the Hamiltonian $H=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\sigma_x^{(i)}\otimes\sigma_x^{(i+1)}$ with periodic boundary conditions, where $i=1,2,\cdots,N$ and $x=N$, for $N$-qubit systems containing up to 12 qubits. These findings indicate that the proposed SMT method is well-suited for characterizing quantum channels that generate states closely resembling the ground states of many-body Hamiltonians. Additionally, we illustrate the method's applicability to quantum gates by reconstructing the controlled-NOT (CNOT) gate using 2-qubit gates. The results suggest that the proposed scheme holds promise for characterizing other significant quantum channels, such as those involved in quantum error correction. Notably, the protocol does not require the measurement of process matrices. Graphene's electronic structure is a subject of intense study due to its unique properties. In this work, we employ the renormalization group method to investigate a Coulomb-interacting bilayer graphene system incorporating a bias potential. Our analysis reveals that the bilayer's band gap influences the renormalization group flow, causing the system to approach different fixed points based on the bias magnitude. Specifically, at zero bias, the system resides in a non-Fermi liquid state, whereas at finite bias, it transitions into a Fermi liquid. Furthermore, the renormalization group analysis indicates that the bilayer's band gap vanishes at a critical doping level, resulting in a new non-Fermi liquid fixed point. These findings offer a theoretical basis for the experimentally observed shift between Fermi liquid and non-Fermi liquid states in graphene as the band gap is tuned. Additionally, our results demonstrate that the bilayer system exhibits a variety of non-Fermi liquid states, characterized by distinct scaling exponents and power-law behaviors for physical quantities. Finally, we predict the existence of multiple critical doping levels where the bilayer transitions between Fermi liquid and non-Fermi liquid regimes. These predictions can be experimentally verified by measuring the Hall coefficient and resistivity as functions of carrier density. The methodology employed in this study is applicable to other interacting electron systems. The structural and electronic characteristics of endohedral fullerenes are significantly influenced by their encapsulated atoms. This study utilizes scanning tunneling microscopy and a combination of density functional theory and GW methods to reveal that the conformation of the Sc2TbN@C80(3,4,5,6) isomer changes in response to temperature. GW calculations indicate that the spectral properties of both the molecular orbitals and the C80 cage vary depending on the specific configuration. Furthermore, GW results demonstrate that the energy of the highest occupied molecular orbital (HOMO) is more sensitive to configuration changes than that of the lowest unoccupied molecular orbital (LUMO). These findings offer a comprehensive explanation for the observed conformational switching and provide a basis for developing molecular electronics. Additionally, this research offers a new perspective on the design of molecular sensors. The Internet of Things (IoT) encompasses a vast network of interconnected devices capable of communication, data exchange, and control. These devices are typically embedded with microcontrollers, which are small computers designed to execute specific tasks. Among them, low-energy microcontrollers represent the most prevalent category, though they are constrained by limited processing power and memory. Consequently, executing conventional encryption and authentication protocols on these low-energy IoT devices is often impractical. Lightweight Cryptography (LWC) offers robust security while significantly lowering computational and memory overheads, making it an ideal solution for resource-restricted environments. This survey examines the current state of LWC, analyzing existing algorithms and their performance metrics such as area, energy consumption, and speed. Furthermore, it evaluates recent literature that deploys LWC on IoT hardware platforms. Finally, the report addresses open challenges and future research directions within the rapidly expanding field of LWC for IoT systems. Given the swift advancements in both LWC and IoT technologies, this area remains highly dynamic and promising. By compiling recent progress, this survey serves as a valuable resource for researchers and students interested in pursuing careers in LWC for IoT devices. Additionally, it provides a comprehensive list of relevant tools and libraries, including NIST's latest LWC standards. This work is intended to be a timely and extensive reference for those seeking to contribute to LWC research and development in the IoT sector. Keywords: Internet of Things (IoT), Embedded Systems, Lightweight Cryptography (LWC), Low Energy IoT Devices, NIST LWC.

Rabi series experiments, which involve sweeping through multiple cycles of resonance frequencies, are fundamental in quantum information science. A prevalent approach, known as the Ramsey series experiment, utilizes these sequences to prepare and measure quantum states. This study introduces a Bayesian adaptive Ramsey series design capable of determining the overlap of two quantum states with high precision using a minimal number of trial measurements. By integrating a Bayesian framework with sequential decision-making, the proposed method establishes a theoretical limit for the asymptotic information gain achievable through adaptive measurements. Furthermore, we demonstrate the scheme's effectiveness by applying it to prepare the W-state. This work provides the foundational principles and tools necessary for executing quantum experiments with maximum efficiency. Additionally, our results establish a lower bound on the number of trial measurements required to prepare the W-state, thereby offering a benchmark for assessing the performance of various quantum state preparation techniques. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this scheme to enable sequential design experiments that adaptively determine overlaps for arbitrary quantum states. Overall, this research offers practical tools for executing efficient quantum measurements and establishes performance benchmarks for diverse quantum technologies. The concept of triangle inequality is fundamental to the theory of metric spaces, which are defined by adhering to specific rules, one of which is the triangle inequality. This concept is also pivotal in network theory, where networks are conceptualized as metric spaces, and the triangle inequality serves as a criterion for identifying the most significant nodes. However, nodes that maximize centrality by minimizing the distance between other nodes often violate the triangle inequality by forming shortest paths. Consequently, nodes that are most central to a network's structure and function typically do not act as bridges between other nodes but rather as the "center" of the network. To address this, we introduce the Gromov importance metric, which quantifies importance through triangle inequality surplus. We demonstrate that this metric exhibits a strong positive correlation with betweenness centrality, calculated via the all-pairs shortest path method, across various synthetic and real-world networks. Furthermore, Gromov importance is positively correlated with the reciprocal of network betweenness, revealing a strong inverse relationship between these two metrics. We also establish that Gromov importance is positively correlated with the reciprocal of the betweenness coefficient, as derived from a tensor-based method for computing betweenness using the distance Laplacian matrix. Additionally, we show that Gromov importance correlates positively with the reciprocal of the average betweenness coefficient, which is computed using the distance algebraic Laplacian matrix. Finally, we demonstrate that Gromov importance is positively correlated with the ratio of the algebraic Laplacian to the distance Laplacian. These findings indicate that Gromov importance is a multi-layer metric for network centrality that leverages the triangle inequality to capture the structural and functional roles of nodes. By utilizing distances rather than direct connections, Gromov importance avoids the bias inherent in degree-based measures. Furthermore, it is shown that Gromov importance is positively correlated with the ratio of the distance algebraic Laplacian to the distance spectral matrix across various networks. These results suggest that Gromov importance serves as an effective metric for assessing node importance in both synthetic and real networks. This paper introduces a new approach to unifying electric and magnetic phenomena, which we term the Azimuthally Uniform (AZU) theory of gravity. In this framework, the conventional Newtonian gravitational potential $\phi$ is supplemented by additional scalar potentials $\phi_{+}$ and $\phi_{-}$, alongside the usual Newtonian field vectors $\mathbf{A}$, $\mathbf{B}_{+}$, and $\mathbf{B}_{-}$. The vector $\mathbf{A}$ adheres to the standard inverse-square law, whereas $\mathbf{B}_{+}$ and $\mathbf{B}_{-}$ function as azimuthally symmetric analogs of electric and magnetic fields, respectively. These fields collectively constitute a symmetric tensor that generalizes the Poynting vector. The components of this tensor are governed by a set of symmetric Maxwellian equations. The AZU fields and their corresponding equations of motion provide a comprehensive framework for describing both gravitational and electromagnetic phenomena. This theoretical structure is complete and self-contained, requiring no external reference to Newtonian gravity. The initial portion of our prior publication, \emph{Azimuthally Uniform Theory of Gravity (AZU)} (arXiv:2009.07717v1 [astro-ph.HE]), established the foundational framework. The current study expands upon those findings by deriving the equations that govern matter within the AZU theory. We subsequently apply the AZU framework to various physical systems, including point particles, continuous matter distributions, and the interior of a star. The AZU theory also offers a symmetric description of light propagation, yielding the same result as General Relativity: the bending of light. This concept was recently introduced by Demetrescu et al. (ESA 2018), who demonstrated a linear-time algorithm to determine the existence of such a tree and an algorithm requiring $O(n \log n)$ space to construct one. Their findings led to a novel $O(\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the diameter problem, achieving a runtime of $O(n^{5/2+\varepsilon})$. In this work, we extend these results to graphs with bounded expansion and distance graphs exhibiting similar traits. Specifically, we demonstrate that when $G=(V,E,d)$ originates from a minor-free graph with unit edge weights, the distance treewidth is $O(\log n)$. Furthermore, we provide a linear-time method to compute a spanning tree $T$ whose minimum spanning path between any $u,v \in V$ has a length matching the distance $d(u,v)$. Leveraging these contributions, we derive a novel $O(\varepsilon)$-approximation algorithm for the diameter problem applicable to graphs with bounded expansion, including all minor-free graphs. The algorithm operates within $O(n)$ space and achieves a runtime of $O(n^{2+\varepsilon})$. Additionally, we present a straightforward reduction from the Euclidean Traveling Salesman Problem to the metric TSP on graphs with bounded expansion, which, combined with existing bounds, yields the first subquadratic algorithm for finding a Hamiltonian cycle in this class of graphs. This finding enables a more efficient dynamic programming algorithm for the Steiner Tree problem on distance graphs with bounded expansion. We have identified extensive traits of discrete-interval systems that generalize prior findings within the standard scalar interval setting. Specifically, we demonstrate that for any discrete-interval system defined by $x_{n+1}=f(x_n)$ where $f$ is both strongly monotone and k-times differentiable, the limit sets are invariably global attractors. Furthermore, we establish the existence of a unique globally stable fixed point when $f'$ is continuous, or a unique globally stable monotonic cycle when $f'$ lacks continuity. Additional results concerning $\omega$-limit sets and periodic fixed points are also provided. The significance of these findings stems from their broad applicability to any interval map $f$ satisfying the stated conditions, encompassing many strongly monotone functions that do not admit closed-form expressions. Consequently, our methodology enables the analysis of limit sets and global stability for such systems, a capability not achievable through existing techniques in the single-interval case. Our primary findings are detailed in [1], while this work offers supplementary details regarding limit sets and periodic fixed points, which are also relevant to other applications.

Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) represent a promising method for solving complex problems on near-term quantum hardware, yet their performance is often hindered by the lack of a reliable initial point in the cost function landscape, leading to suboptimal solutions. This study investigates a cost function landscape characterized by a series of local minima, where the optimal solution is located in the deepest minimum. We introduce a qubit-excitation-driven adaptive VQA (QAV) designed to locate the optimal solution by sequentially exciting qubits from the computational basis state. This approach is benchmarked against a standard VQA, showing that the QAV successfully finds the global minimum with significantly fewer variational parameters and greater robustness. Furthermore, the QAV demonstrates superior performance compared to a recently proposed qubit annealing algorithm. The results indicate that the QAV is highly effective for the phase separation problem, which serves as a real-space representation of the Fermi-Hubbard model. Finally, we outline potential applications of this QAV in quantum machine learning and chemical simulations. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/Quantum-Machine-Learning-Group/QAV. Representational similarity analysis (RSAs) is a technique that characterizes neural representations by examining representations' similarities. We present a Bayesian framework to represent neural activity patterns as a mixture of Gaussian distributions. This approach enables a concise characterization of neural representations, facilitating their manipulation and simulation. Crucially, the framework allows for the inference of latent variables from neural patterns, an advancement that permits the decoding of task-relevant information. We validate this method using both simulated data and neural recordings from the primary visual cortex. Our findings demonstrate that neural representations can be succinctly modeled as a mixture of Gaussians, and we successfully recover information about orientation using Bayesian inference. Furthermore, this framework offers additional capabilities for simulating and manipulating neural representations. Finally, we illustrate how this approach can inform and enhance neural network architectures. Collectively, these results indicate that a compact representation of neural representations, derived from neural recordings, is sufficient to capture task-relevant information. Additionally, this method provides a powerful tool for manipulating and simulating such representations. Finally, the framework offers insights for representing information within neural networks. Recent data from the NANOGrav pulsar-timing array suggests a common-spectrum process in the nanohertz range, which could indicate gravitational waves. Concurrently, the Advanced LIGO-Virgo detector has established an upper limit on gravitational-wave strain at tens of hertz. This study demonstrates that a single inflationary model can simultaneously account for the NANOGrav findings and satisfy the LIGO-Virgo constraints. The mechanism involves quantum fluctuations generated with fixed amplitudes during inflation, followed by exponential amplification post-inflation. The resulting spectrum of long-wavelength gravitational waves exerts a tidal force on binary systems, producing a strain consistent with the observed Hubble tension. Furthermore, the model predicts a gravitational-wave backdrop that will evolve over time, a phenomenon that could be detected by pulsar-timing arrays in the coming years. The analysis also explores the implications of this model for other precision cosmology measurements, including the cosmic microwave background, big-bang nucleosynthesis, and late-time cosmic expansion. Finally, the study examines the potential for testing this model through gravitational waves from black-hole mergers observed by LIGO-Virgo. The model's viability is supported by the recent detection of a supermassive black-hole binary by the Event Horizon Telescope and the growing evidence of Hubble tension. The paper concludes with a discussion of the model's broader implications. The code used in this analysis is available at https://github.com/zhijun-liu/accuracy_cosmology. Keywords: cosmology: early universe, cosmology: theoretical, inflation, gravitational waves, Hubble tension. arXiv e-print: 2305.01001 [astro-ph.CO].

This study reports the first interferometric observations of cometary gas emissions using a radio astronomical instrument. By employing the ALMA Atacama Compact Array, we detected 13CO, 12CO2, CS, and SO emissions from Comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS) at a distance of 2.0 AU from the Sun. The spatial distribution of 13CO reveals a narrow, elongated structure aligned with the comet's trajectory, indicating a production rate of 1.1 × 10^28 s^-1. The observed CS production rate of 1.2 × 10^27 s^-1 is consistent with values recorded for other comets, whereas the SO rate of 1.0 × 10^26 s^-1 is at least an order of magnitude lower. These findings suggest that CS is not merely a photodissociation product of HCS, but rather a primary species released from the nucleus, implying that the comet's parent body once possessed a mantle containing CS. Furthermore, the detection of CS in cometary nuclei supports the hypothesis that the molecular cloud from which the solar system formed was enriched by a CS-abundant protostellar outflow. The results also indicate that the CS abundance in the comet's mantle is at least 100 times greater than that of SO. These observations provide a novel method for investigating cometary composition and offer a new perspective on the formation of carbon monosulfide in the interstellar medium. The data are accessible at https://doi.org/10.1051/0004-4349/20214170. This study introduces a straightforward and efficient method for unsupervised speech generation, utilizing a combination of cycle-consistent adversarial training and diffusion models. Unlike current approaches that rely on cycle-consistent training, our method employs a similar noise consistency training scheme; however, it integrates diffusion models to enhance both the quality and intelligibility of the synthesized speech. Furthermore, our approach eliminates the need for an intermediate latent space, streamlining the process and boosting overall efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that the generated speech aligns well with speech characteristics within the training corpus, achieving a state-of-the-art performance. Additionally, the proposed method is more efficient than existing alternatives, as it avoids mapping noise to an intermediate latent space and utilizes a simpler architecture. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in real-world scenarios, yet their nature makes them challenging because they lack a single optimal solution. Instead, these problems yield a set of non-dominated solutions, each representing a different trade-off among conflicting objectives. The proposed method integrates the NSGA-II population into the Branch and Bound search process, ensuring that the final output consists exclusively of non-dominated points. Extensive numerical tests were conducted to validate the approach's effectiveness and computational performance. The results confirm that the proposed method is highly effective for solving this class of problems. Furthermore, comparisons with the hybrid Branch and Bound combined with the $\epsilon$-Constraint Method demonstrate that the proposed approach yields superior outcomes. Finally, the paper applies this methodology to a multi-objective solid oxide fuel cell reformer optimization problem. The application of the proposed approach to identify the Pareto Front results in the elimination of 99% of the search space. Aspect-based emotion analysis involves identifying an aspect within a sentence and determining its corresponding emotion tone. However, existing research often overlooks the critical challenge of modeling the interdependence between aspects and their emotions. To address this, we introduce the task of learning hidden sentiment representation in the context of aspect-based emotion analysis. This approach not only directly tackles the aforementioned interdependence issue but also holds significant potential for enhancing the performance of models used in related domains. We present HGS-ABEA, a framework that employs a guided contrastive learning strategy to effectively capture hidden sentiment representations. This framework comprises two modules: the Aspect Emotion Extraction Module and the Sentiment Consistency Regularization Module. The former is designed to extract aspects and emotions while accounting for their interdependence, whereas the latter facilitates the learning of sentiment representations through a contrastive loss function. We also report preliminary experimental results on the LG.com dataset, demonstrating the framework's effectiveness. Furthermore, we explore the application of this framework in semantic role labeling and aspect-based sentiment analysis, with experimental findings indicating substantial performance gains. Our source code is accessible at: https://github.com/chenchen1998/HGS-ABEA. The paper can be found at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.07002.

Mediation analysis seeks to determine how an exposure influences an outcome through specific pathways. A critical component of this process is the recognition and estimation of the direct effect, which represents the impact of an exposure on an outcome independent of the mediator. Because the direct effect is essential for a comprehensive mediation analysis, understanding its behavior is vital. However, direct evidence regarding the exposure's direct effect on an binary outcome is scarce. This study evaluates the direct effect within case-control designs utilizing a binary mediator. We first derive recognition and consistency conditions for the direct effect when the exposure is either binary or continuous. Furthermore, we introduce a direct effect estimator designed for stratified case-control samples with a binary mediator and exposure. Through extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we assess the direct performance of this proposed estimator. Finally, we apply our method to two real-world case-control datasets to illustrate its practical utility. Our findings indicate that the direct effect is not always identifiable and that the direct effect interaction does not necessarily exist. Nevertheless, we demonstrate that the direct effect can be effectively estimated using our proposed method across both binary and continuous exposure scenarios. This paper examines the application of hindsight summaries to enhance machine learning models' understanding of insights. We investigate whether these summaries can improve comprehension of actions taken and decisions made by models. Additionally, we explore if such summaries can reveal decisions made by models that are subsequently discarded through techniques like ensemble methods, caching, or pruning. Our results indicate that executing the operations actually performed by a model, rather than merely executing their opposites, yields significant improvements in human understanding. Furthermore, executing these operations and caching the resulting decisions within a model's memory appear to boost the model's performance. Finally, we demonstrate that executing insights and caching them in memory can facilitate more effective decision-making. We refer to this methodology as "executing insights." We validate our approach by comparing it against model outputs, demonstrating that executing insights produce results that are more similar to model outputs. Additionally, we show that caching insights leads to higher accuracy, lower computational costs, and reduced error rates. Our findings suggest that executing insights may constitute a form of meta-learning, where models learn about their own operations and decisions. We also show that executing insights can assist models in learning from mistakes, thereby improving their ability to learn from errors. We refer to this mechanism as learning from mistakes. In conclusion, executing insights represent a novel method for enhancing machine learning models' understanding of their operations and decisions, which can subsequently lead to improved accuracy and efficiency. We anticipate that executing insights will have broad applications across various domains, including but not limited to healthcare, finance, and education. We also expect that executing insights will facilitate the development of more interpretable machine learning models, which is crucial for building trust between humans and machines. Finally, we believe that executing insights will enable the creation of self-aware machines capable of understanding their own actions and decisions.

The solar breeze, a plasma flowing from the Sun, exhibits distinct characteristics that set it apart from the solar wind. This breeze displays greater variability in its dynamic behavior, with its interaction with the interstellar medium shaping the conditions of the heliosphere. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) is designed to investigate how this variability influences the interstellar medium and the heliosphere. This study examines the initial Parker Solar Probe data to identify energy transfer mechanisms and their potential impact on the heliosphere. We analyze the energy transfer between magnetic field and plasma in the inner heliosphere, specifically for distances $r \leq 40$ AU, using the PSP's FIELDS and SWP instruments. Our analysis of the cross-helicity $H_c$ and the Alfvénicity parameter $A$ indicates that the inner heliosphere is populated by Alfvénic fluctuations. We further explore the energy transfer between magnetic field and plasma via the PSP's mean electric field, calculating the magnetic and plasma energy transfer rates. These rates are compared against the PSP's total energy density variation rate to determine the relative significance of each. Additionally, we assess the contribution of magnetic reconnection to energy transfer by calculating the reconnection electric field and the associated magnetic energy transfer rate. Finally, we compare these rates with the plasma energy flux to evaluate their significance. Our results suggest that the Parker Solar Probe's variability is driven by the interaction between magnetic field and plasma, a process that may affect the heliosphere. This analysis is based on data from the first four years of the mission. Future Parker Solar Probe data will be analyzed to determine if these findings hold true across a broader range of inner heliosphere distances. Furthermore, we will investigate how these results vary with solar activity and the solar cycle. In the R-matrix representation of rotor Hamiltonians, R-matrix elements correspond to transition matrix elements between single-particle states. By interpreting these elements as effective potentials, we demonstrate that R-parity defines the parity of the potential within each well. Consequently, the eigenstates of the Hamiltonian exhibit either positive or negative R-parity, leading to the classification of these states as benign or malignant, respectively. This framework establishes a direct correspondence between the nature of the eigenstates and the spectral ordering, a relationship that is vividly illustrated by the adverse scissors mode arising in a two-body cranking Hamiltonian when it is deformed along two axes. Furthermore, we show that the adverse scissors mode can be derived from a simplified model consisting of a malignant and a benign rotors coupled together. This insight offers a valuable perspective on the connection between the adverse scissors mode and the particle-hole gap. Additionally, the analytical derivation of this simplified adverse scissors mode provides a new method for calculating energy gaps in rotor Hamiltonians. Finally, the paper includes a discussion of the limitations inherent in this approach. (Keywords: Nuclear collective motion, Nuclear rotors, R-matrix formalism, Nuclear energy gaps) (arXiv ID: 2109.07700v1)

This study introduces a cell-mean-based neural network approach designed to address both hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs). Unlike traditional methods, the proposed technique avoids reliance on boundary fitting or the imposition of boundary conditions. Instead, it utilizes finite difference schemes to discretize PDE cells and employs feed-forward neural networks to approximate these cell values. To handle boundary conditions, the values of neighboring cells adjacent to the boundary are adjusted to satisfy the required conditions. The method's efficacy is validated through numerical experiments involving both linear and nonlinear PDEs, including the heat equation, wave equation, Laplace equation, Burgers equation, Fisher-KPP equation, and Burgers-Fisher equation. Results demonstrate that the approach yields highly accurate numerical solutions for both time-dependent and steady-state PDEs, regardless of the initial or boundary conditions provided. Furthermore, the technique exhibits robust performance across varying grid resolutions and remains effective for both low- and high-frequency problems. For instance, in the case of the Burgers equation, the method produces accurate results even with coarse grids. Additionally, the approach is applicable to both one-dimensional and multi-dimensional PDEs. The paper concludes by outlining potential extensions to other PDE types, such as the Schrödinger equation, reaction-diffusion equations, and the Black-Scholes equation. Finally, the study provides guidance on selecting activation functions and network architectures to suit specific PDE problems. Overall, this cell-mean-based neural network framework offers a versatile and precise solution for solving PDEs. **Keywords:** cell-mean-based neural network, hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations, numerical solution. **Mathematics Subject Classification:** 65M70, 65L20, 65N30, 65N35, 65N99, 65T50, 65T60. **AMS Subject Classification:** 65M70, 65L20, 65N30, 65N35, 65N99, 65T50, 65T60. **Keywords:** cell-mean-based neural network, hyperbolic and elliptic partial differential equations, numerical solution. **Mathematics Subject Classification:** 65M70, 65L20, 65N30, 65N35, 65N99, 65T50, 65

The hard spectral state of Cyg X-1 is characterized by a dominant steeper power-law component in the X-ray spectrum, a feature attributed to the "stellar breeze"—a stream of material from the companion star directed toward the black hole. This study investigates the spectral and timing implications of this breeze using NuSTAR and XMM-Newton data from a 2017 observation. The analysis reveals a steep power-law component with a photon index of $\Gamma \sim 2.2$, which is significantly steeper than the $\Gamma \sim 1.7$ typical of the standard hard state. We interpret this enhanced steepness as evidence of the stellar breeze's influence on the hard X-ray component. Furthermore, we examine the timing properties of the source and explore the potential impact of the breeze on these characteristics. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for models describing the formation of the stellar breeze and the conditions within the accretion flow during the hard state. This work represents the first application of the "stellar breeze" hypothesis to explain the spectral and timing properties of Cyg X-1. Our findings suggest that the breeze may be a more prevalent phenomenon than previously believed, potentially affecting other sources in the hard state. Consequently, we propose that future research should focus on the impact of the stellar breeze to better understand the intrinsic properties of the hard state. Additionally, we suggest that this phenomenon could play a significant role in the physics governing mass accretion onto compact objects. To test this hypothesis, we recommend conducting a systematic spectral and timing analysis of the hard state in Cyg X-1 using a large dataset. Such an analysis would provide a comprehensive view of the hard state and help determine whether the spectral and timing signatures of the breeze are present. This approach would also help identify the specific physical conditions under which the stellar breeze influences the hard state. Furthermore, we propose that the impact of the stellar breeze should be investigated in other X-ray binaries in the hard state to assess its universality. This investigation would help identify the physical conditions required for the breeze to form and explore its broader implications. Finally, we recommend that the future development of mass accretion models for black holes and neutron stars incorporate the impact of the stellar breeze. This inclusion would enhance our understanding of the physical processes governing mass accretion onto compact objects. We conclude that the impact of the stellar breeze is a critical factor in understanding the hard state of X-ray binaries and its influence on the physics of mass accretion onto compact objects. We investigate tidal features in early-type galaxies (ETGs) to assess the impact of mergers on their evolution. Utilizing data from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Pan-STARRS+ Subaru Strategic Program, we identified 1,000 ETGs with redshifts between 0.01 and 0.15 and absolute magnitudes ranging from -22 to -24. We quantified tidal characteristics using the flux ratio ($\Delta S_{\rm F}$) and tidal radius ($\Delta S_{\rm F}^{1/2}r$), defined as the difference in surface brightness between an ETG and its nearest neighbor. Our analysis reveals that 10% of these galaxies exhibit significant tidal features, with mean $\Delta S_{\rm F}$ values spanning $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-1}$ mag arcsec$^{-2}$ and $\Delta S_{\rm F}^{1/2}r$ values from 0.01 to 0.1 mag arcsec$^{-1}$. These features are predominantly observed in galaxies with $-22.5 < M_{\rm F} < -23.5$ mag and $0.03 < z < 0.08$. Furthermore, the frequency of galaxies displaying strong tidal features scales with neighbor mass ratios ($M_{\rm neighbor}/M_{\rm self}$) of 0.1 to 10, indicating that strong features arise from interactions with neighbors of comparable mass. Finally, we estimate the merger rate for strong tidal features to be approximately $10^{-2}$ Gyr$^{-1}$, suggesting that such features result from relatively recent encounters. These findings align with the hypothesis that strong tidal features in early-type galaxies are the flux signature of recent mergers. Additionally, the observed dependence of tidal feature frequency on mass ratio supports the view that these features reflect the dynamical state of the galaxies. This conclusion is reinforced by the fact that the frequency of strong tidal features peaks at mass ratios of 1 to 3, consistent with the expectation that tidal features are more prominent in equal-mass mergers. Consequently, our results indicate that strong tidal features in early-type galaxies are the flux manifestation of major mergers. The similarity between the tidal feature frequency and the merger rate further implies that the timescale for tidal features to fade is comparable to a Hubble time. This study introduces a novel gravitational framework, the Azimuthally Symmetrical Theory of Gravitation (ASTG), by extending the existing theory to incorporate azimuthal symmetry. ASTG successfully accounts for a broad spectrum of gravitational phenomena, including the dynamics of the solar system, stellar and galactic rotation, galactic morphology, and supernova explosions. A key innovation of ASTG is the introduction of the concept of bipolar ejection. This mechanism posits that the angular momentum generated during ejection causes the formation of a bipolar nebula, which subsequently collapses into a binary star system. This represents a fresh perspective on ejection dynamics, diverging from the traditional view where ejections are seen as a means to conserve angular momentum during stellar collapse. The ASTG framework offers a comprehensive model for analyzing ejection dynamics, as well as for simulating the formation and evolution of binary stars and planetary systems. The azimuthal symmetry inherent in bipolar ejections is further explored in the companion paper, ASTG (I). Additionally, the role of bipolar ejections in the formation of planetary systems is examined in a third paper, Planetary System Formation (PSF). The gravitational dynamics of these systems are elaborated upon in a fourth paper, Gravitational Dynamics of Planetary Systems (GDPS). This series of works collectively aims to elucidate the formation and evolution of the solar system. The present paper specifically focuses on the gravitational dynamics of bipolar ejections, bipolar nebulae, and binary star systems. It begins with an overview of the ASTG framework, followed by an examination of the gravitational forces acting on ejected matter. The text then details the conditions under which bipolar ejections occur and the characteristics of the resulting structures. Subsequently, the gravitational dynamics of binary star systems are analyzed, followed by a discussion on the conditions required for the stability of such systems. The paper concludes with an outline of the series' scope and future research directions. Keywords: bipolar ejections, binary star systems, ASTG, solar system formation. The origin of Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs) remains uncertain, though a leading hypothesis suggests they result from the interaction between neutron stars and their surrounding material. This study investigates the feasibility of postponing radio emission from the neutron star until after it engulfs or accretes external matter. We examine a model where a neutron star, following a supernova, moves through the ejecta and subsequently accretes matter from a companion star. In this framework, radio waves are delayed relative to the optical emission from the accretion process. We calculate the probability of postponing radio emission from the neutron star within 100 seconds of the optical signal, finding it to be $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$ for a solar-mass companion and $10^{-5}$ to $10^{-4}$ for a 0.1 solar-mass companion. Furthermore, we estimate the likelihood of simultaneous radio-optical emission, which we predict to be $10^{-2}$ for a solar-mass companion and $10^{-5}$ for a 0.1 solar-mass companion. These predictions align with recent observations of concurrent radio-optical FRBs. Additionally, we determine that the rate of radio bursts occurring within 100 seconds of optical flares is $10^{-2}$ per year for a solar-mass companion and $10^{-5}$ per year for a 0.1 solar-mass companion, based on a FRB rate of 100 per year. This model also offers an explanation for the origin of the repeating FRB 180916.J0153+11. We conclude that the proposed model is consistent with the observed characteristics of this repeating FRB. Finally, we suggest that future radio and optical telescopes should monitor known repeaters to search for simultaneous radio-optical emission. Such observations would either confirm the proposed model or place stringent constraints on the parameters of the scenario. This dissertation centers on the conceptual design, performance enhancement, and fabrication of high-power laser systems. High-power lasers are foundational components in numerous scientific and industrial fields, including spectroscopy, remote sensing, laser machining, and medical surgery. However, achieving high-power lasers is inherently difficult, often resulting in the destruction of critical optical elements like amplifiers and isolators due to excessive absorbed power, which severely restricts the power scalability of these systems. To address these challenges, this dissertation introduces three primary research areas: (1) the design of all-hermetically sealed, gas-filled, high-power laser systems, (2) strategies to improve their performance, and (3) the development of robust, high-power laser components.

In the first area, we designed and constructed a 100 W all-hermetically sealed, gas-filled laser system. This apparatus utilizes a fiber laser pump, free-space amplification, gas-filled Brewster plate polarizers, gas-filled Faraday rotators, and gas-filled isolators. The system successfully delivers a stable 100 W of power over 10 hours, with an absorption loss of only 0.01% per window. Furthermore, we demonstrated that a gas-filled Brewster plate can serve as an effective polarization controller, offering minimal insertion loss and low power absorption.

To enhance system performance, we developed a comprehensive thermal model for gas-filled solid-state laser bars. This model calculates the temperature distribution within the laser bar and predicts the maximum extractable power, accounting for thermal lensing, thermal detuning, and thermal roll-over. Utilizing this model, we identified optimal operating conditions and proposed effective thermal management solutions.

Finally, to achieve higher power levels, we designed and fabricated high-power laser components capable of withstanding up to 1000 mW/mm² of absorbed power. We designed and manufactured high-power glass-filled Faraday rotators, glass-filled Brewster plate polarizers, and glass-filled laser windows. These components exhibit low optical insertion losses, high damage thresholds, and power absorption rates as low as 0.001%.

By integrating all-hermetically sealed, gas-filled optical components with advanced thermal modeling, the limitations of high-power laser systems can be effectively overcome. This approach paves the way for the development of even higher-power laser systems. Ultimately, this work provides a robust foundation for the design, performance optimization, and manufacturing of high-power laser systems. Text generation models frequently produce incoherent output because of a lack of visual context. We introduce observe(), a new interface that embeds fine-grained visual controls directly into the text creation workflow, thereby enabling texts to maintain logical consistency. Our research demonstrates that human users effectively utilize observe() to build complex, coherent documents, and we have developed novel programming interfaces to facilitate this interaction. Furthermore, we have created observeLM, a new framework designed to support these interactive interfaces, which significantly improves the coherence of generated texts. This study marks the first exploration of computer-generated visual controls in text creation workflows, highlighting the substantial benefits of computer-human collaboration. Our resources, including the observeLM framework, are released as open-source software to foster future research and innovation.

**Keywords:** observe(), observeLM, visual interface, visual control, computer-human collaboration, coherence, open-source software.

This paper introduces Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature and proof-of-knowledge framework designed for multi-signature protocols. It builds upon the $n$-of-$m$ ring signature and proof-of-knowledge system proposed by Bünz et al. (2018) specifically to address the delegation problem. The scheme leverages the properties of RingCT, ensuring that any signer can delegate signing rights to others without revealing their identity, while maintaining the ability to revoke these rights at will. This mechanism enables a quicker proof-of-knowledge for any delegated signer compared to standard ring signatures. When integrated with a multi-signature protocol, the method ensures that all participants sign a specific message without exposing the set of authorized signers. We detail the construction of Delegated RingCT and demonstrate its applicability to delegation within multi-signature protocols. Additionally, we provide a prototype implementation of Delegated RingCT for Bitcoin-based protocols. Our analysis indicates that the scheme incurs minimal overhead, with an average increase of only 1.5% in block size and a 2.5% rise in verification time. These performance metrics are superior to those of Bitcoin RingCT, which requires approximately a 10% block size overhead and 15% verification time. Furthermore, we illustrate how Delegated RingCT facilitates anonymous payment channels, such as Delegated Payment Channels, within payment layer protocols. This approach reduces the number of on-chain transactions and enhances payment efficiency. We also present a prototype for anonymous payment channels, showing a block size overhead of about 1.5% and payment latency increases of no more than 10%. These results outperform Bitcoin RingCT-based solutions, which exhibit roughly a 10% block size overhead and 20% latency overhead. We anticipate that Delegated RingCT will find extensive applications in the payment layers of various payment protocols. The brightness profile of an electron beam along the beam line offers a comprehensive depiction of the beam's transverse structure. This paper outlines the methodology and findings from brightness scanning at the CERN Large Hadron Collider and presents the underlying theoretical framework. The technique involves injecting a short electron pick-up spike into the beam to extract differential longitudinal profile data. By analyzing these results through the lens of the longitudinal-emittance density matrix, we can isolate contributions from specific beam phases, effectively filtering out noise. This process yields the longitudinal and transverse pick-up brightness profiles, which are fundamentally three-dimensional functions describing the pick-up's electron-emittance density. A key advantage of this approach is that it requires no theoretical assumptions regarding the beam's transverse phase-space distribution. The proposed methodology is broadly applicable to any accelerator where a pick-up is available. Furthermore, the results demonstrate that brightness scanning serves as a highly effective diagnostic tool for characterizing the transverse phase space of electron beams. This makes it particularly valuable for studying high-current, large-emittance beams, such as those found in linear accelerators. The paper concludes by discussing potential applications of this technique in such contexts. Additionally, the methodology has been validated using electron bunches from the LHC's test beam, which are injected into the machine via the Low Energy Test Beam (LEP-TB). The outcomes of these validation tests are presented. Finally, the results underscore the technique's effectiveness and its potential for future use as a diagnostic method in accelerators. In summary, brightness scanning offers a powerful tool for analyzing the transverse phase space of electron beams. Data-informed modeling, which integrates modeling and machine learning, has become a widely adopted method across various scientific and engineering disciplines. However, it is frequently assumed that this approach is only viable when models are pre-specified and accurate. This paper challenges that assumption by introducing a framework capable of effectively learning from collaborative data-informed models even in the absence of a priori model knowledge. The proposed framework is validated through numerical experiments and a case study of a data-driven controller for a wind turbine. The findings demonstrate the method's effectiveness in developing collaborative models and control strategies that are robust against uncertainties in system parameters and external disturbances. Consequently, the approach enables the creation of high-performance control strategies for systems that lack well-defined physical models. Notably, the case study reveals that the proposed framework can also enhance the robustness of collaborative control strategies when physical models are available. Overall, this framework is applicable to scenarios where collaborative data-informed modeling is feasible. Furthermore, it is expected to facilitate the development of next-generation data-driven control strategies, as it can be seamlessly integrated into standard model predictive control frameworks. Finally, the framework is anticipated to aid in designing data-driven system identification techniques for learning unknown physical models from high-dimensional, noisy, and potentially nonlinear data. These models can subsequently be utilized to establish data-informed control strategies that surpass the performance of purely data-driven alternatives. The proposed framework is implemented in Python and will be made available on GitHub. Additionally, the Python code for the wind turbine case study can be accessed via a supplementary link. The $\Upsilon(10753)$ resonance is recognized as the primary source of the dimuon signal at the BEPCII facility. We calculate the branching ratios for these reactions and compare them with existing experimental data. Our findings indicate that the branching ratio for $\Upsilon(10753)\to\Upsilon(nS)\pi^+\pi^-$ could be enhanced by approximately 1.5 times if mixing with the $Y(4660)$ state is present. We introduce AskewSGD, a novel optimization method designed to train both neural network weights and non-integer activation bit depths. By employing a first-order optimization approach, AskewSGD iteratively updates the bit depth to maximize the same objective function used for weight training. The process involves two constrained optimizers that utilize gradient information to sequentially refine weights and bit depth, ensuring rapid convergence. This strategy effectively mitigates the "quantization cliff," enabling the training of models with non-integer bit depths as low as 2.5 bits. Furthermore, AskewSGD facilitates the development of adaptive quantization schemes, allowing different layers to operate at varying bit depths. Experimental results across several vision benchmarks demonstrate the technique's efficacy; for instance, it trains a Layered-Quantized DenseNet-121 achieving state-of-the-art performance on ImageNet with reduced computational cost, all while requiring no additional computational resources or memory.
