Soft robotics is a rapidly evolving field characterized by the design of robots with materials and control strategies that mirror the physical properties and behavioral capabilities of biological organisms. The inherent compliance of these robots enables them to perform tasks and adapt to their environments in ways that rigid robots cannot. This distinctive characteristic necessitates a thorough understanding of the relationships between the robot's deformable structure, the external forces acting upon it, and its resulting behavior. Consequently, soft robots are typically governed by models that capture the mechanics of their compliant materials. This paper reviews the current state of practice regarding model-driven control methods for soft robots and identifies key open issues in control theory and mechanics that must be resolved to advance the discipline further. Specifically, we address three critical challenges: (i) the development of new control strategies for under-actuated systems, (ii) the design of controllers for robots operating within non-rigid environments, and (iii) the application of soft robots in deformable object manipulation. Finally, we propose a research agenda aimed at fostering future advancements in model-driven control for soft robotics. (This work was presented at MDMC 2021, held in conjunction with the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Robotics and Automation, ICCAD 2021, and the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Advanced Intelligent Systems, ICRA 2021, and ICAS 2021, respectively, in Singapore.) Table-oriented fact validation involves verifying factual claims within the context of specific spreadsheet environments. Although many current methods for this task adopt a "disintegration" strategy—extracting text from the spreadsheet to form natural language questions paired with the original claim and then answering via large language models (LLMs)—we identify a critical limitation in this approach. Specifically, the textual information extracted this way is often insufficient for LLMs to accurately validate the facts. To address this, we propose leveraging the native tabular understanding capabilities of LLMs to directly validate facts while retaining structural information. We present FActCheck, a new benchmark designed to evaluate this integrated methodology. FActCheck utilizes the FActCheck dataset, featuring a more diverse range of claims and annotations that better reflect real-world scenarios. Our analysis reveals that FActCheck's fact validity distribution is heavily skewed toward "may be true," a nuance that previous datasets failed to capture adequately. We further demonstrate that FActCheck serves as a more rigorous benchmark, exposing dataset biases that prior works overlook. The code and data for FActCheck are accessible at https://github.com/roberta-factcheck/FActCheck.

Confrontational Networks (CN) are a deep metric learning framework designed to learn discriminative features by simultaneously contrasting pairs of samples labeled as either "similar" or "dissimilar." While the standard approach conditions these networks on desired embedding characteristics using one-hot encoded descriptors, we propose a method to perform Confrontational Learning within a lower-dimensional, continuous latent space instead. We introduce two variants of this approach: one that conditions on specific attributes and another that is entirely unconditional. Our framework is highly adaptable and effectively integrates with various standard Confrontational Learning configurations. Experimental results demonstrate that our methods yield discriminative embeddings capable of learning discriminative features even under extreme intra-class and inter-class variability. Furthermore, we show that this framework can train discriminative feature extractors for tasks involving semi-supervised classification, image retrieval, and object recognition. Finally, we highlight the approach's ability to train generative models that synthesize realistic images and recover latent representations. Phase samplers are compact, high-performance devices that generate precise timing signals for phase-locked loops. In this study, we compare two distinct designs of such samplers, which employ different techniques to mitigate the phase noise of the oscillator. The first design utilizes a direct digital synthesizer (DDS) to digitally sample the oscillator output at a high rate, storing the data in on-chip memory. A digital filter then averages this sampled data before outputting the result. The second design passes the oscillator signal through a resistive divider, converts it to a digital format at a lower sampling rate via an analog-to-digital converter (ADC), and subsequently outputs it digitally. To evaluate the sampling mechanism, we subjected both samplers to a hierarchical sampling test, measuring the phase noise of a 10 MHz oscillator at various offset frequencies. The test setup comprised a signal generator, a dual-channel vector signal analyzer, and a custom-built measurement system. The results indicate that both samplers successfully suppressed the oscillator's phase noise, with the ADC-based sampler achieving a greater reduction. Furthermore, we analyzed the characteristics of the samplers, including their sampling rates, resolution, and other parameters, to identify the trade-offs inherent in each design. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these samplers and their advantages over traditional measurement systems. The hierarchical sampling approach presented here offers a promising avenue for developing more efficient and accurate phase noise measurement systems. Additionally, the comparison between the two samplers provides valuable insights into the design trade-offs involved in creating phase samplers for phase noise analysis. This work is expected to contribute to the ongoing research and development of phase samplers as critical components in phase noise measurement systems. The source code for the measurement system is available on GitHub to facilitate reproducibility and transparency. By providing a detailed description of the measurement system and its results, we enable other researchers to replicate the study and compare their own samplers against our results. This transparency is essential for advancing the field of phase noise measurement and promoting the development of more effective and reliable measurement systems. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/yourusername/hierarchical-sampling-measurement-system. We hope that this research will inspire further investigation into phase samplers and their applications in phase noise measurement. We present a resilient tagging scheme for the vertices of a graph $G$ that enables distance computation between any pair of vertices $u$ and $v$ using only their tags. Specifically, we achieve a bit-length of $O(\log n + \log^* w)$ for graphs with $n$ vertices and maximum edge weight $w$. Our primary advancement is a $O(\log n + \log^* w)$-bit tagging scheme that remains resilient to a constant number of faults in general graphs. This is accomplished by first assigning tags of $O(\log^* w)$ bits, which allow vertex distances to be rounded to the nearest power of 2 with an error of at most 1. Subsequently, we round these $\log^* w$-bit tags to integers, enabling the calculation of rounded distances between any two vertices. We then incorporate fault tolerance into this process, demonstrating that the failure of a constant number of vertices does not prevent the accurate computation of rounded distances between any pair. Finally, we apply these tags to graphs with a bounded genus, such as planar graphs, and show that the $O(\log^* w)$ bit length can be reduced to $O(\log n + \log^* w)$. This approach surpasses the previous best $O(\log w)$-bit scheme for general graphs and the $O(\log n)$-bit scheme specific to planar graphs. This study introduces a two-entity correlation model for a lossy Bose-Hubbard system driven by an external force. The correlations are defined as joint distributions of boson number differences between mode entities, and their time evolution is analyzed using moment-based approximations within a quantum master equation framework. The results are interpreted through the lens of the master equation, highlighting the strengths and constraints of the moment approach. Specifically, the model is applied to a ring of four modes to investigate correlations in both number and momentum domains. While spectrum-domain correlations can be intuitively understood via the master equation's eigenmodes, their dynamics in the number domain are more complex. In the weak-dissipation limit, the moment approach accurately reproduces the exact solution's qualitative features, though it fails to capture the dynamics of entanglement entropy. Conversely, in the strong-dissipation limit, the moment approximation introduces significant deviations from the exact behavior. These findings underscore the necessity for a more rigorous correlation model that remains consistent with the Liouvillian dynamics of the open bosonic system. Finally, the study examines the potential of this two-entity correlation framework for analyzing many-body localization in driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard systems. The moment approach successfully reproduces the emergence of number-domain correlations at resonance with momentum-domain ones, offering a viable alternative to exact methods. However, the study also notes that the moment approach cannot yet explain the suppression of these resonant correlations under strong dissipation. Consequently, the moment model is currently best suited for analyzing number-domain correlations under weak-dissipation conditions. This work is anticipated to serve as a foundation for future research on Bose-Hubbard systems subject to external forces and dissipation. Additionally, the code used for numerical calculations will be made publicly available. **Keywords:** Bose-Einstein condensation; Bose-Einstein correlations; Bose-Einstein condensation in mesoscopic rings; correlations in momentum space; correlations in number space; symmetry in number and momentum space. **Abbreviations:** BEC: Bose-Einstein condensation; BEC$_1$: symmetry in number and momentum space; BEC$_2$: correlations in momentum space; BEC$_3$: correlations in number space; BEC$_4$: moment approach. **Symbols:** $a_j$: annihilation operator for mode $j$; $n_j$: number operator for mode $j$; $b_{kl}$: correlation between modes $k$ and $l$; $B_{kl}$: 2-entity correlation between mode $k$ and $l$

This work investigates the existence and regularity of weak solutions to the divergence-form elliptic equation $-{\rm div}(A(x,\xi)\xi) = {\rm div}f$ within $L^2$-currents. The results extend the findings of Giacomini, Hayman, and Paroni (arXiv:1905.07700) to a broader setting. Specifically, we demonstrate that for an elliptic matrix $A$ exhibiting $(p,q)$-growth with $q < 2$, and a source term $f$ belonging to a $L^2$-current $T$ such that $\xi \in f$ lies in $L^{1,\alpha}(\Omega)$ where $\alpha = \alpha_0 = \frac{n}{2} + \frac{2-p}{p}\cdot 2$, a solution $\xi$ satisfying $\xi \in L^{1,\alpha_0}(\Omega)$ exists. The matrix $A$ is assumed to be countably $\rho$-H\"older continuous in $x$ for some $\beta > 0$, where $\beta = \beta_0 = \frac{4}{3}$. Furthermore, the primary innovation of this paper lies in a novel technique that enables the extension of divergence-structure equation results to $L^p$-currents. This method is applicable to any $p$-current $T$ provided that the dimension of the domain $\Omega$ satisfies ${\rm dim}(\Omega) < p < 2$. Our findings rely on the recent work of Arosio, Garofalo, and Lin (arXiv:1905.07700), which addresses divergence-structure equations in $L^2$-currents. Additionally, our primary growth condition is $\frac{p-2}{p-1} < \mu < 2$, where $\mu = \mu_0 = \frac{p-2}{2} + 1$. This study introduces decision functions for out-of-distribution (OOD) detection within Gaussian process (GP) models. We begin by reviewing standard GP frameworks, including those for OOD detection, and propose an alternative based on Gaussian Oja processes. Our primary contribution lies in formulating decision rules that rely exclusively on Oja process parameters, ensuring computational efficiency. We further extend this methodology to Gaussian process regression over manifolds (GPRM) and Gaussian process classification (GPC), with the latter extension serving as our technical contribution. We assess the efficacy of these proposed methods against state-of-the-art approaches using a collection of OOD detection benchmarks. The results demonstrate that our methods perform comparably to leading solutions on many datasets while maintaining a significantly lower computational footprint. Additionally, we illustrate the utility of these frameworks in a real-world application focused on OOD detection for medical imaging. All code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1998/decision-rules-gp. The findings presented here stem from the first author's doctoral thesis. Keywords: Out-of-distribution detection, Gaussian Oja process, Gaussian process regression, Gaussian process classification, Gaussian process classification over manifolds.

Periodic driving of a quantum system typically induces heating, a phenomenon known as Floquet heating, which causes the system to evolve toward an infinite-temperature state where all states are equally probable. However, in open quantum systems, dissipation can suppress this heating. This study demonstrates that dissipation can also halt Floquet heating within specific quantum many-body systems, allowing the system to reach a steady state at a temperature significantly below infinity. We illustrate this through an experimental and numerical analysis of a Bose-Einstein condensate dissipationally coupled to a driven, optical-lattice structure, which supports a scissor-like mode. This mode is considered a prototypical scar-like state, characterized by low entropy and an inability to thermalize. We find that incorporating an engineered dissipative coupling to the lattice's center enables the system to achieve a temperature orders of magnitude lower than the steady-state temperature of the driven isolated lattle. This approach represents a promising avenue for controlling quantum states and temperatures, with potential applications to various quantum-matter models. Furthermore, our findings may extend to other scar-like states, including those arising from many-body localization and time-crystalline phases. Finally, our research may inspire the development of novel quantum devices that operate at temperatures far lower than those achievable through conventional refrigeration methods. The Alexandrov maximum theorem established a key link within the theory of generalized convex functions. In the context of the Monge-Ampère equation, Alexandrov's solution exhibits profound connections to concepts such as absolute continuity, Holder continuity, and uniform integrability. This article introduces a refined version of Alexandrov's theorem, termed the "Enhanced Alexandrov Maximum Theorem," which demonstrates the uniform Holder continuity of functions falling within its scope. Applied to the Monge-Ampère equation, this improved theorem yields a novel proof for the absolute continuity, uniform integrability, and uniform Holder continuity of solutions when the right-hand side is constrained. These findings represent significant advancements in the theory of functions of several variables and the theory of generalized convex functions. Furthermore, the proof methodology employed in this work is versatile and can be adapted to derive other conclusions. The technical approach is also robust and applicable to various problems in partial differential equations. The enhanced Alexandrov maximum theorem is anticipated to have extensive applications in diverse fields. This paper is structured into ten sections. Section 1 provides an overview of the topic and related research. Section 2 defines generalized convex functions and examines the convexity of function compositions. Section 3 outlines fundamental properties of multivariate functions. Section 4 presents the enhanced Alexandrov maximum theorem. Section 5 investigates the uniform convergence of sequences of functions with constrained second-order difference quotients. Section 6 proves the uniform Hölder continuity of the Monge-Ampère equation's solutions under a constrained right-hand side. Section 7 establishes the equivalence between the Alexandrov maximum theorem and the convexity of function compositions. Section 8 explores the uniform convergence of sequences of functions where second-order differences are bounded from below. Section 9 applies the enhanced Alexandrov maximum theorem to the Monge-Ampère equation. Section 10 concludes the work. This study develops a statistical time-domain framework to characterize the temporal fluctuations of a generic, aperiodic light source. The description relies on a real-valued, time-dependent amplitude and a time-dependent phase, with the latter defined via the phase diffusion process. The source's time structure is quantified using an amplitude diffusion function and an phase (or phase diffusion) correlation function. These statistical properties are derived from the source's autocorrelation function using a novel decomposition technique. The efficacy of this approach is validated by analyzing both a non-repetitive optical pulse train and an optical clock based on a semiconductor laser. Notably, the proposed statistical description is applicable to any aperiodic optical source. The methodology is supported by an open-source Python package, pyphase, which is available on GitHub. Pyphase enables the calculation of the amplitude and phase structures of optical sources and the simulation of their aperiodic optical clock performance. Furthermore, pyphase can model the fluctuations of repeating lasers, making it a versatile tool for characterizing laser light. The package is also valuable for simulating optical frequency comb systems, including optical frequency metrology setups. By facilitating the simulation of various laser noise models, pyphase allows researchers to evaluate the impact of different noise characteristics on measurement results. This paper details the construction of the pyphase package and provides pyphase-compatible simulations for fluctuation models, including white phase noise, random walk phase noise, and the non-repetitive optical clock system. Additionally, pyphase can be utilized to assess the effects of white frequency noise and random walk frequency noise on optical frequency metrology. This work establishes pyphase as a versatile instrument for characterizing aperiodic optical clocks and optical frequency metrology systems. Finally, pyphase is freely available for users to develop their own models for aperiodic light sources and optical frequency metrology systems. This paper introduces a fog-assisted dynamic network architecture designed to enhance Service Function Chaining (SFC) resiliency, resource efficiency, and Quality of Service (QoS). The proposed framework relies on distributed, real-time decision-making at the edge to recover from network failures and mitigate faults. By integrating cloud and fog resources, the system achieves a distributed, low-latency recovery mechanism that minimizes the impact of network failures. Faults are categorized into two types: those triggering network recovery and those, such as packet loss or congestion, managed by asset management strategies. To address the latter, the system employs energy-efficient techniques to manage network assets, including traffic engineering and asset scaling. This architecture is particularly well-suited for real-time applications like Virtual Reality (VR) and autonomous vehicles, which demand resilient and efficient edge resources. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed system significantly improves recovery time and QoS for SFC, surpassing both standalone fog and cloud solutions. Furthermore, it offers resource and cost advantages over virtualized cloud systems by leveraging fog and, when necessary, cloud resources. The architecture also supports QoS-driven traffic engineering and the dynamic scaling of assets, such as virtual machines. Finally, the system is applicable to future 6G networks, which are expected to integrate multiple 5G access technologies to support diverse services. A key challenge in 6G will be resource management, which this system addresses through distributed, real-time decisions utilizing both fog and cloud resources. The paper concludes by outlining current limitations and proposing future research directions. Keywords: Fog Computing, SDN, SDN-VIM, QoS, QoS-aware Traffic Engineering, Asset Scaling. 1. Introduction The Software Defined Network (SDN) paradigm has facilitated the widespread adoption of network virtualization, enabling the creation of virtualized services over physical infrastructure. This has been instrumental in supporting various applications, from basic web services to advanced real-time applications like Virtual Reality (VR) and autonomous vehicles. VR, for instance, is increasingly popular in gaming and entertainment, offering an immersive experience that enhances user engagement. However, VR is highly sensitive to network conditions, as it requires the transmission of high-resolution images and low-latency control signals. Consequently, VR applications are best deployed in environments with high bandwidth and low latency, such as data centers. Nevertheless, VR demand is not uniform across all locations; it is typically higher in urban areas than in remote regions. This disparity presents a significant challenge for network operators, as provisioning data center resources to meet peak demand incurs substantial costs.

This paper introduces a novel algorithm designed to alter gradient flows during the training of deep neural networks. By adjusting the standard gradient update rule, the proposed method enables the exploration of sample-wise or channel-wise training using a single base model. The study investigates the impacts of gradients modified in both the input and output spaces, with the output space analysis incorporating diverse loss functions. Extensive numerical experiments were conducted across several datasets, including CIFAR10, CIFAR100, FashionMNIST, and ImageNet. The results demonstrate that sample-wise and channel-wise approaches yield promising outcomes, while the use of different loss functions in specific training scenarios proves effective. Furthermore, the research explores the influence of base model architecture and training configurations on numerical performance. Ultimately, this work aims to facilitate the systematic evaluation of sample-wise and channel-wise training methodologies. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/SeokminKwon/GradManip. Additionally, the authors have published a companion tutorial offering a comprehensive guide to the various training schemes and model architectures examined in this study. We introduce a new holographic error correction model, the hyper-invariant MERA (HIMERA), which maintains bulk connectivity via multiple paths even when subsets of boundary qubits are missing. This characteristic stems from power-law associations between boundary and bulk qubits within our tensor network framework. As a stabilizer code, HIMERA exhibits exponential code degeneracy and can be interpreted as a continuous-deformation code through a specific mapping. Furthermore, we establish the code distance and demonstrate that HIMERA can be prepared using a constant depth quantum circuit, rendering it feasible for current quantum hardware. Additionally, we investigate a family of parametric HIMERA networks and analyze their performance as a continuously-deformable code, revealing a phase transition within the code space. Finally, we extend HIMERA into a continuous-deformation code with a linear code distance, which can be viewed as a generalization of the HaPPY code. This generalized code, the holographic invariant tensor network code (HITNC), is prepared using a single layer of boundary quantum error correction. We establish its stability, determine its code distance, and identify a phase transition within its code space. These codes hold significant potential for advancing holographic quantum information theory and have practical applications in quantum computing. Specifically, we outline a method to construct a fault-tolerant universal quantum computer by leveraging these codes. This approach, known as holographic hardware, is expected to surpass the capabilities of existing quantum error correction architectures. Our methodology is detailed in a companion paper, which also provides a comprehensive analysis of these quantum computing systems. This study examines the three-dimensional distance distribution among Galactic Core Fibers, utilizing a sample of 100 fibers selected from the Population of the Galactic Core Fibers (PGCIF). Distances are calculated between all fiber points within a 10 pc radius of each fiber's center. The analysis reveals that the cumulative distance distribution aligns with a power law, characterized by a slope of $\alpha = 1.15 \pm 0.05$ for distances $d < 100$ au and $\alpha = 1.25 \pm 0.05$ for $d > 100$ au. Furthermore, the distance distribution between points within the same fiber is also well-described by a power law, with a slope of $\alpha = 1.15 \pm 0.05$ for $d < 10$ au and $\alpha = 1.25 \pm 0.05$ for $d > 10$ au. These findings indicate that the fibers within PGCIF represent gravitationally bound structures. Additionally, the observed distance distribution between separate fibers is consistent with the Parker model of a gravitationally unstable, self-gravitating gas cloud. Finally, the statistical properties of fiber separation distances in PGCIF are compared against those of the Orion molecular cloud. This analysis demonstrates that fibers in PGCIF are more compact than those in the Orion cloud, exhibiting a more pronounced separation distance distribution. These results further support the hypothesis that fibers in PGCIF are more gravitationally bound than those in the Orion cloud. Overall, the statistical distance distribution properties of fibers in PGCIF are consistent with the Parker model of a self-gravitating cloud. Consequently, the fibers in PGCIF are likely more gravitationally bound than those in the Orion cloud. This conclusion is supported by the fact that the radial velocity dispersion in the Orion cloud is approximately 0.2 km/s, whereas in PGCIF it is only about 0.05 km/s. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings. The research was conducted using the Apache Commons Math and Matplotlib software. This paper introduces a novel Ideal Conservation Voltage Reduction (ICVR) scheme designed for primary distribution networks, which are interconnected with secondary networks via voltage regulators. The objective of ICVR is to lower active energy losses by adjusting node voltages to an ideal, lossless profile while maintaining power flow continuity. Unlike traditional conservation voltage reduction (CVR) methods that rely on centralized optimization, ICVR is distributed, enabling its deployment in large-scale systems without incurring high computational costs. To facilitate integration with secondary networks, the ICVR formulation incorporates both non-linear and linear power flow constraints. Furthermore, to handle the non-linear constraints distributedly, we develop two distinct distributed algorithms: one utilizing consensus optimization and another based on model predictive control (MPC). Simulation results demonstrate that both proposed algorithms converge to the optimal solution within a finite number of iterations. Finally, to ensure robustness against communication delays, we propose two distributed schemes capable of tolerating both primary and secondary network disruptions. Extensive simulations confirm the algorithms' convergence and their ability to achieve near-optimal solutions under various network disruption scenarios. Additionally, the application of these schemes to a real-world system is demonstrated. (Corresponding author: M. R. Iravani) Keywords: Conservation Voltage Reduction, Model Predictive Control, Optimization, Power Distribution Networks. (Corresponding author: M. R. Iravani)

This study demonstrates that in a nonrandom bandit setting, a specialist can surpass the regret of a baseline policy—even one that is adaptive—provided the specialist employs an arm-dependent lag. This finding stands in contrast to random bandit environments, where lag does not influence regret. The analysis further extends to settings where arms exhibit time-varying variances, resulting in specialized policies that utilize time-dependent lags. Additionally, the paper examines the impact of nonparametric priors on regret outcomes. Finally, it establishes that the asymptotic behavior of the posterior distribution remains consistent with that observed in random bandit scenarios. To validate these theoretical results, the study includes both synthetic and real-world experiments. The code is accessible at https://github.com/akshaykumar1997/NonRandomBandits. Accurately modeling loads on offshore wind turbines is essential for their cost-effective deployment. While proxy models offer a viable solution by circumventing the need for physics-based simulations, they must remain probabilistic to quantify uncertainties stemming from environmental variables like wind speed and direction. This study employs linked Gaussian processes to build proxy models for offshore wind-turbine stresses. Specifically, the correlation between parent and child models is represented as conditional linked Gaussian processes, with their parameters optimized using likelihood functions. By utilizing the mean and covariance functions of the parent and child models, the correlation's mean and covariance are derived, and the latter is integrated into the linked Gaussian process framework. Furthermore, an uncertainty quantification analysis was conducted on stress models for a turbine situated at the NREL's Barrow Island test site. Results indicate that the linked Gaussian process effectively propagates model uncertainty, yielding uncertainty metrics that align with those of standard Gaussian process models. Additionally, the barometric pressure is recognized as a critical environmental factor influencing turbine stresses, a relationship that the linked Gaussian process successfully captures. Consequently, the proposed linked Gaussian process model demonstrates potential for cost reduction in the development of proxy models for wind-turbine stresses. Turkey and Kazakhstan experienced a simultaneous earthquake on February 6, 2023, generating significant global interest. This study investigates how social media reacted to these events, specifically examining the distribution of user participation from Istanbul and Almaty. Our findings indicate that the two cities were affected differently, with Istanbul showing distinct user behavior compared to its neighbor. Additionally, we analyzed the topics trending in Istanbul both before and after the earthquake. The analysis was conducted using the Twitter API. Our results reveal that prior to the event, users in Istanbul were primarily interested in football and elections, whereas interest surged on social media platforms following the earthquake. Ultimately, this research demonstrates how social media can be leveraged to assess the impact of natural disasters. The code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ozgurkaya2000/IEEE-Access-Earthquake. Given that social media is increasingly integral to daily life, this study holds significant relevance for disaster management. Future work will expand the analysis to include other nations and events, such as the Turkey-Syria earthquakes and the 2010 Haiti earthquake. We aim to replicate this study on various countries and disasters, thereby proving its applicability to disaster management. Furthermore, we plan to incorporate sentiment analysis to examine user opinions regarding the earthquakes. This research was conducted by Ozgur Kaya, Hasan Kurt, and Mustafa Tasdemir. Kaya's contribution focused on data collection and analysis, Kurt on topic modeling, and Tasdemir on sentiment analysis. We investigate the $R_\infty$ characteristic of generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups $G(a_1,\ldots,a_n)$ by analyzing their nilpotent quotients. Specifically, we examine the case where $n=2$, demonstrating that the number of infinite Morse sequences associated with any nontrivial nilpotent quotient of $G(a_1,a_2)$ is either infinite or constant and nontrivial. Consequently, for these groups, there are no finite nilpotent quotients possessing a constant $R_\infty$ characteristic. This finding extends previous work where the $R_\infty$ characteristic for nilpotent quotients of nilpotent generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups was determined. Furthermore, we provide an upper bound for the nilpotent length of such groups, which supports the conjecture that generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups do not admit finite nilpotent quotients with a constant $R_\infty$ characteristic. Time-resolved spectroscopy is a powerful method for probing dynamic processes in chemical and biological systems. However, reconstructing system evolution from experimental data is difficult because of inherent noise and variations in measurement conditions. This study introduces a forward-optimization (FO) approach to invert time-resolved data, contrasting it with the conventional method that minimizes the $\chi^2$ distance between simulated and experimental signals. The primary advantage of the FO method is its utilization of all information within the time-resolved signals. By employing a Monte-Carlo ensemble of trajectories, the approach is robust against stochastic fluctuations in both the observed signals and the initial conditions of the system. Furthermore, the FO method is straightforward to implement and can be integrated into the same statistical framework as standard simulations. The efficacy of this inversion strategy was validated using both synthetic and published experimental datasets. The proposed approach is applicable to time-resolved experiments across various fields, including chemistry, biology, and material science. The FO method was implemented in Python and is available as a standalone open-source package. Additionally, a Jupyter notebook demonstrating how to apply the method to both synthetic and real experimental data is provided. This method is particularly valuable for analyzing time-resolved data from complex systems, such as those involving heterogeneous environments or initial conditions. Boundary conformal field theory serves as a powerful framework for characterizing conformal field models defined on domains with boundaries. This theory is particularly valuable for investigating interface phenomena, including capillary effects, surface anomalies, and the reflection of bulk operators. In this study, we examine the reflection of operators at the boundary, specifically focusing on their two-point correlation functions and boundary reflected entropy within 2D boundary conformal field models. Our methodology relies on the conformal mapping of 2D correlation functions, the selection of appropriate boundary conditions, and the analysis of entropy via the replica trick. As a concrete application, we calculate the boundary reflected entropy for the 2D Ising model across various scenarios, such as different boundary conditions, the reflection of operators near a boundary, and reflections influenced by external magnetic fields. Furthermore, we extend our analysis to 3D interface conformal field theory, applying the same principles to 3D Ising models. Finally, we present numerical results that confirm the validity of our analytical findings. These results represent a novel application of boundary conformal field theory, offering new insights into the reflection of operators and boundary entropy. Additionally, our approach may hold significance for quantum information theory, as reflected entropy is a recognized information-theoretic quantity. The Individual Energy Assessment (IIA) theorem and stochastic efficiency function (SEF) were originally proposed to offer a non-invasive method for measuring the work performed by molecular motors. This study extends the IIA theorem to broader stochastic processes and presents a practical technique for work measurement that avoids external probes. The approach is validated through simulations of Brownian motors and experimental data from DNA helicases. In both scenarios, the average error in estimated work scales with the square root of the motor's internal state transition count, indicating that high precision requires a large number of states. Consequently, this non-invasive method is applicable to any molecular motor, including those that are not biological in origin. The proposed strategy involves analyzing current fluctuations and applying the IIA theorem, which allows the work value to be determined without directly probing the system. We demonstrate that the SEF can be calculated from current fluctuations that exhibit a linear relationship with the thermodynamic driving force. Additionally, we show that systematic errors in work estimates can be significantly reduced by incorporating non-equilibrium free energy differences. These findings suggest that molecular motors operate near the SEF = 0 limit, meaning their performance can be greatly enhanced by minimizing fluctuations in non-equilibrium free energy. Ultimately, this research advances the understanding of non-invasive work measurements in molecular motors and provides a foundation for developing more efficient artificial molecular motors. Mobile applications utilizing Bluetooth for national contact tracing have emerged as a critical component of the global fight against the COVID-19 pandemic. This study evaluates the confidentiality of the Coronav\'irus-SUS application, demonstrating the significance of analyzing the complete privacy architecture rather than concentrating solely on discrete components. The Coronav\'irus-SUS app was constructed using the Flutter framework, which necessitates the inclusion of a proxy server to facilitate communication between native Android applications and the central server. We identified the proxy server as a critical vulnerability, showing that it failed to employ cryptographically strong random number generation. Consequently, an attacker could intercept Bluetooth-based interactions occurring between the application and the proxy server. This breach allows an adversary to monitor both the geographic locations of infected individuals and their Bluetooth device identifiers. Furthermore, we provide a detailed analysis of the app's privacy design and outline the specific steps required to enhance its confidentiality. To our knowledge, this represents the first design analysis of a national COVID-19 contact tracing application in Brazil. Our findings underscore the necessity of involving security experts in the design and development of such applications to guarantee the confidentiality of the populations they aim to protect. We have made the full source code of the Coronav\'irus-SUS application available on GitHub to support these research efforts. Additionally, the source code for the proxy server is included in an annex. We hope these findings will assist other security researchers in their investigations into similar applications. This study introduces a quantum-enhanced neural network architecture designed to boost the expressive capabilities of classical networks. The proposed quantum data format is generated using quantum states prepared via gate-based quantum computers, offering the advantage of not requiring quantum hardware with native qubit connectivity. We demonstrate the format's efficacy through two experiments on quantum data consisting of qubits and two-qubits, utilizing both gate-based and trap-based state preparations. The results indicate that the proposed architecture can achieve the equivalent capacity of classical neural networks containing 20 to 100 qubits using just 4 to 9 qubits. Furthermore, the effectiveness of the proposed quantum data is validated through classification tasks on MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets. These findings suggest that the proposed quantum data format holds potential for enhancing the performance of quantum-enhanced neural networks. Additionally, the methodology for evaluating the capacity of quantum data via quantum-enhanced neural networks can be extended to other types of quantum data. Unlike existing work that typically requires non-trivial modifications to standard C code to accommodate a machine-oriented formalism, our approach features a superficial embedding of C constructs into ACL2, allowing programmers to write code with only minor adjustments. This study analyzes the orbital elements of 39991 Iochroma, a member of the outer asteroid main belt, to identify potential resonances affecting its evolution. We examine the short-term fluctuations in its orbital period and semi-major axis, as well as the long-term drifts in eccentricity and inclination. We also assess the impact of mean motion resonances (MMRs) on the asteroid's behavior. The analysis of short-term fluctuations reveals that, in addition to general non-gravitational forces, Iochroma is subject to the 3:1 and 5:2 MMRs. The observed long-term drifts in eccentricity and inclination are attributed to chaotic diffusion caused by these same resonances. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the asteroid's evolution is influenced by a complex web of MMRs, with the 3:1, 5:2, and 7:3 resonances having the most significant effects. Finally, we show that the current position of Iochroma places it at the intersection of the 3:1, 5:2, and 7:3 resonances, a scenario that explains the object's chaotic behavior. These findings are supported by frequency map analysis and fast Lyapunov Indicators. Additionally, we estimate the remaining lifetime of the asteroid and the time required for it to be ejected from the 3:1 resonance. We also calculate the probability of Iochroma crossing the inner and outer edges of the main asteroid belt, as well as crossing the Earth's orbit. The study concludes that the 3:1, 5:2, and 7:3 resonances are the most critical for explaining the observed behavior of 39991 Iochroma. These resonances are also the most likely to cause the asteroid's ejection from the 3:1 resonance and its ebb and flow between the inner and outer edges of the main belt. Finally, the most probable scenario for the asteroid crossing the Earth's orbit involves a chaotic diffusion process driven by all three resonances. A recent surge of interest has emerged in applying machine learning to solve central problems within algebraic topology, a field focused on classifying mathematical structures based on their shape and holes. This methodology is essential for analyzing complex datasets in physics, chemistry, and biology, where understanding the underlying dataset's topology is critical. This review examines recent advancements in applying supervised and unsupervised machine learning to algebraic topology, with a specific emphasis on applications in physics and chemistry. We identify key challenges and propose promising future research directions. The review is designed to be accessible to mathematicians, physicists, chemists, and computer scientists, aiming to inspire collaboration across these disciplines. The synthesis of this work draws from over 200 papers, with detailed references provided. Although the 6-digit personal identification number (PIN) in the secure messaging app Signal is designed to verify a user's identity, an analysis of 1,050 Signal conversations revealed that only 18% of these exchanges involved the sharing of PINs. To understand why users bypass PIN protection despite the app's security-focused marketing, this study employed think-aloud protocols to examine how enthusiastic and casual users perceive PINs within their daily communications. The findings indicate that users primarily view PINs as a minor, internal hurdle rather than a robust security measure. Their justifications for skipping PIN protection varied, including a lack of awareness about the feature's protective capabilities, a belief that it serves no real purpose, and a perception that it hinders communication. These insights into user cognition regarding built-in security features can guide developers in designing more effective security communications to educate users on the value of their own PINs. Furthermore, this research underscores the value of the "inside-out" approach, which prioritizes the perspectives of enthusiastic and casual users to uncover the nuanced ways security features are adopted in everyday social interactions. By centering research on how users actually perceive security, this method offers a pathway to developing security features that are both valuable to users and feasible to implement. Ultimately, this study demonstrates that engaging with users who actively integrate security features into their workflows provides critical insights into the complex, often unanticipated ways these features are used in practice. The authors advocate for an iterative, user-centered design process that iteratively tests security features with enthusiasts and casual users to refine their design and implementation. This approach ensures that security features are not only technically sound but also align with the needs and perceptions of the people who use them. By balancing technical expertise with user insights, this methodology fosters security features that are both effective and accessible to a broader audience. The authors believe that the inside-out approach is essential for the successful design and implementation of security features, as it bridges the gap between technical design and user perception, ultimately enhancing the security of digital communication for everyone. This study introduces an algorithm designed to precisely and rapidly compute integrals of the form $\int_0^T f(t)w(t)dt$, where the weight function $w(t)$ adheres to a solar day period. The proposed method, termed solar GQ (SGQ), is a specialized adaptation of Gaussian quadrature. We derive recurrence relations for the moments of the weight function and provide numerical examples to validate SGQ's accuracy and efficiency. Furthermore, applying SGQ to reconstruct the hourly solar irradiance profile from a single measurement yields an average relative error of 0.0011, a significant improvement over the 0.145 error produced by existing linear approximations. Zero-shot object localization involves identifying instances of object classes that are absent from both the training and validation datasets. This letter introduces ZCOPL, a novel framework that localizes these object classes by leveraging class-level attributes rather than relying on specific example images. ZCOPL operates by estimating class-specific endmember positions within an image, subsequently predicting the locations of object instances based on these endmembers and their associated class traits. Accurate traffic forecasting is essential for traffic management, planning, and control. Conventional methods typically rely on historical data from individual sensors, but the Internet of Things (IoT) now enables access to vast, heterogeneous traffic datasets. This paper introduces a new forecasting framework designed to predict traffic volumes across all road links within a network. The approach leverages similarity metrics to identify representative historical patterns for specific time periods and geolocations, utilizing these patterns to forecast future flows for each sensor. By training a single generalized model to predict every link, the system significantly reduces computational complexity. The study validates the method using real-world data from a real-time traffic management platform in London, comparing its performance against traditional techniques. Results indicate that the proposed approach is both computationally efficient and accurate, achieving a 90% reduction in computational cost while improving prediction accuracy by 10%. Furthermore, the method was benchmarked against state-of-the-art forecasting tools, demonstrating that it surpasses all compared approaches. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1994/similarity-driven-attribute-extraction. This work is supported by the EPSRC grant (EP/R003040/1). Additionally, the authors are currently developing a new open-source Python package for traffic forecasting, which will be released on PyPI under the license. The package employs a similarity-driven attribute extraction strategy to identify representative historical traffic patterns for prediction. It begins by loading real-time traffic data, optionally from multiple providers, into a dictionary. Users can then define time periods and geographic locations for forecasting. The system allows for the selection of either a generalized model or a separate model for each location, with a dedicated function to predict traffic volumes for the specified locations during the given periods. Finally, a visualization tool is available to display the predicted results. The authors welcome any feedback or suggestions. Please contact ahmed.hassan@imperial.ac.uk. This paper introduces CuratedMovieData, a newly compiled dataset designed to enhance the analysis of current movie performance. Built from the 2010-2020 period, it includes detailed box office metrics such as global gross revenue, budget, running time, and genre, alongside box office-specific indicators like domestic gross, opening weekend earnings, and the number of theaters. The origin of the ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray excess in blazar spectra remains unresolved, with various models proposed to explain it. This study investigates inverse Compton scattering (ICS) of the extragalactic background light (EBL) by relativistic electrons within relativistic jets. We introduce a novel Monte-Carlo algorithm to efficiently simulate the scattering process, accounting for electron motion and partial polarization of the EBL. Our results indicate that both the electron distribution and the polarization state of the EBL significantly influence the resulting spectrum. Furthermore, we demonstrate that polarized EBL can generate a distinct spectral feature resembling a soft X-ray excess. Finally, we suggest that a combination of EBL Emission Resonance Scattering (BERS) and Emission Resonance Scattering (ERS) offers a viable explanation for the soft X-ray excess observed in certain blazars. These findings may assist in interpreting future polarimetric data from blazar spectra. (Abridged) (Machine Translated)

We present a method for calculating the analytic extension of a complex scalar field in the presence of an external potential, extending our earlier work which addressed only constant potentials. Furthermore, we develop an efficient algorithm to construct the analytic extension, enabling its rapid application. Our study includes an extensive analysis of the method's performance across various potential types. Finally, we demonstrate the technique's utility for simulating black hole accretion fields. This study addresses the challenge of distinguishing between two unknown, symmetric pure states using a single copy through an optimal measurement. Given the lack of knowledge regarding the specific states, the prior probabilities for the alternative hypotheses must also be unknown. Consequently, the problem is formulated as a two-user Bayesian decision task with unknown prior probabilities. By applying the concept of virtual users, this is transformed into a standard Bayesian decision problem. The resulting virtual detection task is modeled as a Markov decision process, yielding a virtual detection strategy that serves as an upper bound for the original single-user scenario. For a single copy, this strategy indicates that the prior probability of the alternative hypotheses should be inferred from the overlap between the two states; specifically, the prior probability is zero if the overlap exceeds 2/3 and 1/(2-o) otherwise. This approach reduces to the well-known pretty good states measurement when the overlap equals 2/3. Furthermore, the Bayes risk for this virtual detection problem is calculated, and an asymptotic expression for the average error probability is provided. These findings are applicable to distinguishing between two unknown symmetric pure states across general scenarios, including cases involving multiple copies. Notably, when dealing with a single copy of two unknown symmetric pure states with an overlap of 2/3, the average error probability is exactly 1/3. This result aligns with the average error probability for two known states under the optimal pretty good states measurement. Additionally, the derived upper bound is demonstrated to be asymptotically optimal for a large number of copies. Finally, the optimality of the virtual detection strategy is illustrated through an example involving two unknown symmetric pure states formed by superimposing two known basis states. Baryon production is investigated through the quantized splintering of a helical QCD string. In this process, a brane emerges from the string's horizon, carrying baryon charge while the remaining string retains the diquark charge. The QCD string is modeled as a 2+1 dimensional quantized massive gauge theory featuring a Chern-Simons term. By applying the Witten formula for baryon charges, the diquark's contribution to the string's angular momentum is calculated. Furthermore, quantum corrections arising from massive gauge fields are derived. These findings suggest that, analogous to a collapsing star, a brane can form within the string's horizon due to these corrections, resulting in baryon creation. Additionally, the influence of quantum effects on the brane's mass is explored. Finally, the scenario of splintering into multiple branes is examined. This analysis relies on the assumption that a helical string configuration exists, which could be triggered by the Chern-Simons term in the presence of a strong magnetic field. Consequently, this model may offer a potential explanation for the creation of multiple baryons. Keywords: QCD string, helical string, baryon charge, quantum corrections. We analyze the relationship between these travel times and the orientation of active regions, specifically comparing regions intersecting the solar equator with those having perpendicular alignments. Our results indicate that the travel-time variations caused by sunspot currents align with the equator-perpendicular asymmetry previously identified by Stello et al. (2008). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the amplitude of this asymmetry correlates with the total surface area of the active regions. These findings confirm the conclusion drawn by Stello et al. (2008) that active region structures influence helioseismic travel times, while also supporting the specific hypothesis that currents surrounding sunspots contribute to this effect. Consequently, the equator-perpendicular asymmetry in travel times can be interpreted as evidence for the presence of strong sunspot currents. Finally, we show that the amplitude of this asymmetry is consistent with the observed correlation between the strength of magnetic fields and sunspot size. Collectively, these results suggest that currents within sunspots possess a strength comparable to that of the magnetic field and a size similar to the sunspot itself. Practical single-source light field image compression is largely dependent on model-based techniques, where the performance of compression algorithms is directly tied to the precision of underlying models. Although deep learning has enhanced the quality of these models, it has not yet yielded significant improvements in compressed size, rendering such approaches less viable for real-world applications. To address this, we introduce a displacement-aware model that integrates the displacement information from corresponding pixel pairs to refine the model estimation process. This information is extracted using a technique called learning-driven practical parameterized prediction coding. Our approach leverages the geometric characteristics of light field images to optimize the residual coding strategy. Experimental results demonstrate that, compared to the PCC baseline, our method achieves a 10% reduction in compressed size at equivalent objective metrics. Furthermore, our method outperforms other state-of-the-art techniques in both geometric accuracy and residual coding efficiency. Finally, we have released an open-source implementation of the learning-driven parameterized prediction coding disparity view model at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/LPCC. This work holds potential for advancing practical applications in light field compression. Source code is available at https://github.com/Chenchenchenchen/LPCC. Interactive and non-interactive methods represent the two primary frameworks for information retrieval. Interactive approaches enable users to engage with the system to adapt results to their specific needs, whereas non-interactive methods rely on pre-defined rules to maintain consistent and predictable rankings. This paper introduces a vector-based cross-language information retrieval (CLIR) framework that integrates strengths from both paradigms. Specifically, it employs sparse vectors derived from multilingual term alignment for non-interactive querying, while utilizing dense vectors generated through a non-native speaker's paraphrases for interactive queries. We applied this method to the TREC CLIR tracks in 2019 and 2020, achieving new state-of-the-art performance on all evaluated tasks. The code for our TREC CLIR submissions can be found at https://github.com/roberta/interactive-querying. Furthermore, the paper outlines the mathematical foundations of our interactive querying technique, which may prove valuable for other domains such as private or domain-specific search applications. Given the current challenges in global information access, our technique is expected to be particularly beneficial for non-native English speakers. This study introduces two estimation techniques to generate reliable health metrics from sparse data, with a specific focus on the 2015 Ethiopia Demographic and Health Survey (EDHS). The first approach employs a spatial kriging model to estimate regional indicators, while the second utilizes a spatial Bayesian Bayesian Hierarchical Model (BHM) for the same purpose. Using the EDHS dataset, the research compares the performance of these methods against the Direct Estimation (DE) approach. The analysis reveals that both the spatial kriging and spatial Bayesian BHM strategies yield more precise and reliable estimates than direct estimation, particularly within small regions characterized by low sample sizes. The findings demonstrate that integrating spatial information and accounting for small-area, low-power contexts significantly enhances the accuracy of health metric estimation. The study concludes that spatially informed methods are essential for deriving reliable estimates from complex survey data in low- and middle-income countries. Additionally, it offers practical guidance for researchers aiming to apply spatial techniques to estimate reliable health metrics. All estimation code is accessible via a GitHub repository. Keywords: Bayesian estimation, Ethiopia, kriging, low and middle-income countries, small regions, spatial Bayesian estimation.

To accurately model energy alignments, we applied a self-consistent Hubbard $U$ parameter derived from constrained density functional theory. Our findings indicate that the Hubbard $U$ value varies with the specific element, showing a general trend of increasing across the rows and decreasing down the columns of the periodic table. Additionally, we observed that the Hubbard $U$ required to align the valence band maximum of monolayer MA$_2$Z$_4$ with that of monolayer graphene is consistently lower than the value needed to align with graphene in a graphene/graphene/ graphene sandwich structure. This reduced screening within the sandwich geometry explains the higher Hubbard $U$ value in that system. Furthermore, the quasiparticle exciton energy of MA$_2$Z$_4$ is found to be stacking-independent. Finally, the quasiparticle exciton energy of MA$_2$Z$_4$ is compared with that of graphene/graphene/graphene sandwiches. These results are expected to aid in the rational design of materials for optoelectronic applications. This similarity suggests that MoSi$_2$N$_4$ sandwiches could serve as a viable graphene substitute in optoelectronic devices. Additionally, the calculated exciton energy of WGe$_2$N$_4$ sandwiches is about 0.1 eV, indicating strong tunability of exciton energy through chemical engineering. These insights regarding dielectric constants are expected to facilitate the rational design of dielectric materials. This study presents the first observation of the decay $\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-$ using 9 fb$^{-1}$ of $pp$ collision data collected by the LHCb detector. The measured branching fraction is ${\cal B}(\Sigma^+ \to p \mu^+ \mu^-) = (1.0 \pm 0.3 \pm 0.1) \times 10^{-7}$, which aligns with Standard Model predictions. Additionally, the lepton lepton energy distribution is found to be consistent with the product of two Dalitz plots representing the intermediate two-step decays. No evidence for time-dependent CP violation was found, and no significant deviations from Standard Model expectations were detected in the branching fractions for related decay modes. Furthermore, the form factor ratio $t_1/t_2$ was determined to be $-0.10 \pm 0.11 \pm 0.01 \pm 0.04$, where $t_1$ and $t_2$ represent hadronic form factors, with the last error term accounting for hadronic form factor correlations. The hadronic form form factor ratio $f_0(0)/f_+(0)$ was also derived. These findings facilitate a more precise determination of the hadronic form factor ratio at the $\Sigma^+$ resonance compared to other methods. The result, $f_0(0)/f_+(0) = 0.90 \pm 0.10$, is in good agreement with Lattice QCD calculations. Consequently, this provides a stringent test of the Standard Model and constrains the parameter space of beyond Standard Model scenarios. The hadronic form factor ratio is sensitive to SU(3) flavor symmetry breaking, and its value is consistent with the prediction derived from the $\Sigma^- \to \Lambda \mu^+ \mu^-$ decay. Finally, the hadronic form factor ratio is also sensitive to the quark flavor dependence of the axial-vector coupling constant, a parameter that could be measured in future experiments. This work represents a significant advancement in the study of hypernucleon decays and contributes to the broader field of flavor physics. The results are published in Phys. Rev. The majority of stars form within dense cores created by the gravitational collapse of molecular clouds. Recent observations indicate that these central protostars are typically encircled by protoplanetary disks, which are believed to originate from the direct fragmentation of the collapsing core. This study investigates the dynamics of disk formation through numerical simulations of the collapse of a prestellar cloud fragment. We demonstrate that a protoplanetary disk can emerge from the rupture of a prestellar nucleus, a process that simultaneously creates a central protostar. Our findings suggest that the rupture of a prestellar nucleus offers a viable mechanism for generating protoplanetary disks around central protostars. Additionally, we show that the central protostar is enveloped by a dense envelope of material that has not yet accreted. We contend that this structure represents the initial evolutionary stage of the classical star and planetary disk formation process. Furthermore, the characteristics of the central protostar and its surrounding disk are contingent upon the physical conditions of the prestellar nucleus at the time of rupture. Consequently, this proposed formation mechanism may account for the diversity of observed star-disk systems. Finally, we emphasize the critical need for further research into the dynamics of disk formation. Specifically, we suggest that the initial conditions of the prestellar nuclei, such as their magnetic field strength and turbulence, significantly influence the subsequent evolution of the central protostar-disk system. Therefore, we advocate for a more comprehensive examination of the initial conditions of prestellar nuclei to better understand disk formation. Atmospheric scattering significantly influences astronomical images, but current modeling techniques are often inadequate for analyzing these effects. This study presents a novel atmospheric scattering model derived from on-sky observations of atmospheric air mass. We conducted these observations using the 1.6-meter telescope at the Observatorio Astronómico Nacional de San Pedro Mártir, employing a CCD camera equipped with a central mask to block the star image. The mask's edge creates a sharp transition from the stellar point spread function (PSF) to the surrounding sky, enabling the measurement of scattered light intensity across various air masses. By analyzing images taken through broad-band filters, we determined the sky surface brightness at different air masses. Our results indicate that the surface brightness of the scattered light halo adheres to a power law with respect to angular distance from the star, where the power law index is governed by another power law as a function of air mass. Furthermore, the sky surface brightness at a specific angular distance remains constant at a given air mass but follows a power law when considered as a function of angular distance. These findings suggest that the sky surface brightness at a fixed angular distance can be described by an atmospheric scattering model based on the air mass. Additionally, we discuss the implications of these results for future atmospheric scattering models. This work is part of a series; the following paper will detail the parameters of the models fitted to the observed data. The subsequent paper will apply these fitted model parameters to future atmospheric scattering models. Finally, we will compare our results with those from other studies. This manuscript is available in Spanish. Keywords: Scattering - Planetary Atmospheres - Planetary Rings - Planetary Satellites - Planetary Atmospheres - Planetary Rings.

We introduce a multi-term temporal sequence modeling approach designed to capture diverse temporal patterns. This method employs Bayesian inference to automatically assign a prior that enforces sparsity within the model parameters. By utilizing Bayesian Variational Inference (BVI), we efficiently approximate the posterior distribution of the parameters, thereby enabling the modeling of temporal sequences across various time scales. Experimental results on two sequence datasets demonstrate that these multi-term models effectively learn parameters at different time scales. Furthermore, we find that Bayesian priors enhance performance on short sequences, whereas Gaussian priors are more beneficial for long sequences. Finally, the multi-term framework yields improved results on the original BVI task and outperforms existing state-of-the-art sequence modeling techniques on two additional tasks. The rise of federated learning has made it feasible to train models across multiple parties holding confidential data. Nevertheless, the risk of data leakage persists, potentially compromising user privacy. This paper introduces an adversarial framework where a malicious client attempts to extract private information from a target by querying other honest clients. We demonstrate that if the target possesses justice, a simple query strategy can reliably recover the target class even with a limited number of queries. Furthermore, we show that when justice is absent, the target can exploit differential confidentiality gaps to design a complex leakage scheme capable of inferring the target class. These findings are validated through experiments conducted on both image and text datasets. Our research underscores the necessity of ensuring honesty among participants in federated learning environments. Additionally, we offer a novel proof-of-concept code available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi1997/Federated-Training-Encounters-Justice-and-Differential-Confidentiality}. We establish a supersymmetric minimal framework for $E_6$ grand unified theories that extend the standard model with a $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry associated with right-handed neutrinos. Incorporating a non-abelian $SU(4)_C$ color group, our model successfully accommodates all 15 Higgs doublets required by the $E_6$ classification within a single adjoint representation, thereby minimizing fine-tuning issues. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the baryon asymmetry observed in the universe can be explained through leptogenesis driven by a light scalar neutrino, with the remaining right-handed neutrinos responsible for dark energy. Our analysis indicates that the neutrino masses and dark energy density can be derived from the mass of the lightest right-handed neutrino, which lies in the few TeV range. Consequently, these neutrinos may be directly detected at upcoming collider experiments. Additionally, we examine the model's phenomenological implications, including the lightest supersymmetric particle dark matter candidate, flavor-changing neutral currents, and the masses of additional supersymmetric partners. We conclude that these features can be investigated at the high-luminosity large hadron collider. Finally, we present a comprehensive particle and superspectrum for a representative mass scenario and explore its potential to address the muon $g-2$ anomaly. A detailed phenomenological study will be presented in a forthcoming publication. Finally, the $U(1)_X$ gauge symmetry is found to be anomalous-free and capable of unifying all three standard model gauge couplings at a relatively low scale of approximately 10 TeV. All model parameters are determined through a global fit. The full framework is defined by 15 fundamental parameters, which are fixed by 15 experimental observables, including eight neutrino-related parameters. This approach offers a complete, economical, and predictive solution to numerous problems in particle physics and cosmology. This paper introduces a new wireless communication framework designed to enhance throughput by integrating intelligent reflecting surface (IRS) and energy harvesting. The proposed system aims to boost both throughput and energy efficiency in high-traffic, energy-constrained environments. Specifically, the study investigates an IRS-assisted network where a power-deprived user harvests energy from a point-to-point link shared with a primary user. The network's dual objective is to maximize harvested energy for the user while ensuring the primary user maintains a specific quality of service (QoS). To achieve this, an unsupervised learning approach is employed to optimize the IRS phase shift matrix and the power allocation coefficient, thereby improving throughput. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed scheme yields significant gains in throughput and energy efficiency compared to existing methods found in literature. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits low computational complexity, making it suitable for real-time implementation. Consequently, this work offers a promising solution for high-throughput, energy-constrained scenarios. Finally, the paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions. Keywords: Intelligent Reflecting Surface (IRS), Wireless Powered Communication, Throughput, Energy Harvesting, Unsupervised Learning. We introduce a unified framework that interconnects the dark sector leptogenesis with dark matter, dark energy, and the Hubble tension. In this model, the dark sector comprises two interacting components: dark matter and dark energy, which are linked to the heavy right-handed neutrino responsible for leptogenesis. The interaction between dark matter and dark energy is governed by a small dimensionless parameter $\alpha$, while the neutrino masses are dictated by the same heavy state. Furthermore, the dark energy equation of state, $w_{\rm DE}$, is established as $-1-\frac{2}{3}\alpha(1-q_0)$, where $q_0$ represents the present Hubble parameter. Our analysis demonstrates that the parameter $\alpha$ can be constrained by combining leptogenesis requirements with Hubble tension data and Planck observations. Additionally, we find that the model's parameter space allows for an interaction between dark matter and dark energy, with the neutrino mass range satisfying the constraints imposed by the thermal scenario of leptogenesis. Finally, we show that this framework can simultaneously resolve the Hubble tension, generate significant leptonic asymmetry, and establish dark sector interconnections. Consequently, the thermal scenario of leptogenesis remains a viable framework. Finally, we discuss the implications of future surveys for testing our proposed model. Specifically, the Hubble Space Telescope (HST) and the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) will be able to constrain the dark sector interaction parameter $\alpha$ to a precision of approximately $10^{-2}$ and $10^{-3}$, respectively. This level of precision is sufficient to test the model's parameter space, provided that the Hubble tension persists. However, if the Hubble tension is resolved, the model's parameter space would be restricted to the non-interacting limit. In this case, the neutrino mass would be bounded from above by $0.015$ eV, consistent with the thermal scenario of leptogenesis. This upper bound can be further constrained by the next-generation Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) experiment, CMB-S4, which will probe the neutrino mass range down to $0.001$ eV. Additionally, we note that the model's parameter space can be further constrained by the Cosmic Microwave Background (CMB) power spectrum. Reinforcement learning (RL) has demonstrated significant potential for deriving control policies from data, yet it often demands extensive trials to achieve a specific objective. This paper introduces a data-informed control framework that accelerates policy learning by integrating prior knowledge. The method constructs an augmented state space incorporating supplementary data and designs a policy that leverages this additional space. Furthermore, the framework utilizes supplementary information to define an augmented reward function. To validate the approach, the study applies it to three challenging real-world problems—underwater swimming, bipedal walking, and flying through a narrow gap—utilizing data from physical robots. The results indicate that incorporating supplementary data enables policies to acquire new skills with substantially fewer training trials. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenchenWu/DDIC. Additionally, videos demonstrating the behaviors learned by the proposed method can be found at https://vision.csail.mit.edu/projects/data-driven-intelligent-control/. Finally, the paper discusses the application of this framework to high-dimensional control tasks. Supplementary materials are available at https://vision.csail.mit.edu/projects/data-driven-intelligent-control/. This work investigates a two-dimensional non-unitary conformal field theory involving three scalar fields, where the coupling constant is identified with the complex structure of the underlying Riemann surface. By computing three-point correlation functions, we determine the Ward relations. These relations are subsequently formulated within the language of conformal blocks and established dressed vertex operators for the mathematical link associated with the $\mathfrak{sl}_3$ Toda lattice. Finally, we examine specific cases of the derived Ward relations. Although general conformal Ward relations for a collection of primary fields in a two-dimensional conformal field theory are typically characterized by $c$ independent equations, the specific structure of this theory results in only two independent equations. This reduction is attributed to the fact that certain three-point correlation functions vanish. Furthermore, we explore the non-trivial nature of these Ward relations through numerical calculations. Finally, the paper concludes with several remarks and a discussion of potential future research directions. Additionally, an appendix provides a complete set of recursive equations for two- and three-point correlation functions. These equations were developed to address a conjecture by Bershadsky, which posits that conformal blocks in two-dimensional conformal field theory can be defined recursively. The proposed conjecture offers a straightforward method for calculating correlation functions. We validate this conjecture by comparing its predictions against our explicit computations of two- and three-point correlation functions. This approach not only confirms the validity of the conjecture but also enables the calculation of n-point correlation functions. Consequently, this suggests that conformal blocks within two-dimensional conformal field theory may indeed possess a recursive definition. Finally, our findings indicate that Bershadsky's conjecture holds a broader generality than previously recognized. Specifically, the recursive construction for correlation functions can be extended to a broader class of models.
