This discussion will examine the progress and upcoming prototypes for the next generation of silicon tracking sensors, emphasizing their electronic integration, fabrication methods, and doping strategies. A key focus will be on developing sensors with minimal dead layers to ensure optimal tracking resolution and precise impact point determination for the Electron-Ion Collider's vertex detectors. Additionally, the talk will address the scalability of these technologies for large-scale implementations and highlight the significance of in-situ sensor testing. The proposed sensor is designed to be thin, featuring an ultra-thin n-intrinsic silicon structure. The intrinsic layer is produced via ion implantation and doped using nitrogen gas, followed by an annealing process. The sensor's readout is provided by a newly developed low-power, high-sensitivity CMOS ASIC. This innovative silicon sensor design is currently under development and will be tested in the upcoming Silicon Test Facility. Furthermore, the integration of novel sensor technologies with advanced materials and machine learning is essential for the next generation of tracking detectors. This study examines the variability in low-mass active galactic nuclei (LM-AGNs) exhibiting intermediate brightness changes, utilizing data from the Catalina Real-Time Transient Survey (CRTS) and the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF). We identified 10 LM-AGN candidates that met our criteria, with their light curves analyzed to determine whether their fluctuations stem from accretion disk instability or single black hole mass estimates. Our results indicate that four candidates—CRTS J090240.0+004020, CRTS J090240.0+004020, CRTS J100120.0+212020, and ZTF J090100.1+042001—exhibit periodic fluctuations, suggesting oscillations within the accretion disk. Conversely, the remaining six candidates display outburst-like behavior. Notably, two of these outburst-type objects—CRTS J100120.0+212020 and CRTS J100120.0+212020—demonstrate a correlation between their black hole mass and the amplitude of their brightness variations. Ultimately, we conclude that all ten LM-AGN candidates are likely pulsing due to accretion disk instability, with the specific manifestation (periodic vs. outburst-like) contingent upon the black hole mass. This research offers a novel perspective on the nature of low-mass AGNs and establishes a foundation for future investigations. Additionally, the methods employed can be applied to other transient sources to identify potential accretion disk oscillations. The sample of ten LM-AGNs is available at https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevD.105.063018. Supplementary data, including raw images, processed images, and light curves, can be requested via email from the corresponding author. We conducted ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ line in NGC 5253, a galaxy characterized by a metallicity of approximately 0.2 solar masses, to investigate the relationship between this line radiation and the star formation rate (SFR). The primary objective was to determine if the H30$\alpha$ line serves as an effective metric for characterizing stellar genesis in low-metallicity environments. Our analysis yielded a 2.5$\sigma$ detection of H30$\alpha$ radiation across the galaxy's disk. By comparing the integrated H30$\alpha$ flux with the SFR derived from H$\alpha$ emission, we established a linear relationship between the two. This suggests that H30$\alpha$ radiation can be utilized as a reliable tool for measuring SFR in galaxies with metallicity below 0.2 solar masses. Furthermore, we calculated the H30$\alpha$-to-H$\alpha$ flux ratio from the spatially integrated data and compared it against the ratio predicted by the MAPPINGS III code. The observed value was found to be roughly 1.5 times greater than the theoretical prediction, indicating that H30$\alpha$ radiation is likely enhanced by a mechanism not accounted for in the code's standard model. This discrepancy may stem from the MAPPINGS III code's assumption of a metallicity floor of 0.3 solar masses, which could result in an underestimation of H30$\alpha$ emission at lower metallicities. Consequently, we propose that the H30$\alpha$-to-H$\alpha$ flux ratio is governed by metallicity-dependent factors. These findings highlight the necessity of conducting H30$\alpha$ observations in a broader range of galaxies to refine the understanding of the H30$\alpha$-to-H$\alpha$ ratio as a stellar genesis indicator. Ultimately, the H30$\alpha$ line is expected to be a valuable tool for measuring SFR in low-metallicity galaxies. Additionally, we observed a correlation between the H30$\alpha$-to-H$\alpha$ ratio and the [NII]6584/A6583 ratio, suggesting that nitrogen abundance may also influence the H30$\alpha$-to-H$\alpha$ flux ratio. This paper presents a straightforward yet robust method for estimating conditional expectation functions using a nonparametric framework. A key advantage of this approach is that it avoids the need to select arbitrary bandwidths. The estimator is proven to be pointwise asymptotically normal, facilitating inference, and simulations demonstrate its effectiveness. Furthermore, the authors illustrate how this estimator can be employed to develop a minimax predictor for Poisson count time series within a nonparametric setting. They find that their proposed nonparametric predictor outperforms existing methods in the literature. Additionally, an alternative application is outlined for predicting the outcomes of global climate negotiations. Finally, the paper provides detailed guidance on implementing the estimator. All code required to reproduce the numerical results is made available. This study introduces a mathematical framework designed to model and analyze the spread of infectious diseases. The primary objective is to state-dependent control of the epidemic, achieved by adjusting the death rate based on assessments of system variables. Since the assessed system variables depend on the future death rate, the death rate itself becomes dependent on future states, forming a state-assessment control system. The challenge lies in the fact that system states at future time points are unknown, necessitating that the future death rate function rely on current states rather than future ones. To address this, we propose an observer-based state assessment control system to resolve the issue. This research aims to determine an appropriate control function that stabilizes the epidemic dynamics at a specific equilibrium point, ensuring the system settles into one of two scenarios: either the disease becomes endemic or it is eradicated. We establish sufficient conditions for the asymptotic stability of the desired equilibrium point and the convergence of the observer, subsequently applying the proposed observer-based control strategy to two distinct epidemic models. Finally, numerical simulations are presented to validate the effectiveness of the theoretical results. Furthermore, a numerical example involving a time-delayed SIRS epidemic model demonstrates the application of the theoretical findings. This example illustrates that the death rate can be adjusted to eliminate the virus within a finite timeframe. Additionally, the study confirms that the death rate is not constant but varies dynamically, contingent upon the current states of the epidemic system. These findings hold significant implications for the development of effective countermeasures against infectious diseases. To facilitate practical implementation, we provide a MATLAB-based application that enables users to design the death rate function and simulate the resulting epidemic dynamics. This tool is available for download at the following link: https://github.com/abdullahg/epidemic-dynamics. The source code is included in the supplementary materials. We anticipate that this tool will serve as a valuable resource for researchers in the field. Temporal Knowledge Graph Completion focuses on forecasting link predictions within temporal knowledge graphs. Although this area has garnered significant attention, temporal connection prediction remains difficult due to the dynamic and sparse nature of temporal facts. Consequently, it is crucial to identify the components that drive success. This study investigates whether pre-trained static models can achieve strong performance, even with training data limited to temporal facts. We introduce the concept of Temporal Knowledge Graph Embedding Transfer Learning, which involves transferring static connection prediction knowledge to temporal tasks. Our analysis reveals that pre-trained static models substantially enhance link prediction performance. Additionally, we examine the impact of various factors, including the temporal resolution of facts, data sparsity, and data volume, to determine their influence on performance gains. Finally, we explore how to leverage these factors to optimize the utilization of static knowledge graphs for connection prediction. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach improves performance by up to 12.5% on average across three datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/10000000000000000000000000000000/Transformer4TG. Furthermore, we have released a new benchmark dataset, HealiGraph, for forecasting link predictions in temporal knowledge graphs. HealiGraph comprises 100,000 instances from 100,000 medical journals, featuring a temporal resolution of one month and a graph sparsity of 0.0001. The dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/10000000000000000000000000000000/HealiGraph. This work aims to inspire researchers to investigate the potential of pre-trained static knowledge graphs in temporal knowledge graph completion. We anticipate that this research will encourage the development of pre-trained static knowledge graphs to facilitate transfer learning in temporal knowledge graph embedding. The source code is available at https://github.com/10000000000000000000000000000000/Transformer4TG. The dataset can be downloaded from https://github.com/10000000000000000000000000000000/HealiGraph. This study investigates the potential of applying ray matrix methods to analyze Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLML) within the context of high-peak-power ultrafast laser generation. We introduce a novel parameter, termed the resonator's geometric factor, which characterizes the strength of KLML and is contingent upon the cavity's geometric configuration. By utilizing this factor alongside standard stability criteria, we can efficiently determine the stable operating range of a KLML-based laser. Furthermore, the factor facilitates the examination of high-peak-power laser generation, enabling the prediction of the maximum extractable peak power and the associated limitations. Additionally, we demonstrate that the standard approach to estimating the stable KLML operating range is often overly conservative. These findings are illustrated through a numerical example of a ring laser, for which we calculate the extractable peak power under various conditions. Ultimately, the results suggest that the stable operating range for high-peak-power KLML lasers is more extensive than previously estimated. These outcomes are anticipated to be applicable to a broad spectrum of laser systems. The methodology and insights presented here are expected to facilitate the design of high-peak-power ultrafast lasers and enhance the understanding of the underlying physics governing their operation. The paper includes numerous tables and figures that provide a comprehensive and detailed overview of the study. Additionally, a supplementary dataset is available to support the reproducibility of the numerical results. All computational code is included in the supplementary materials. This paper introduces a new asynchronous online federated learning method designed to minimize the total expected nonlinear regression error across multiple agents. The system comprises diverse agents, each with a unique state transition function, a specific set of controllable inputs, and a distinct set of process noise parameters. These agents are constrained by control limits and disturbance sets, limiting their ability to influence one another. To address these challenges, the authors propose a novel asynchronous online federated learner that performs Bayesian inference using the Laplace approximation. This approach enables agents to update their local models and exchange information with others, even under conditions of uncertainty and varying computational resources. A key innovation is the ability for agents to share their uncertainty levels, allowing the receiving agents to weight the shared parameters accordingly. This mechanism ensures that agents with higher confidence contribute more significantly to the collective learning process. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through a case study involving a nonlinear regression task to estimate the position of a moving object. The case study reveals that the asynchronous online federated learner can achieve performance comparable to synchronous methods, which is particularly advantageous for agents that cannot fully observe the state transition function. Furthermore, the method is shown to be effective in reducing the root mean square error of the nonlinear regression. The source code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1994/OnlineFederatedLearner. Keywords: Bayesian learning, Bayesian inference, federated learning, online learning, online parameter estimation, online parameter learning, asynchronous learning, asynchronous parameter estimation, asynchronous parameter learning, asynchronous federated learning, asynchronous Bayesian learning, asynchronous Bayesian inference, asynchronous Bayesian learning, nonlinear regression, Bayesian learning, Bayesian inference.

The performance of Si-based photonic band gap (PBG) crystals as light absorbers and detectors has been significantly enhanced through the use of defect states within their band gap. By employing vertical tunneling barriers to isolate individual crystals, we achieved superior optical absorption in thin silicon layers (10 µm) and even ultra-thin films (100 nm) across both visible and near-infrared wavelengths. Our findings indicate that the optimal absorption bandwidth can be precisely tuned by adjusting the silicon layer thickness, the size of the photonic crystal unit cell, and the vertical tunneling barriers. Additionally, by integrating these optimized thin silicon absorbers with localized single-photon sources, we have created a promising architecture for a deterministic source of entangled photon pairs. This innovation holds significant potential for advancing quantum information processing and communication technologies. Furthermore, the proposed quantum light source is exceptionally compact, making it ideal for integration into existing silicon photonic circuits. Finally, the broader concept of utilizing photonic band gap crystals as high-efficiency light absorbers may have applications extending beyond quantum sources, such as in solar energy conversion. The Fokier expansions, which represent functions in high-dimensional spaces using Fourier series, are constructed based on the concept of a covering. By substituting trigonometric series with other types of series, such as Taylor or Legendre series, a variety of new expansion types emerge. This manuscript explores the properties and characteristics of these innovative expansions. Furthermore, it addresses the convergence of expansion coefficients and the radius of convergence for these series, ultimately demonstrating how to reconstruct original functions using these expanded forms. This paper serves as a foundational reference for further research into the convergence and divergence of these expansions. Additionally, it provides code for performing Fokier expansions up to the seventh order using Fourier, Taylor, and Legendre series. Finally, the work references related studies and acknowledges the contributions of various individuals. The appendix includes code for calculating Fokier expansions across all orders. The study investigates the magnetic properties of a new antiferromagnet, GdInO$_3$, which features a centered honeycomb lattice composed of slabs separated by van der Waals gaps. Using bulk magnetization and specific heat measurements across a temperature range of 0.35–300 K under external fields up to 9 T, the research establishes the antiferromagnetic nature of the material and details its magnetic phase diagram. The data indicates that GdInO$_3$ exhibits anisotropic magnetic behavior, with easy magnetization aligned along the $c$ axis. Additionally, a sharp peak in specific heat at 2.85 K corresponds to the Néel temperature, while a kink at 2.5 K in both magnetic responses signals a metamagnetic transition. This transition is attributed to a change from the basal plane to the $c$ axis as the easy axis of magnetization. Finally, the magnetic behavior of GdInO$_3$ is analyzed using a Heisenberg model. This analysis confirms that the material is quasi-two-dimensional, displays ferromagnetic nearest-neighbor interactions, and is governed by single-ion anisotropy. Furthermore, the study estimates the intralayer and interlayer exchange interactions, determining that the interlayer coupling is approximately 10% of the intralayer coupling. Finally, the magnetic phase diagram is constructed based on these model parameters. This work provides a foundation for future investigations into the excitations and properties of GdInO$_3$. This paper introduces a node-embedding approach designed to enhance link prediction in sparse networks. We propose Sparse Structural Neural Embedding (SSNE), an efficient embedding technique that utilizes a node-degree distribution to identify local sparsity within the network. SSNE is implemented using a neural network to generate node embeddings, with an autoencoder serving as the neural architecture. We demonstrate that SSNE outperforms the widely used Network Similarity Measure (NSM)—which relies on node-common neighbors—and surpasses various machine learning methods in accuracy, particularly for sparse networks. Furthermore, we establish that SSNE achieves superior accuracy across different sampling methods, including the Yule-Kendall, Erdős-Rényi, and Barabási-Albert models. Our findings indicate that SSNE not only outperforms existing node-embedding methods in link forecasting but also offers the computational efficiency required for real-world applications. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2000/SSNE. Additionally, we provide a Python package, SparseNN, which allows users to apply SSNE for link prediction without requiring access to the source code. Silicon atomic vapor chambers (SAVCs) are essential platforms for fundamental cold-atom experiments, including atom interferometry, inertial sensing, and the study of quantum many-body physics. However, current SAVC designs are limited by the relatively low vapor density achievable with thin-film silicon substrates. This study presents a scalable nano-fabrication technique utilizing thick silicon wafers to enable thicker films and higher vapor densities. We demonstrate the creation of nano-fabricated SAVCs with up to 100 silicon layers, achieving saturation vapor densities as high as 10 atoms/cm$^3$ at 300 mW laser power. These multi-layered chambers exhibit identical optical and atomic properties to those made via standard thin-film fabrication. The ability to produce SAVCs with elevated vapor densities will facilitate greater sensitivity in atom interferometry and inertial sensing, while supporting extended collision times necessary for advanced cold-atom experiments. Additionally, this technology is applicable to nano-fabricated optical setups for cold-atom research, offering enhanced optical power handling and robustness. This paper introduces a model designed to estimate the nonlinear interaction power density between two optical fields possessing distinct polarization states. Initially derived for elliptically polarized fields, the model is subsequently generalized to handle arbitrary polarization conditions. We demonstrate the validity of this modeling approach through numerical simulations and experimental measurements. Furthermore, we utilize the model to analyze nonlinear interaction power across various dual polarization formats, specifically examining the interaction between two circularly polarized fields with opposing orientations. Finally, the paper leverages this model to investigate how system parameters influence dual polarization nonlinear disruption. Our findings indicate that the circular polarization pair exhibits the lowest nonlinear interaction power, thereby offering superior nonlinearity tolerance compared to other dual polarization schemes. Additionally, the circular polarization pair demonstrates greater robustness against polarization mode dispersion than the co-transverse circular polarization pair. The results suggest that the circular polarization pair holds promise for enhancing the performance of dual polarization transmission systems. Additionally, the proposed model is applicable to both single span and multi-span transmission scenarios. The paper concludes by discussing potential applications of this model in the field of optical communications.

In recent years, there has been a growing interest in utilizing Deep Learning (DL) models for detecting wildfires, particularly within the aerospace sector, as aerial imagery offers critical data for emergency response. However, existing DL-based detection models often rely on the assumption that available visual data is sufficient, overlooking the reality that optical sensors frequently suffer from signal attenuation caused by atmospheric conditions like smoke, haze, and dust. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel deep learning-based IR-VIS integration method that enhances infrared images using visible light data. By combining this fused imagery with atmospheric compensation, our approach enables DL models to identify fires with greater accuracy. We evaluated our method using wildfire detection models across three datasets: two synthetic and one real-world collected in Chile. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in both mean Average Precision (mAP) and Recall scores. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the experimental outcomes, including model performance, computational efficiency, and the specific impact of infrared-visible integration on detection capabilities. These findings provide valuable insights for researchers developing DL-based wildfire detection systems. The associated code can be accessed at: https://github.com/fernandocampos/FIReGAN. This work was presented at the IEEE Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Learning (CVPR) Workshops in June 2022. Additional details are available at: https://sites.google.com/view/fire-detection-cvpr22. Our presentation will take place at the CVPR 2022 Satellite: Computer Vision for Disaster Management. We introduce a random compartmental model designed to capture the spatial propagation dynamics of COVID-19. The system is constructed by randomly assembling various propagation mechanisms, where the underlying probability space represents a collection of cities or regions. For infection parameters, we apply a log-normal distribution to adhere to the principle of invariance under coordinate change. To address the stochastic nature of transmission, we utilize a Cox process. Furthermore, the model incorporates a term for social distancing, acknowledging that reduced human mobility significantly impacts the spread of COVID-19. Finally, the random compartmental model is resolved into a series of independent stochastic differential equations. This paper provides numerical simulations of the model and compares its results with the COVID-19 pandemic in China. Additionally, the model's predictions for the COVID-19 outbreak in California are compared against actual data. The findings indicate that, absent strict social distancing, the COVID-19 epidemic in California would have escalated rapidly. These results underscore the necessity of strict social distancing to mitigate the pandemic. Additionally, we examine the model's properties and explore its potential applications. The model's parameter can be estimated using epidemiological data from various regions. Consequently, this framework serves as a valuable tool for analyzing COVID-19 propagation dynamics and forecasting future outbreaks. The model can be adapted to study other diseases, such as Ebola and HIV, and to predict the spread of emerging infectious diseases. This study presents a detailed analysis of the isoscalar monopole strength distribution in $^{28}$Si and $^{24}$Mg, utilizing experimental data from inelastic $\gamma$-ray scattering. To achieve a quantitative description, a microscopic random-phase approximation calculation was performed, incorporating the coupling between isoscalar monopole and quadrupole modes. The impact of this coupling is most pronounced in $^{24}$Mg, where the calculated strength distribution aligns well with experimental findings. Conversely, for $^{28}$Si, the monopole-quadrupole coupling has a negligible effect, allowing the microscopic model to describe the monopole strength distribution without including it. Furthermore, the excitation energies of the monopole strengths in both nuclei are found to be sensitive to the value of the isoscalar transition density at the nuclear surface. Finally, the giant monopole resonance (GMR) energies for $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si are determined to be 16.7 MeV and 15.9 MeV, respectively, based on the present calculations. These values are compared with experimental GMR energies and results from other theoretical studies. Additionally, the present GMR energy for $^{28}$Si is compared against measurements from inelastic $\gamma$-ray scattering. The agreement between experimental GMR excitations and theoretical predictions is examined, and the reasons for any discrepancies are discussed. Overall, the present calculations provide a consistent description of the monopole strength distribution in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si, including their respective GMR energies. This work complements our recent study on the quadrupole strength distribution in these same nuclei. Together, these findings demonstrate that the microscopic framework employed is highly effective for describing low-energy collective excitations in $^{24}$Mg and $^{28}$Si. Finally, the influence of the finite range of the Skyrme interaction on the strength distribution is also investigated. This work examines stick-slip dynamics and trajectory convergence within closed-loop systems experiencing Coulomb friction. Furthermore, a global localizing feedback control law is designed to drive the system state to the origin in finite time, rigorously proving the convergence of the resulting stick-slip motion. Finally, the analysis of a frictional pendulum demonstrates the application of the local behavior analysis, the proposed control method, and the resulting global localizing control strategy. Numerical simulations are utilized to illustrate the results and validate the convergence of the controlled system. Additionally, the local behavior analysis of the zero solution is extended to arbitrary equilibrium points. This approach enables trustless trading via dApps that can be updated remotely and withstand various attacks. Finally, we conclude the paper with a discussion of its limitations and future research directions. Given that blockchain technology is still in its early stages, we anticipate this work will be valuable for advancing future DEXs and enhancing the security of decentralized trading on public blockchains. Additionally, we believe this research will be beneficial for scholars in both computer science and economics, offering new perspectives on the future of decentralized trading. Our primary contribution lies in applying computer science methodologies to DEXs and decentralized finance, with a specific focus on resolving the critical issue of smart contract security. We aim to foster interdisciplinary collaboration between computer science and economics to drive future blockchain research. Finally, we hope this paper will inspire further investigation into new solutions for trustless DEXs, with a strong emphasis on security. This paper introduces the E-value, a utility designed to assess the sensitivity of probabilistic inferences when data is missing. By leveraging the decentralized and transparent nature of Blockchain, BFL offers an effective solution to the challenges faced by IoV. The study's primary contributions are as follows: (i) A comprehensive review of existing FL research within the IoV context; (ii) An analysis of the advantages and limitations of Blockchain for IoV applications; (iii) A thorough examination of the proposed BFL framework; and (iv) A detailed discussion of BFL's benefits and constraints in addressing IoV challenges. The paper concludes by outlining the framework's potential for IoV and suggesting directions for future research. By integrating Blockchain with FL, this approach provides a robust solution for secure and privacy-preserving data exchange in IoV applications. Furthermore, BFL enhances the security and privacy of vehicular networks by enabling vehicles to share data without exposing raw information. This cryogenic infrastructure includes a 160-liter dilution refrigerator, where the cold stage accommodates up to 20 helium-vapor-cooled shielding layers for up to 128 qubits. The installation process was completed in just 12 hours, and the system has already achieved an internal temperature of 10 millikelvin. This paper details the design and construction of the cold system, as well as the strategies employed to minimize thermal loads during installation. Additionally, it outlines the current status of a comprehensive testbed program aimed at demonstrating the scalability of large-scale, high-performance quantum computing systems. Specifically, the paper addresses the design and implementation of a high-performance refrigeration system capable of cooling up to 128 qubits, analyzes the thermal constraints for both qubit interconnects and on-chip control electronics, and describes an integrated testbed system designed to evaluate the scalability of superconducting quantum processors. Furthermore, the paper presents an initial characterization of a high-performance refrigeration system, demonstrating that a 120-liter dilution refrigerator can cool an integrated qubit-testbed system to 10 millikelvin. Finally, it presents a high-performance quantum computing testbed system, which was established in the coldest stage of a newly installed 160-liter dilution refrigerator at Fermilab. This testbed features a quantum processor with a quantum capacity of up to 128 qubits, utilizing a two-dimensional planar transmon architecture. The processor is controlled by a fully superconducting, multi-channel, high-bandwidth RF-multiplexed architecture, and the system demonstrates the ability to perform qubit initialization, coherent control, and readout at 10 millikelvin. This testbed system is designed to facilitate the study of large-scale, high-performance quantum computing systems. The paper concludes by discussing the current status of this testbed system, including its capability to cool up to 128 qubits, the integration of a quantum processor with up to 128 qubits, and the implementation of a high-bandwidth RF-multiplexed architecture for qubit control and readout. The testbed system is currently being used to demonstrate the scalability of large-scale, high-performance quantum computing systems. The paper also discusses the future of the testbed system, including plans to upgrade the quantum processor to up to 256 qubits

Cryptocurrency, a digital asset functioning as a medium of exchange, has garnered significant interest from both the public and the programming community. This surge has led to a proliferation of libraries and resources designed to facilitate the creation of cryptocurrency-related software. However, these resources often contain errors, and developers frequently lack awareness of these flaws, resulting in the deployment of buggy applications. While numerous studies have examined how developers discover cryptocurrency misinformation, there remains a gap in understanding how such misuses actually occur. This paper presents an investigation into Python cryptocurrency misuses extracted from the Python Package Index. Our analysis reveals that most misuses stem from incorrect code usage, with a substantial portion being vulnerable to security threats. Furthermore, we demonstrate that code coverage testing is an effective method for identifying these misuses, even in scenarios where existing tests are scarce. This research is the first of its kind to examine real-world cryptocurrency misuses, offering valuable insights for developers to prevent the introduction of flawed applications. Additionally, it underscores the utility of code coverage testing for detecting such issues. To support this research, we have released a novel dataset comprising Python cryptocurrency packages and their corresponding misuses, which is publicly accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1999/py-crypto-misuses. The code used for analysis is available on GitHub at https://github.com/abhishekgupta1999/py-crypto-misuses. Our findings are also published as a news item on the ACM News website: https://news.acm.org/article/2022/09/28/extracting-real-world-cryptocurrency-misuses-with-code-coverage-testing. Our source code is also featured in the Code4SE repository: https://github.com/CodeSE/Codes4Research/tree/main/PyCryptoMisuses. Additionally, this work is included in the News item Extracting Real-World Cryptocurrency Misuses with Code Coverage Testing, available at https://news.acm.org/search/search-result?query=Extracting+Real-World+Cryptocurrency+Misuses+with+Code+Coverage+Testing. The repository https://github.com/CodeSE/Codes4Research/tree/main/PyCryptoMisuses is also featured in the news item Extracting Real-World Cryptocurrency Misuses with Code Coverage Testing. Finally, the paper is also presented in the publication PyCryptoMisuses: A Dataset of Python Cryptocurrency Packages and Their Misuses, which can be found at https://dl.acm.org/doi/10

Semantic tag prediction relies on images paired with extensive datasets containing image-text pairs. While current approaches typically depend on manual annotations, we introduce WORTH, a novel system that automatically generates semantic tags by integrating three distinct sources: (i) an image encoder that extracts features from visual input, (ii) a large-scale encoder trained on textual Wikipedia articles, and (iii) human-contributed local knowledge from crowd-sourced question-answering platforms. WORTH demonstrates a significant reduction in training time compared to existing methods while maintaining or exceeding semantic tag generation performance. The WORTH framework includes a WORTH core model for tag prediction and an auxiliary model for image retrieval. We trained the WORTH core model on the VisualWiki dataset, which contains over 1.5 million image-text pairs. Our results indicate that WORTH outperforms other state-of-the-art methods in tag generation accuracy and achieves state-of-the-art performance in image retrieval on the Wikipedia Image Search (WIS) dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepLearningRadboud/WORTH.

This study introduces NuSPAN, a novel class of proximal mean networks designed for the seismic reflectivity recovery task. Sparse modeling is a widely used approach in this domain, typically relying on the $l_0$ norm to enforce sparsity. However, directly minimizing the $l_0$ norm is computationally prohibitive; consequently, the relaxed $l_1$ norm is often employed as a surrogate. While effective for signal detection, the $l_1$ norm introduces non-zero values at non-analytic signal interfaces, which degrades the accuracy of interface location estimation. To address these limitations, we propose a new family of models termed "nonuniform sparse models," which are specifically tailored to the seismic reflectivity recovery problem. We then develop a new family of proximal mean models, NuSPAN, which serves as a proximal mean representation of nonuniform sparse models. NuSPAN is constructed to be amenable to efficient mean-type optimization. Furthermore, we establish a universal proximal mean architecture for NuSPAN and devise a universal mean-type algorithm to solve the corresponding optimization problem. Experimental results demonstrate that NuSPAN outperforms existing methods in terms of both sparsity and recovery accuracy. The source code is publicly accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenchenWang1994/NuSPAN}. Additional details regarding the NuSPAN model and code can be found in our preprint \cite{wang2021nonuniform}. The preprint is available at \url{https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.00001}. This paper serves as a technical report on our work described in \cite{wang2021nonuniform}. This paper presents semigroups of composition operators acting on the space BMOA$\Gamma$(\phi), which consists of analytic functions possessing square-integrable non-tangential gradient extensions to the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, where $\Gamma$(\phi) is defined by an integrable weight function $\phi$. We derive sufficient conditions for BMOA$(\phi)$ to remain closed under these composition operators and investigate the conditions under which such operators are compact and bounded. Furthermore, we examine semigroups generated by linear composition operators and operator integrals linked to holomorphic self-maps of $\mathbb{D}$. Our analysis focuses on the compactness and boundedness of these semigroups and establishes criteria for the strong and uniform convergence of their orbits. Additionally, we explore the compactness of linear composition operators and their adjoints on BMOA$(\phi)$, as well as their commutators and weighted commutators. Finally, we address the compactness of integral operators associated with holomorphic vector fields on BMOA$(\phi)$. Throughout the study, we provide sufficient conditions for operators to be compact, bounded, or quasi-nuclear, incorporating a variety of novel examples and counterexamples. Notably, our findings extend to other spaces, including Q$(K)$, $\mathcal{B}$(\phi), and Dir$(\phi)$. Key concepts encompass BMOA$(\phi)$, holomorphic vector fields, and the compactness of weighted operator commutators. We introduce a data analysis technique designed to identify universal finite-size corrections in ground state wavefunctions of integrable models. This method amalgamates data from two distinct integrable models by matching their wavefunction overlaps. As a proof-of-concept, we apply this approach to the XXZ spin chain, successfully isolating the Haagerup model. By analyzing the universal finite-length corrections specific to the Haagerup model, we derive its conformal data. Furthermore, this technique enables the extraction of conformal data for other integrable models without requiring prior knowledge, facilitating a straightforward classification based on the extracted parameters. Finally, we demonstrate that this method can be applied to extract the conformal data of the critical Ising model. This data extraction procedure is implemented via an open-source Python package named `universal_corrections`. Part-of-speech (POS) tagging, which assigns categorical labels to words, has traditionally been treated as a deterministic task. However, we argue that uncertainty inherent in sparsely covered historical corpora should be modeled as a stochastic process. To achieve this, we introduce forecasting, a new method for generating future time series. We present Forecasting-Tagging, a framework that adapts a state-of-the-art forecasting model to dependably handle the uncertainty in historical collections. Evaluated on the Old English Corpus, our approach demonstrates that Stochastic Fisher-Tanner tagging, when enhanced with forecasting, delivers reliable POS annotations for terms outside the scope of modern reference data. Furthermore, our method surpasses the current leading stochastic Tagger, achieving state-of-the-art performance in both accuracy and reliability. These superior characteristics make our system the most dependable tool for annotating historical collections, particularly for terms absent from modern linguistic resources. The code and datasets are available at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/Forecasting-Tagging. We extend the concepts of weak and renormalized solution integrity to cover a broad spectrum of nonlinear elliptic and parabolic PDEs, encompassing those with superlinear growth. Our approach leverages the concept of precompactness derived from the abstract theory of Sobolev-orthogonal dynamics. We apply these generalized integrity principles to classical models, such as double phase double growth problems, anisotropic nonvariational double phase issues, and anisotropic $q$-Laplace double phase problems. Furthermore, we address $p$-Laplace type problems featuring a drift term, anisotropic $p$-Laplace double phase equations with drift, divergence form $p$-Laplace type problems with absorption, and a specific class of $p$-Laplace type problems with reaction terms. In the context of parabolic equations, we examine anisotropic $p$-Laplace type problems with reaction terms, focusing on their $L^\infty$ well-posedness. Additionally, we investigate anisotropic $p$-Laplace double phase problems with reaction terms, analyzing the regularity of their weak solutions. Finally, our analysis of $p$-Laplace type problems with reaction terms explores the connection between the vanishing of the reaction term and the existence of global weak solutions. Throughout these discussions, we also address the associated isoperimetric inequalities. Finally, we consider the $p$-Laplace double phase problem subject to a fractional Sobolev constraint. In this scenario, we demonstrate that the energy functional is both precompact and Fréchet differentiable, and we examine the dynamics of its associated Euler-Lagrange PDE. This analysis leads to an examination of the spectrum of the corresponding eigenvalue problem. Furthermore, we analyze the spectrum of a related fractional problem, which involves a nonlocal operator defined by a variable exponent. In this specific case, we establish the existence of a positive principal eigenvalue, which is characterized as the smallest positive root of a polynomial. The associated eigenfunctions are identified as the normalized positive eigenfunctions that maximize the eigenfunctions' $L^p$-norms. Additionally, we explore the relationship between the fractional Sobolev exponent and the Lebesgue exponent. Finally, we demonstrate that the Sobolev embedding constant for anisotropic $p$-Laplace double phase functions is bounded by the Sobolev embedding constant for anisotropic $p$-Laplace functions.

To address this, we introduce a novel error reduction strategy utilizing concealed inverse errors, which enhances the performance of existing quantum processors without requiring extra qubits. This enhanced system can subsequently achieve full error correction through quantum codes by increasing code distances. We demonstrate the utility of this proposal on quantum circuits for variational quantum algorithms and Grover's search, evaluating their error resilience on the publicly accessible IBM quantum computer, QASM-14. The results indicate that the average fidelity of our proposed method is 1.5 times higher than that of the standard approach. Furthermore, we show that this method can resolve the data-encoding problem in image search operations within a 200-qubit framework. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work to other quantum tasks. Our findings suggest that this strategy is applicable to near-term quantum processors and can be readily implemented through software updates. Additionally, the proposed approach offers a pathway toward full error correction in superconducting quantum processors with minimal hardware costs. A key challenge in analyzing multivariate data is modeling the dependence within extreme values. This becomes particularly critical in spatial statistics, where understanding the behavior of spatial extremes is essential for practical applications. In marine engineering, for instance, predicting extreme sea conditions is vital for assessing the reliability of offshore structures. This paper addresses spatial extremal dependence by predicting extreme values at specific locations given a realized vector from the remaining spatial points. To achieve this, we introduce a new class of multivariate spatial conditional peak models, which are non-parametric, non-negative, and possess a closed-form expression. The methodology is validated using a synthetic dataset and an observed dataset of significant wave heights from the North Sea. To assess uncertainty, we develop a confidence interval for the predicted response and employ a coverage probability metric to evaluate its performance. Finally, the spatial conditional peaks are applied to forecast future sea states in the North Sea. Current pre-trained vision-language models (VLPs) frequently struggle to capture the intricate details of visual data when processing image-text pairs. This limitation primarily stems from the text encoder's reliance on natural language, which often fails to align with how humans perceive images. To address this, the VT-CLIP framework generates supplementary text descriptions guided by the input image to augment standard annotations. Specifically, during pre-training, VT-CLIP integrates these extra descriptions with conventional text prompts to enhance the learning of fine-grained visual features. In fine-tuning, a visual-directed feature is extracted from the text encoder and merged with the image embedding within a contrastive learning framework to boost the model's generalization capabilities. Extensive experiments across multiple datasets demonstrate that VT-CLIP consistently surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both pre-training and fine-tuning scenarios. Controlling quantum systems is fundamental to quantum information, yet environmental noise often restricts the precision of these operations. This study introduces a universal open-loop control framework designed for noisy quantum systems governed by arbitrary matrix-valued Hamiltonians. The method employs operator switching to generate approximate dynamics for target unitaries, achieving an exponential improvement in approximation quality compared to current approaches. Additionally, the technique is applicable to a wide range of noisy systems. Simulation results demonstrate the method's effectiveness on a non-trivial example: a noisy rotation of a quantum state using a system with an unknown Hamiltonian. The paper concludes by outlining potential future extensions. Keywords: Quantum control, Open-loop control. We provide a concise proof of the Segments theorem extended to the quaternionic case, utilizing an alternative approach that deepens our comprehension of the theorem's nature and reveals its intrinsically algebraic core. Additionally, we derive a corollary that offers a novel proof of the original Segments result using standard real inner product space techniques, while a second corollary demonstrates that the theorem remains valid within an abstract framework where the inner product is merely required to be anti-linear. Finally, we present a new perspective on the proof by employing techniques from topological K-theory. Throughout this paper, we explicitly track the coefficients and models used; in fact, we construct spectral versions of both Clifford algebras and their associated Grassmannians. Our approach leverages the recently developed Boardman-Holm type model for quaternionic Plateau cylinders, which is constructed from a spectral version of the Grassmannian of 1-dimensional subspaces. We establish that this spectral Grassmannian is equivalent to the Boardman-Holm model based on our findings. Furthermore, we have formulated spectral versions of both the Segments and Plateau theorems. We anticipate that this work will facilitate the formulation of "quaternionic Boardman-Holm techniques" within homotopy theory. Ultimately, we believe that spectral real inner product spaces will become an essential component of topological algebra. This manuscript is a revised and expanded edition of the author's PhD thesis. Quantitative analysis in radiology and digital pathology frequently involves intricate annotations by clinicians and AI models, such as pixel-level segmentation, bounding boxes, and performance metrics. These annotations are essential for evaluating AI performance and guiding clinical decisions. However, the current landscape of annotation formats is fragmented, with various tools supporting diverse and non-interoperable standards. This diversity creates significant hurdles for researchers and clinicians, particularly in multi-institutional settings where quantitative results must be shared. To address this, we introduce Highdicom, a Python framework designed to encode image labels and machine learning results within the DICOM standard. As an extension of the established medical imaging standard, DICom facilitates seamless interoperability and compatibility with existing medical imaging infrastructure. Highdicom offers a comprehensive suite of classes for creating and managing annotations, alongside a library of sample datasets to streamline development. The framework includes a validator to ensure strict DICOM compliance and a converter that generates standard JSON output for compatibility with popular annotation tools. By providing a robust and accessible solution for encoding image labels, Highdicom serves as a valuable resource for the broader medical imaging community. This paper introduces a new surface term for the Einstein-Hilbert action specifically for extremal surfaces. When integrated over the extended domain of an extremal surface—defined by the vanishing of both its induced metric and extrinsic curvature—this term yields Noether charges that align with those of black hole extremal solutions sharing the same asymptotic symmetry. Utilizing this formulation, we derive the covariant expression for the soft graviton charge associated with an extremal surface. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the soft algebra generated by these charges closes into the Virasoro algebra. Finally, applying the Cardy formula to this soft Virasoro algebra yields the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of black holes. These findings provide additional support for the hypothesis that entanglement entropy corresponds to the entropy of soft gravitons. The study is conducted in four-dimensional spacetime with spherical symmetry. The derived expressions for the soft charge and Virasoro algebra are expected to be generalizable to higher dimensions and more complex solutions. Additionally, the no-ether-bound condition is examined, with the conclusion that entanglement entropy can be interpreted as the Noether charge of an extremal surface located at the boundary of the entanglement region. This extremal surface exhibits a vanishing extrinsic curvature and an induced metric proportional to the square of a small parameter. The analysis also extends to other types of extremal surfaces, including planar and strip geometries. The resulting expressions for soft charges and the Virasoro algebra are subsequently generalized to $D$ dimensions. Finally, the relationship between entanglement entropy and soft charges is explored through the lens of holographic duality. By treating the entanglement region as an extremal surface within the dual AdS space, we show that its area equals the entropy of soft gravitons. This result is further corroborated by the successful derivation of the black hole entropy using the soft charge and Virasoro algebra formulations developed in this work. The conclusion is reached that the soft charge of an extremal surface is fundamentally equivalent to its area. These results are also applicable to other types of extremal surfaces, such as those representing entanglement regions. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these findings for the physics of black holes. Specifically, it is argued that the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy of a black hole can be understood as the entropy of soft gravitons within an extremal surface, thereby offering a potential explanation for the black hole information paradox. The discussion is limited to spherical symmetry. Finally

Deep learning has proven highly effective for DNA sequence analysis, yet most existing models rely on extensive, specialized training data. Consequently, applying these methods to tasks like identifying transcription factor binding sites or predicting chromatin accessibility is often impractical due to data scarcity. This study introduces a novel unsupervised embedding learning approach for DNA sequences. By adapting self-supervised language models originally developed for natural language processing, we generate sequence embeddings that capture higher-order sequence features. When tested on downstream classification tasks, these embeddings achieve performance comparable to or superior to supervised deep learning models, even when trained on extremely limited datasets. This success is attributed to the embedding model's ability to implicitly learn fundamental biological properties of DNA. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these embeddings can facilitate the discovery of new biological concepts, such as a previously unidentified class of transcription factor binding sites. Finally, we explore the application of this technique to clustering DNA sequences, offering a potential solution to a long-standing challenge in genomics. To support this research, we have released an open-source framework for unsupervised embedding learning, which can be accessed at https://github.com/alextseng/DNA-Embedding. Our code and results are publicly available at https://github.com/alextseng/DNA-Embedding. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation under grant numbers 1908443 and 1943242. The epitaxial synthesis of bulk crystals of V$_2$O$_3$ on Al$_2$O$_3$(0001) has enabled the creation of high-quality, epitaxial ultrathin films. These films exhibit a metal-insulator transition (MIT) upon cooling, which shifts to lower temperatures as the film thickness diminishes. This transition is attributed to the reduced stability of the metallic state in thin films. Conversely, the MIT in surface-modified v$_2$O$_3$ films, specifically those coated with MgO, occurs at significantly lower temperatures than in unmodified films. This observation indicates that the MIT in these systems is not solely governed by thickness. Furthermore, the surface-modified films display a spin-ordered antiferromagnetic ground state even at temperatures below 1 K, a phase that remains elusive in unmodified v$_2$O$_3$ films. This suggests that the interaction between the v$_2$O$_3$ film and the MgO substrate stabilizes the antiferromagnetic metallic phase. These findings underscore the critical role of interfaces in the physical properties of transition metal oxides. The study also confirms that v$_2$O$_3$ serves as an ideal model system for investigating the interplay between interface effects and electronic correlations. Finally, the results demonstrate that the growth of v$_2$O$_3$ films can be optimized to tailor their physical properties. This capability is crucial for advancing the field of oxide heterostructures, where the interaction between two different oxides can be harnessed to generate novel properties. This work was conducted at the Max-Planck-Institut für Struktur und Funktionalität der Materie in Düsseldorf, Germany, and at the Max-Planck-Institut für Festkörperforschung in Stuttgart, Germany. This paper investigates the Lie-Poisson framework for systems adhering to $\mathfrak{g}^*$-equivariant Lagrange 1-forms, where $\mathfrak{g}^*$ denotes the dual of a Lie algebra $\mathfrak{g}$ acting on the Lagrangian. We demonstrate that such systems can be locally transformed into one involving the trivial Lagrange 1-form through what we term a \emph{clebsch conjugation}. This process involves a gauge transformation of the Lagrange 1-form followed by a non-linear canonical transformation of the underlying coordinates. We show that this clebsch conjugation can be realized through either of two equivalent methods: (1) solving the associated Euler-Lagrange equations to derive a Lie-Poisson vector field, followed by identifying a gauge-equivalent vector field within the same equivalence class; or (2) utilizing the correspondence between equivariant Lagrange 1-forms and their associated geometric Lagrange functions. Furthermore, we provide a characterization of the admissible equivariant Lagrange 1-forms based on Fréchet derivative considerations, which can inform the selection of suitable forms for specific problems. Finally, the paper includes several examples to illustrate the procedure. One of these examples involves a system on the rigid body dual $SO(3)$, which, following the clebsch conjugation, can be locally reduced to a system on the affine space $\mathbb{R}^3$. We also examine the relationship between this newly identified class of Lie-Poisson frameworks and those previously explored by Bolsinov and Omel'yanov. Additionally, we demonstrate that the established equivalence between Lagrange and Poisson frameworks applies in the context of equivariant Lagrange functions and is compatible with the clebsch conjugation. Finally, we show that the dynamics of both examples can be described using Hamiltonian vector fields on appropriate cotangent bundles. These findings are particularly relevant for the study of Hamiltonian extensions of Lie-Poisson systems, as they significantly expand the pool of candidate extensions. Specifically, we illustrate how to generate candidate extensions for a Lie-Poisson vector field equivalent to that of the Euler top by performing a Hamiltonian extension on the locally equivalent system defined on $\mathbb{R}^6$. Finally, we provide evidence suggesting that the Lie algebra of the resulting extended system is not the semi-direct product of the original algebra with $\mathbb{R}$, contrary to the standard case. Similar extensions have been identified in the literature

We introduce a thorough investigation of 2018 sub-prime-field planetary anomalies detected by the Korean Microlensing Exoplanet NTeWorkSystem (KMTNet), aiming to establish a robust framework for future direct planetary research. Our analysis incorporates 118 light curves, with 2018 events serving as the foundation for this study. We present the most extensive and precise set of planetary parameters for 68 events, including 20 planets with well-constrained parameters and 45 planets featuring poorly-constrained parameters. Additionally, we identify 128 planets with poorly-constrained parameters that are likely to be resolved by upcoming data releases. We have developed a novel method for calculating planetary parameters, which will be the sole approach used for future KMTNet direct-planet analyses. This work represents the first step toward a more rigorous examination of KMTNet microlensing planets. The extensive list of planets with well-constrained parameters offers a unique opportunity to study the statistical properties of the planetary mass function. We have compiled all available data for 68 events, enabling the calculation of planetary parameters and the subsequent analysis of the resulting planetary population. The analysis of the planetary population derived from well-constrained events is presented in the companion paper (Paper VII). This paper is part of a series; the sequence is as follows: Paper I, II, III, IV, V, VI, and VII. This paper is also referenced in the following: Paper VIII. Building upon the previous paper in this series, we introduce conservation principles for comoving entropy, comoving Burgers' equation, specific entropy, and specific enthalpy. These principles serve as necessary and sufficient conditions for the adiabaticity of a fluid. In the context of the compressible comoving frame, these principles are equivalent to the adiabaticity condition expressed via the specific enthalpy, as detailed in the subsequent paper in this series. For specific applications, such as stellar models, we demonstrate that the conservation of comoving entropy is equivalent to the von Zeipel theorem. Furthermore, we show that the conservation of specific entropy within a comoving frame is equivalent to the first law of thermodynamics in that same frame. Finally, we provide an overview of various conservation principles from this series and their respective applications. A notable outcome is the derivation of the Hubeny equation, which provides an explicit formula for the luminosity gradient in adiabatic stars. Additionally, we establish an equivalent formulation of the first law of thermodynamics for the compressible Euler equations, which is particularly useful for numerical computations. This work is the second of two companion papers; the first will derive the conservation principles of this series, while the third will generalize these principles to barotropic compressible fluids. The remaining series will be completed by the fourth paper, which will generalize the principles to the compressible Navier-Stokes equations, and the fifth paper, which will apply these principles to the shallow water equations. The final paper in the series will summarize the entire collection. This manuscript serves as a companion to the first paper in this series, which will derive the conservation principles discussed here. The third paper in the series will utilize these principles to derive the conservation laws of the comoving frame for the compressible Navier-Stokes equations. Subsequently, the fourth and fifth papers in the series will apply these conservation laws to the conservation equations of the compressible Navier-Stokes equations and the shallow water equations, respectively. Finally, the fifth paper will conclude the series by summarizing all results from this collection. This study evaluates the performance of various machine learning algorithms in predicting whether a bank loan will default. We processed a binary-coded NPL dataset by applying feature engineering and selecting significant variables through feature importance analysis using the Random Forest model. Subsequently, we trained and tested multiple classifiers—including Random Forest, KNN, Decision Tree, SVM, Naive Bayes, and Logistic Regression—on the processed data. The results indicate that the Random Forest algorithm achieved the highest accuracy at 96.11%, followed by KNN at 95.23%. Based on the analysis, Random Forest is determined to be the most effective model for this specific dataset. Finally, we propose several strategies for future enhancements. We anticipate that these models will prove valuable for assessing default risks and aiding decision-making processes. Additionally, the insights regarding feature significance may assist in formulating new policies. This research aims to empower small and medium enterprises (SMEs) to make more informed decisions. Ultimately, the proposed machine learning models are expected to enhance operational efficiency and effectiveness within banking institutions.

This work presents an extended abstract of a recent paper that defines the colorfull symmetric functions of Dyck paths with a specific number of peaks of a given length, as well as Young tableaux where no two cells in the second column share the same color. These concepts correspond to the case $q=1$, which represents the weight of Dyck paths under a weight function that increments by $q$ each time a horizontal step is taken, and denotes the evaluation of a $q$-rook polynomial on a specific shape. Leveraging $q$-rook theory, we establish a bijection between colored Dyck paths and non-rectangular partitions to demonstrate that the resulting functions are complete Sheffer sequences within umbral calculus. Furthermore, they are identified as the complete Bell polynomials with a scaling factor of $-1$, which encompass Stirling numbers of the first kind. Additionally, we provide an explicit expression for the generating function of colorful symmetric functions based on peaks, utilizing q-Stirling numbers of the first kind, and offer a bijection that proves the combinatorial identity linking Bell numbers to Stirling numbers of the second kind. Finally, we present a novel combinatorial interpretation for the combinatorial sum formula of Stirling numbers of the first kind. Finally, we demonstrate that the generating function for colored Bell numbers corresponds to the evaluation of a $q$-rook polynomial on a staircase shape. As a consequence, we derive a new combinatorial identity for Stirling numbers of the first kind. This research was conducted in collaboration with J. Bonilla, J. Bonilla, J. Bravo, and J. J. Bravo. This paper introduces a novel convolutional architecture designed to streamline image recognition processes. By leveraging orientation-based calculations, the method reduces the dimensionality of convolutional filters, thereby cutting down the total number of parameters. The proposed model was successfully applied to three standard benchmark tasks: MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet. The findings indicate that while the orientation-based model features fewer parameters and lower computational costs, it delivers comparable or superior performance in terms of accuracy and F1 scores. Notably, the most significant improvements were observed on the MNIST dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1993/obcnn. Let $G$ be a finite group acting on a finite set $X$. We define the novel concept of a *$G$-curved linear interval* as a specific subset $I \subseteq X$ satisfying certain $G$-invariant properties. For any $G$-curved linear interval $I$, we derive a formula expressing the cardinality of $I$ using the linear characters of the stabilizer subgroups $G_x$ for each $x \in I$. This approach yields new formulas for determining the sizes of sets defined by entrywise inequalities in permutation matrices, as well as sets determined by inequalities among monomial counts in monomial matrices. Furthermore, this work introduces a novel relative trace equation for linear characters of finite groups, which serves as a non-central extension of the classical sum of values of a linear character equation. The theory of $G$-curved linear intervals is supported by geometric intuition regarding affine spaces over finite fields under finite group actions. Finally, we outline potential generalizations of this work to other areas within representation theory and finite group theory. The relative trace equation is anticipated to find applications in the design of symmetric designs, coding theory, and design theory. The novel formula for the cardinality of $G$-curved linear intervals is expected to have applications in probability theory, combinatorics, and related probability fields. Additionally, the proposed framework may benefit finite geometry, combinatorial designs, and designs with specified parameters. The study may also have implications for finite mathematics, algebra, and calculus. Finally, the theory of $G$-curved linear intervals could contribute to the fields of statistics and stochastic processes. This work may also influence the theory of random graphs, random matrices, and random matrices with specific eigenvalue distributions. The theory of $G$-curved linear intervals is expected to have applications in the study of finite fields, algebraic curves, and surfaces. The proposed framework may benefit the study of projective spaces, algebraic varieties, and their associated cohomology theories. The theory of $G$-curved linear intervals is anticipated to have applications in the study of modular forms, automorphic forms, and their associated L-functions. The proposed framework may benefit the study of arithmetic statistics, analytic number theory, and combinatorial number theory. The theory of $G$-curved linear intervals is expected to have applications in the study of dynamical systems, ergodic theory, and measure theory. The proposed framework may benefit the study of ergodic methods

This study presents a substantial re-examination of the top quark mass, incorporating the most precise measurements of the differential cross section for single top quark production. The analysis is grounded in the framework of the Standard Model effective field theory (SMEFT), which facilitates the systematic inclusion of higher-dimensional operators that may arise from physics beyond the Standard Model. By employing the latest results from the ATLAS and CMS collaborations regarding inclusive and semi-inclusive (lepton+jets) differential cross sections for single top production, we determine the numerical values of relevant SMEFT coefficients. These coefficients directly influence the top quark's decay width and the kinematic distributions of its decay products. Our findings indicate a 10% deviation in the Standard Model prediction for the decay width, which translates to an approximately 2 GeV difference in the corresponding invariant mass of the decay products. This level of precision is comparable to the masses of other charged Standard Model fermions, suggesting that the electroweak symmetry breaking sector and/or its connection to fermion masses warrants further investigation. Additionally, we establish a lower limit of 468.5 GeV for the mass of the lightest neutral fermion, assuming the decay proceeds through a dimension-7 operator. This result is consistent with prior studies conducted under similar assumptions. Given that the top quark's mass and couplings are intrinsically linked to the electroweak sector, our findings may also have broader implications for the electroweak sector itself. Finally, we outline the potential for this approach to be applied to Higgs boson couplings, which are also tied to the electroweak symmetry breaking sector. The findings of this work could have significant implications for the future of the LHC and the development of the next generation of particle accelerators. The accompanying Jupyter notebook provides a detailed, step-by-step reproduction of the analysis. A graph $G$ is defined as nearly regular if the disparity between its maximum and minimum degrees does not exceed 1. In 1998, Chetwynd and Schellwoll demonstrated that any $k$-regular graph $G$ with an even number of vertices $n$ admits a vertex partition into two sets $V_1$ and $V_2$ such that the minimum degree $\delta(V_1)$ and maximum degree $\Delta(V_2)$ within the induced subgraphs are both at least $k(n-2)/2n$. Building upon this finding, we generalize it to apply to nearly regular graphs. Furthermore, we establish a local extension of this result by showing that for nearly regular graphs, a sufficiently large subset $V_1$ can be identified such that there exists a subgraph $H$ where $V_1 \subseteq V(H)$, satisfying $\delta(H) \ge k(n-2)/2n$ and $\Delta(H) \le (k+1)(n-2)/2n$. Additionally, we introduce the concept of consecutively edge-tinted graphs, proving that every nearly regular graph $G$ with $n$ vertices admits a coloring of its edges using $k+1$ colors such that the sum of degrees of any vertex across all colors falls within the range $[k(n-2)/2n, (k+1)(n-2)/2n]$. Finally, we examine random nearly regular graphs, demonstrating that with high probability, any partition of the vertex set $V$ into two subsets results in induced subgraphs where the degree of every vertex is at least $d(n-1)/2n$. In the probabilistic analysis, we further establish that with high probability, nearly regular graphs $G$ exist where no partition of $V$ into two sets yields induced subgraphs both having a minimum degree of at least $k(n-1)/2n$. The theoretical foundation for our work is the Lopsided Lovász Local Lemma. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread fear and has been addressed through various diagnostic methods, including PCR testing, antigen detection, and serology. Among imaging techniques, Chest X-rays (CXRs) have been utilized to identify the virus. However, due to the superior accuracy of Low-dose Computed Tomography (LDCT) scans in detecting COVID-19, this study aims to leverage LDCT images for diagnosis. We introduce a Two-stage Time-distributed Capsule Network (TD-DCN) designed to classify and localize COVID-19 within LDCT images. The network's first stage employs a Time-distributed CNN (TD-CNN) to extract features from 3D slices, which are subsequently processed by the second stage, the TD-DCN, to classify and localize the disease. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed model achieves a COVID-19 detection accuracy of 99.61%, surpassing existing state-of-the-art methods. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar123456789/TD-DCN. This paper introduces a mathematical framework for spatial efficiency within low-Earth orbit, designed to facilitate a systematic analysis of the strategic and operational dynamics governing the deployment, operation, and termination of LEO constellations. The model incorporates key variables such as orbital altitude, orbital and equatorial inclination, and the counts of active and de-orbited satellites. By generating three-dimensional representations of occupied orbital space, we can comprehensively quantify the volume utilized by a constellation throughout its operational lifespan. We present results for various existing and proposed constellations, including Iridium, Globalstar, and Starlink, and discuss implications for future space traffic management. Additionally, we address limitations in current international legal frameworks regarding the management of orbital and frequency resources. Finally, we propose a computational game theory approach to model the strategic interactions between multiple constellation operators, aiming to identify stable equilibria in fleet size and space requirements. This methodology could provide a scientific basis for regulatory decisions concerning multi-constellation deployments. The findings of this study are applicable to a broad range of LEO missions, including those for global communications, remote sensing, and space-based surveillance. The code used to develop this model is publicly accessible on GitHub. Our methodology and model are also available on arXiv-preprint servers. This study introduces a new framework for generating coarse quadrilateral meshes with uniform element sizes on CAD models. The approach begins by projecting CAD surfaces onto a 3D Euclidean grid, where each voxel represents a surface patch. By treating these voxels as a lattice graph, the method constructs a coarse quadrilateral mesh. The proposed system is an integer linear optimization tool capable of producing high-quality meshes even for complex CAD geometries. Furthermore, the mesh refinement process is entirely automated, eliminating the need for user intervention. Experimental results demonstrate that the tool can efficiently generate coarse quadrilaterial meshes for various CAD models, including those with intricate CAD features. Additionally, the tool is now publicly accessible. The accompanying website offers a user-friendly interface that requires no interaction, allowing users to upload CAD files and download the resulting coarse quadrilateral meshes. This capability facilitates the creation of an open-source mesh database, which can be utilized for training and evaluating automated mesh generation techniques. The entire generation process, from uploading the CAD file to producing the mesh, takes approximately 10 seconds. The results indicate that the tool is highly effective for Coarse Mesh Generation (CMG) and represents a significant advancement toward fully automated CMG workflows. The tool is expected to contribute substantially to research in automated CMG. To our knowledge, this tool marks the first to achieve Coarse Mesh Generation without any requirement for user interaction. This paper derives formulas for the expected value and variance of the sample correlation coefficient under various data arrangements. For each arrangement, we determine an optimal arrangement that maximizes the expected value of the sample correlation through a systematic search. Furthermore, we propose an exact variable transformation to generate data arrangements exhibiting a specified target value for the sample correlation expectation. Additionally, we introduce a general criterion for evaluating the validity of statistical tests for the sample correlation coefficient, regardless of the underlying data distribution. Finally, we recommend a new class of distribution-free tests for the sample correlation coefficient and perform power comparisons against existing tests using various data arrangements. Simulation results indicate that the proposed tests outperform all competing methods in terms of test power. Consequently, these new tests are valuable tools for analyzing paired samples, particularly when the data follows a specific arrangement. To facilitate their application, we provide an R package named \texttt{OptCorr} that includes the implementation of these tests along with supporting functions and data. This package is freely available for download. Additionally, an R package containing simulation results for various tests and data arrangements will be released for download. Both packages can be accessed at: https://sites.google.com/view/optcorr. The contents of this paper are structured as follows: Section 2 reviews relevant literature; Section 3 presents analytical formulas for the expected value and variance of the sample correlation; Section 4 examines different data arrangements; Section 5 proposes new tests for the sample correlation; Section 6 presents simulation results comparing the performance of these tests; and Section 7 provides concluding remarks.
