This paper examines linear bandit frameworks featuring action sets with varying cardinalities, distinguishing between models where the agent selects from all available options and those where selection is constrained. We derive upper bounds on regret for both scenarios and analyze the implications for inference. Furthermore, we introduce a practical method to compute an agent's regret in both settings, leveraging the observation that the bandit problem can be represented as a linear program. Our numerical experiments confirm that this linear programming approach is efficient and capable of generating tight regret bounds. Additionally, our findings indicate that while inference is feasible when actions are chosen from the entire set, it remains an open challenge when action sets are restricted. Finally, we discuss potential extensions of this work. The study is supported by grants from the ANR (ANR-17-CE25-0011), the ERC (724467), and the CNRS PICS (71501P). The associated code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/PranjalNigam/Linear_Bandits}. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews related literature; Section 3 introduces the linear bandit problem and defines regret; Section 4.1 presents a general regret upper bound; Section 5 focuses on a single agent, deriving lower bounds for the $\mathcal{K}$-Armed Bandit and a $\log(n)$ lower bound for the linear program, while also proposing a new lower bound for cases where the agent chooses the subset size; Section 6 addresses multiple agents, deriving a lower bound for $\mathcal{K}$-Armed Bandits and proving that inference is unattainable when agent identities are hidden; the Conclusion begins in Section 7. The initial authors contributed equally to this research. Keywords: Multi-Armed Bandits, Inference, Linear Programming.

In gapless graphene, the valley Chern number lacks physical significance because valley degenerate electrons fail to generate valley-dependent spin- and valley-polarized orbital Hall currents. However, when gap-opening mechanisms break time-reversal symmetry, a finite valley Chern number emerges, enabling a nontrivial valley Hall effect. In this study, we demonstrate that the orbital Hall effect can substitute for the valley Hall effect in certain gap-opening scenarios. Specifically, under a moiré potential, the valley degree of freedom becomes irrelevant, valley degeneracy is lost, and valley-polarized states merge with spin-polarized states. Consequently, a valley Hall effect is impossible under these conditions. Instead, we observe that valley-polarized orbital Hall currents can substitute for both spin- and valley-polarized ordinary Hall currents. Furthermore, we show that the valley-dependent Berry curvature is directly proportional to the spin-dependent Berry curvature of corresponding quasiparticles, which is essential for understanding valley-polarized orbital Hall currents. Finally, our findings indicate that the orbital Hall effect can be substituted for the valley Hall effect in various gap-opening scenarios, including those involving moiré potentials, exchange interactions, and structural defects. Notably, the valley Hall effect in graphene can be restored by introducing a valley-reversing boundary. These results hold significant promise for enhancing valleytronics and spintronics within graphene-based devices. Additionally, our results suggest that the valley Chern number is not a robust topological invariant in gap-opening scenarios where the valley degree of freedom is suppressed. To address this, we propose a novel Chern number formulation that accounts for orbital hybridization, which can be applied to diverse gap-opening scenarios. We also demonstrate that this new definition of the Chern number accurately captures the orbital magnetic moment of band-edge electrons. Finally, we show that this Chern number can be experimentally measured through Hall resistance. These findings are expected to advance the development of graphene-based spintronics and valleytronics. Moreover, our proposed definition of the Chern number is applicable to other two-dimensional materials, such as transition metal dichalcogenides. Our results further suggest that the valley Hall effect in these materials can be enhanced by incorporating structural defects. Overall, our findings provide a foundation for realizing efficient spin- and valley-polarized electronic devices based on two-dimensional materials. Additionally, our Chern number formulation is expected to facilitate the discovery of new Chern insulators and topological superconductors. Graph Neural Architectures (GNA) have recently demonstrated significant potential for various Graph Machine Learning (GML) tasks. However, their susceptibility to data contamination remains an underexplored vulnerability. This paper investigates how graph data contamination can be strategically exploited to compromise GNs. Specifically, we introduce a new reinforcement learning framework designed to automatically identify and label the minimal data required to induce specific target behaviors within a given GNL. Experimental results on real-world graph datasets indicate that our approach is highly effective, successfully achieving the desired behaviors with very small datasets. Furthermore, we find that the method is robust across diverse GNL architectures and graph inducings. Finally, we highlight the implications of our findings for GNL security and propose strategies to mitigate these risks. To the best of our knowledge, this represents the first work to explore data contamination in GN architectures. Accurate alignment of catalogues from different surveys is essential for multi-survey photometric redshift studies. This process involves matching objects across surveys with varying photometric bands and spatial resolutions, which necessitates accounting for systematic differences in positional measurements. We introduce a Bayesian astrometry augmentation method that enhances object position estimation by integrating multi-band photometry. Our approach utilizes a new probabilistic model for point source centroids that leverages the information contained in a survey's PSF. We demonstrate that this model is effective for both ground and space-based surveys. By combining positional measurements from multiple surveys, we achieve more precise source positions, thereby improving cross-survey catalogue alignment. Additionally, we show that our method can be extended to generate mock catalogues for source populations with known luminosity functions, such as quasars and galaxies, which can be tested against real observations. These mock catalogues offer realistic joint position and magnitude distributions for specific source populations, facilitating more accurate pre-processing for alignment and matching. We illustrate the application of our method to a quasar catalogue created from the DESY2015A Y1A data release. We demonstrate the existence of a specific index function that ensures every hypergraph possesses a collection of minimal vertex sets that is both non-empty and countable. Furthermore, a theoretical model is proposed in which the cardinality of the family of all minimal vertex sets can exceed the total number of vertices in the hypergraph. Finally, the conditions under which a hypergraph admits a vertex set that is minimal with respect to any cardinality are explicitly characterized. The study also examines the relationship between the vertex sets and edge sets of a hypergraph. Specifically, an index function is constructed such that the resulting families of minimal vertex sets and minimal edge sets are both non-empty and countable. Additionally, we present a model where, for any infinite cardinal $\kappa$, a hypergraph exists with a family of minimal vertex sets of cardinality $\kappa$ and a family of minimal edge sets with a cardinality strictly greater than $\kappa$. Ontologies serve as formal conceptual conceptual frameworks that explicitly define concepts along with their interrelationships. While ontology visualization is a critical component of the broader ontology engineering workflow, existing visualizations struggle to represent non-hierarchical relationships effectively and fail to scale well for large ontologies. This paper introduces OntoPlot, a new visual approach designed to handle non-hierarchical structures and scale efficiently for ontology visualisation. The method was evaluated using 11 ontologies, ranging from small collections of 100 instances to large ones with over 100,000 instances. The results demonstrate that OntoPlot successfully renders these large ontologies in a readable format, offering both visual and spatial cues to assist users in navigating complex ontology structures. A user study was conducted to assess the usability of OntoPlot, and the findings indicate that the approach is user-friendly. The source code for OntoPlot is publicly accessible at https://github.com/CSSE-EPPOC/OntoPlot. Furthermore, this work is intended to contribute to the field of ontology visualization by providing a new solution and a platform for future research and development. The paper concludes by outlining the method's limitations and suggesting several avenues for future research. We present a method for enhancing semi-supervised end-to-end speech transcription by training an end-to-end model across two speech datasets featuring different noise characteristics. This approach employs a CycleGAN to establish a mapping between these distinct noisy domains and incorporates penalties designed to measure the distributional similarity of latent representations within a bottleneck layer of an autoencoder. Experiments conducted on end-to-end speech transcribers for Spanish and English demonstrate that our method surpasses the standard cross-domain training baseline. Specifically, the system achieves relative Word Error Rate reductions of 12.7% and 10.2% on test sets free of acoustic noise, respectively. Additionally, we show that the mapping network can be utilized for image denoising, attaining performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods in the field. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DeepSpeech/cyclegan-transcription. This research was conducted within the Google Research on AI for Social Impact group. Deduction serves as a fundamental cognitive process enabling intelligent agents to derive new conclusions from existing knowledge, a capability essential for robot perception, action, and navigation. While current deductive navigation approaches depend on manually designed rules and rely on agents possessing extensive world knowledge, this paper presents a framework for active deduction designed specifically for self-governing navigation. We propose a multi-agent deduction model grounded in the epistemic logic of distributed systems. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm for constructing deduction graphs that facilitates active deduction, thereby reducing the necessary number of deduction steps. Leveraging this framework, we develop the PROFOUND algorithm for active deductive navigation. PROFOUND enables robots to navigate efficiently by gathering and utilizing perceptual data. Our simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms state-of-the-art methods in terms of both deduction steps and movement steps. Additionally, PROFOUND exhibits robustness against incomplete world knowledge and partial sensor observations. Finally, we validate the PROFOUND algorithm through physical experiments conducted with a TurtleBot. The PROFOUND source code is available at https://github.com/robertkvasnak/profound-deductive-navigation. This work was supported by the Czech Science Foundation (grant 19-03033S). Thermal fractionation in non-ideal mixtures gives rise to the Soret effect, where concentration gradients form under a temperature gradient. In thermal convection driven by this phenomenon, an internal force drives thermal instability when the Soret coefficient is positive, causing light components to accumulate at hotter boundaries. This paper investigates the Soret effect in flexible colloids, where thermal forces interact with the flexibility of the molecular potential. We demonstrate that the sign of the Soret coefficient can reverse, contingent upon the specific components involved. Furthermore, we show that even when translational Soret coefficients vanish, the thermal segregation of the internal degrees of freedom can still generate a non-zero effective Soret coefficient. These insights deepen our comprehension of thermal transport in non-ideal systems and highlight the critical role of internal flexibility in driving thermal segregation. These theoretical predictions align with existing experimental data and offer new targets for future research. Finally, we examine the implications of these findings for understanding thermal transport in biological systems. To facilitate this, we introduce a framework for modeling flexible molecules that incorporates both external and internal Soret coefficients. The study utilizes a three-particle system consisting of two flexible particles and one rigid impurity, with results corroborated by molecular dynamics simulations. All numerical and computational details are available at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez-ramos/flexibility-and-soret-effect. Supplementary material can be found at https://doi.org/10.48550/arxiv.2303.07001. Additionally, the source code for the theoretical calculations is accessible at https://github.com/alejandro-fernandez-ramos/flexibility-and-soret-effect/tree/main/src. Automated Composition Evaluation (ACE) involves assessing student essays written in a target language, originally gaining significant interest due to the limited consistency of human scoring and the advent of the Evaluation task in the annual IEEE International Conference on Multimedia Learning (ICML). However, the most recent IEEE ACL Multimedia Conference (ACL-M) has not featured this evaluation domain, despite recent advancements in transformer-based language models that have yielded substantial progress in its performance. This study introduces ACE-LM, a novel ACE system built upon a pre-trained transformer-based language model. By fine-tuning a mask language modeling task with a specifically designed loss function, ACE-LM was developed to predict student essay scores. This paper details the construction of ACE-LM and reports its performance on the 2020 ACL-M machine scoring task. The results demonstrate that ACE-LM successfully predicts scores for unseen essays, achieving a Spearman's rank correlation of 0.5004 on the test set. Domain adaptation is frequently employed to enhance domain-invariant features and mitigate performance drops when models are tested on distant domains. However, these techniques often generate spurious predictions, leading to false positives. This paper introduces box reordering, an unsupervised approach for identifying false positives in domain-adaptive pedestrian identification. By leveraging distance metrics derived from state-of-the-art domain-adaptive and pedestrian identification models, box reordering enhances detection efficiency without requiring additional training. The method is straightforward and can be easily integrated into existing pipelines. Extensive experiments demonstrate that box reordering significantly reduces false positives, improving mean average precision by 11.4% on the Market-1501 dataset and 10.3% on person-person matching within the CUHK01-14 dataset. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1997/BoxReordering. Furthermore, the method has been incorporated into the `person_reid` repository, where it is used to compute mean average precision on Market-1501, CUHK01-14, and CUHK03. The results are accessible via the following links: Market-1501 (https://github.com/chenyi1997/BoxReordering/tree/master/results/market1501), CUHK01-14 (https://github.com/chenyi1997/BoxReordering/tree/master/results/cuhk0114), and CUHK03 (https://github.com/chenyi1997/BoxReordering/tree/master/results/cuhk03). The results for CUHK01-14 and CUHK03 are also available in the person_reid repository. This paper introduces a novel approach to music enhancement through spectral image transformation. By converting the spectrogram image of raw audio into the frequency domain and applying standard image enhancement techniques, we achieve improvements to the transformation in inverse space, which is then converted back to the time domain. A vocoder reconstructs the spectrogram from this enhanced domain space, and the final audio is produced by converting this restored spectrogram back into audio signals. Experiments conducted on various raw audio clips demonstrate the superiority of our method, with human evaluations confirming the enhanced quality of the improved audio. Furthermore, utilizing the Music Enhancer on Spotify, our system successfully processed multiple tracks, yielding positive user feedback. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ashwinbhat/SpotifyMusicEnhancer}. Additionally, a demo video is available at \url{https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=4242222222}. This study examines the consequences of releasing an object prematurely or during the mid-throw phase. While prior research has extensively analyzed errors in the early phase, the effects of mistakes in the late phase and the mid-throw stage remain underexplored. Our findings indicate that the late phase is the most resilient to timing errors, whereas both the mid-throw and early phases are more susceptible to timing inaccuracies. Furthermore, we observed that the late phase demonstrates greater robustness against kinematic noise compared to the other phases. Additionally, we developed a method called FauxThrow, which involves throwing a virtual ball in a mixed reality environment as if it were real. This approach facilitates investigations into the errors discussed in this work and allows for interaction with the virtual object. FauxThrow holds promise for enhancing virtual sports training and developing virtual sports games. Finally, we propose integrating this methodology into educational settings to improve learning outcomes. This paper introduces FauxThrow as a novel tool for virtual sports training and education. This paper introduces Tree Formed Decoding (TFD), a technique that integrates a neural machine translation model with a parse tree to produce a sentence-level parsed tree. TFD incorporates an additional convolutional neural network (CNN) to generate syntactic link features, which are merged with the parse tree and the original input features. These integrated features are then fed back into the neural machine translation model to enhance its decoding process. Experiments on the Microsoft Sentence-level Parsing Task demonstrate that TFD effectively improves parsing accuracy while simultaneously performing machine translation. Specifically, TFD yields an average SPM score improvement of 0.52 points across all source languages, with individual language gains ranging from 0.25 to 1.0 points. Furthermore, TFD achieves an average BLEU score increase of 1.0 points over vanilla models, with improvements varying between -0.1 and 2.4 points for specific languages. Finally, ablation studies confirm that the CNN component is essential for forming the parse tree and are crucial for achieving accurate machine translation. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/tao-liu/Tree-Formed-Decoding. Our findings indicate that TFD holds significant potential for future neural machine interpretation and parsing research. Our results suggest that TFD can achieve an average SPM score gain of up to 1.0 points over current state-of-the-art methods. This paper presents a top-down tree-forming decoding approach that leverages syntactic features to improve both parsing accuracy and machine translation performance. We introduce a tree-formed decoding method that integrates a neural machine translation model with a parse tree to generate sentence-level parse trees. By utilizing a convolutional neural network to produce syntactic link features, we embed these features into the parse tree and combine them with original features to guide the decoding process. Our experiments demonstrate that this tree-formed decoding strategy significantly enhances both parsing accuracy and machine translation quality. Source code: https://github.com/tao-liu/Tree-Formed-Decoding. Our results indicate that the proposed tree-formed decoding method can achieve an average SPM score gain of up to 1.0 compared to state-of-the-art methods. This paper details the Binding Energy Assessment Platform (BEAP), a repository of quantum chemical binding energy distributions designed for molecules and molecular fragments relevant to astrochemistry. BEAP is intended to serve as a foundational resource for the astrochemical community, facilitating the evaluation of binding energy data through a user-friendly interface. The platform offers a suite of utilities to streamline the quantum chemical assessment process and to enable data exploration and visualization, thereby supporting both researchers and students. A primary utility is the Molecular Binding Energy (MBE) calculator, which calculates binding energies for molecular systems using established protocols and a predefined library of atomic and fragment geometries. Additionally, the BEAP Explorer allows users to investigate molecular systems and analyze their corresponding binding energy distributions. This document provides an overview of the platform's capabilities and features, with a focus on its assessment and visualization tools. It also outlines the development process, including the design of the binding energy assessment protocol and the selection of atomic and fragment geometries from the MLE-MB26 database. The paper includes a demonstration of MBE calculator usage and the initial BEAP Explorer interface, which displays systems from the BEAP molecular binding energy data repository. Finally, the article concludes with a summary of BEAP's current capabilities and a vision for its future enhancements. A repository of web-based BEAP interfaces is accessible at https://beap.astrochem.org. The platform is under active development, and further details can be found at https://beap.astrochem.org/about. The study by Fushinobu and Takahashi (2019) [1] utilizes a multiplicative stochastic model featuring a sample-related lower bound for Takahashi's stochastic growth model. This framework is especially valuable for analyzing growth processes constrained by a non-zero minimum size. However, Fushinobu and Takahashi (2019) did not address the existence of the model's equilibrium state. This paper investigates the existence of equilibrium states for this stochastic growth model below a sample-related lower limit and explicitly formulates the equilibrium distribution. Furthermore, the paper analyzes the model's long-term behavior by examining the convergence of empirical distributions from simulated trajectories toward the theoretical equilibrium distribution. Finally, the research applies this model to population dynamics, specifically modeling the growth of a newly discovered nematode species. This approach offers a significant advantage over deterministic growth models, as it can analyze the dynamics of small populations where demographic stochasticity is significant. The results indicate that the species' population size stabilizes around the carrying capacity, with the magnitude of fluctuations determined by the variance parameter. These findings demonstrate the model's efficacy in describing growth processes. Additionally, the methodology for stochastic growth models with a sample-related lower limit can be extended to include upper limits. This extension would enable the description of population dynamics constrained by an upper limit, such as the maximum number of individuals in a specific habitat. This capability is highly relevant for ecological studies, where understanding how populations respond to environmental changes is crucial. By determining how both population increases and decreases are constrained, researchers can predict the impacts of various environmental factors on biodiversity. In this context, the proposed stochastic growth model with a sample-related lower limit serves as a valuable tool for ecological research. Although the paper does not address upper limits, this decision was based on the observation that most ecological research focuses on lower limits. This is because populations are often limited by a minimum size due to environmental constraints, whereas they can typically expand to fill available habitats. Consequently, the application presented in this paper is expected to be valuable for researchers in both mathematics and ecology. Specifically, mathematicians can employ this model to study complex systems, while ecologists can use it to investigate the ecological impacts of environmental changes.

Keywords: stochastic growth model, multiplicative stochastic model, lower limit, equilibrium state, ecological impact.

A primary hurdle in the emerging field of quantum advantage testing is efficiently appraising deep quantum circuits. This challenge stems from the prohibitive costs of directly sampling from such deep circuits on current hardware. We introduce a novel approximation technique for quantum advantage tests that leverages the computational power of shallow circuits by employing random projective measurements on intermediate layers. This work presents the first rigorous analysis of the statistical error inherent in this approach. Our findings indicate that the statistical error remains comparable to that of direct sampling, while utilizing circuit depth no greater than half of the original. Additionally, numerical experiments demonstrate that the observed error in our proposal is significantly lower than current experimental benchmarks for verifying quantum advantage. This research offers a fresh perspective on quantum advantage tests and establishes new standards for the benchmarking of quantum processors. Furthermore, our study advances the broader objective of developing new algorithms for verifying quantum advantage. For the Davey-Stewartson II equations, we establish that the reflection coefficient's behavior as $|k| \to \infty$ is governed by the $L^2$-norms of the x and y derivatives of the nonlinearity. This finding contrasts sharply with standard nonlinear Schrödinger equations, where the reflection coefficient is known to be analytic at $|k| = 0$. Consequently, our results provide a comprehensive description of the reflection coefficient's properties for one-dimensional non-stationary Davey-Stewartson equations, thereby extending these findings to a higher dimension. Additionally, this extension relies on the specific property that the DSIIR equation remains non-resonant even at $|\kappa| = 0$. We further demonstrate that the linear source term in the DSIIR equation, which serves as the Dysthe-Kakutani transform of the dbar equation's source, is determined by the second-order derivatives of the input function with respect to both x and y variables. This distinguishes it from the DSI equation, where the linear source depends on first-order derivatives. As a result, the reflection coefficient for the DSIIR equation exhibits significant high-frequency behavior, whereas for the DSI equation, it displays oscillatory behavior. These insights regarding the DSIIR equation are derived from the work of Beals and Rakhmanov. Finally, we show that the high-frequency behavior of the reflection coefficient for DSIIR equations is essential for deriving the Zakharov-Shabat inverse scattering transform transform for DSIIR equations. Meta-learning, defined as learning how to learn, has recently gained significant traction in computer science. Specifically within vision tasks, the objective is to train models capable of adapting to new, previously unseen data distributions through minimal examples. This paper introduces a novel depiction learning task where a single image is sufficient to depict an object in a target environment. Unlike prior work where linear depictions are explicit, our approach trains a model to implicitly learn this mapping. We assess performance using a zero-shot transfer metric, measuring the model's ability to generalize to new environments without additional examples. Our method employs meta-training to minimize the distance between mean representations of objects across various environments, thereby facilitating the learning of consistent linear depictions. Experimental results demonstrate that meta-training significantly enhances transfer performance, with a sparse autoencoder proving more effective than a standard convolutional neural network for this specific task. Furthermore, we validate the methodology's effectiveness through a qualitative examination of the resulting linear depictions. Low-resource languages face significant hurdles in Natural Language Processing, primarily due to the scarcity of data and linguistic resources. This scarcity often necessitates training on a limited subset of languages, resulting in code-switching models that perform multilingual processing across these languages. However, this approach compromises both performance and fairness, as low-resource languages are often excluded from training data. This paper addresses these issues by evaluating the robustness of low-resource machine translation models, specifically examining the impacts of knowledge distillation and low-rank matrix quantization. Our findings indicate that knowledge distillation enhances the fairness and accuracy of the target low-resource language but degrades performance on the source language. Conversely, quantization improves source language performance while degrading that of the target language. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that current state-of-the-models do not generalize effectively to low-resource languages. Finally, we show that our custom low-resource models, when subjected to quantization or distillation, achieve results comparable to those of state-of-the-art systems. Overall, this work underscores the need for more robust models capable of processing low-resource languages. The code and data are available at: https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Quantized-and-Low-Resource-MT.

We introduce the concept of hypergraphs and define their associated Lagrangian function. We demonstrate that the illogical nature of this function provides the motivation for developing a novel hypergraph clustering method. Finally, we examine the hyperisostatic state of hypergraphs, examining how variations in their Lagrangian function give rise to diverse clustering patterns. This analysis effectively illustrates the operating principles of the proposed algorithm and highlights its distinct advantages. Experimental results confirm that the algorithm's efficiency surpasses that of existing competitive hypergraph clustering techniques. Additionally, we apply the proposed algorithm to cluster a newly constructed dataset of 1,000 protein molecules. The outcomes indicate that this approach is not only highly effective for clustering large-scale protein molecule data but also demonstrates robust performance across various other types of data. The computational performance of the proposed hypergraph clustering algorithm is further detailed in our accompanying video. This paper introduces a method for binary segmentation of pulmonary nodules in CT scans that eliminates the need for labeled data. We demonstrate that self-training, when applied to unenhanced scans, yields inferior performance compared to its application to enhanced scans. Consequently, image enhancement stands out as the most critical factor in reducing the reliance on labeled data for binary segmentation tasks. Our primary contribution is a segmentation framework utilizing a U-Net architecture, which is evaluated under three distinct scenarios: using unenhanced images without self-training, using unenhanced images with self-training, and using enhanced images with self-training. The results confirm that while image enhancements are vital for developing robust models, they are not strictly necessary to achieve reasonable segmentation performance. The primary objective of this study is to highlight the significant impact of image enhancements and to establish a benchmark for future research aimed at further decreasing the dependency on labeled data. The code and dataset are accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan12345/CT-Scan-Binary-Segmentation. Keywords: binary segmentation, lung CT scan, image enhancement, self-training, U-Net.

Finally, we release a new dataset, "HumanEvalCap," which evaluates the human manageability of image descriptions. This paper introduces MMLSpark, a new open-source machine learning stack built on Apache Spark that offers adaptable, scalable, and unified solutions for data processing and modeling across batch, streaming, interactive, and batch/streaming hybrid environments. MMLSpark fills a significant gap in the big data ecosystem by providing consistent, optimized data processing and modeling across these four modes, enabling users to develop data pipelines and models in batch, scale them to stream interactively, or evolve them as new data sources and modeling techniques emerge. The system includes implementations of popular algorithms such as Random Forest, Gradient Boosted Decision Trees, Linear and Logistic Regression, K-Means, Principal Component Analysis, Clustering, and Dimensionality Reduction. Additionally, it supports data processing capabilities for functions like filtering, sorting, sampling, and feature engineering. Built from the ground up to ensure consistent, optimized data processing across all Spark modes, MMLSpark facilitates the development of batch pipelines, the creation of streaming models, the easy deployment of batch models as streamlets, and the evolution of these models over time. Furthermore, the batch APIs are designed to be compatible with existing H2O Driver Packages, allowing for straightforward upgrades to streaming capabilities. Given the growing demand for unified data processing and modeling across all Spark modes, we anticipate that H2O will soon acquire and contribute to this project. We invite the community to explore, contribute, and experiment with MMLSpark. For more information, visit https://www.h2o.ai/products/mmlspark. Voice Interpretation (VI) involves converting spoken language from one language into a different language. Currently, machine-based VI is achieved through a multi-task pipeline comprising machine speech recognition, machine translation, and machine speech synthesis. This study focuses on the underlying end-task of machine interpretation, which bypasses speech synthesis and directly translates transcriptions across languages. We achieve zero-shot voice interpretation by jointly training 2D-attention-based sequence-to-sequence models with attention-based encoder-decoder attention mechanisms on parallel multilingual data. Furthermore, by leveraging the inherent self-attention mechanism, the model can interpret a test speech input into a language it has not encountered during training without significantly degrading performance. Experiments conducted on multilingual data from the Multilingual Neural Machine Translation (MN12) dataset demonstrate that our model outperforms the baseline and machine interpretation methods in both CTR and BLEU scores across various scenarios. Additionally, we show that the model can successfully interpret speech inputs into new languages at near-original levels using only a few sentences. Finally, we release the pre-trained model to facilitate future research in end-task voice interpretation. In the specific case of linear problems, this convergence is proven to be smooth. Notably, the system reduces to a well-known model when the boundary memory term is absent. Furthermore, we present numerical results that illustrate the dissipative energy mechanisms occurring at the boundary. Accurate short-term probabilistic aggregate load forecasts are essential for the reliable integration of high shares of renewable energy sources (RES) at both the utility and consumer levels. This study evaluates the impact of incorporating daily historical highs into forecast ensembles on the accuracy of probabilistic grid load predictions. Using one-year of smart meter data from 1,000 German households, we generated daily and hourly probabilistic aggregate load forecasts for the 24 hours ahead, combining both standard and historical high-enhanced models. Results indicate that for the 95th percentile, ensemble forecasts based on standard historical patterns outperform those using historical highs. However, when residual forecasts are combined with historical highs, accuracy improves by 1.5% to 3.5% across percentiles ranging from 5% to 95%. This enhancement is particularly pronounced for the 95th and 99th percentiles, where a 5% improvement is achieved. Consequently, the inclusion of daily highs in ensemble forecasts significantly improves the accuracy of extreme load forecasts. These findings are expected to be applicable to other regions and time scales. Furthermore, the methodology is transferable to the planning and operation of energy storage systems and the dispatch of flexible loads. The data and code utilized in this research are available at: https://github.com/JulianSchuierer/ProbabilisticLoadForecasting. Keywords: Probabilistic load forecasting, ensemble forecasting, historical highs, extreme load forecasting, residential load forecasting. The successful implementation of Machine Learning (ML) within healthcare relies heavily on incorporating domain expertise. This paper presents a blueprint for embedding medical knowledge into ML, grounded in the knowledge representation framework established by Miller et al. Specifically, we focus on the information content portion of the Later-Derived Knowledge (LDK), which includes data derived from observations, reports, and measurements. To facilitate this, we introduce a domain-specific ontology designed to capture LDK in the healthcare sector. Furthermore, we detail a methodology for injecting this domain knowledge into ML processes, demonstrating its efficacy through an application to chest X-ray analysis. Our approach enables the identification and integration of relevant knowledge, such as anatomical structures and diagnostic guidelines, directly into ML training and evaluation. We illustrate this by training and assessing ML models for pneumonia detection, thereby injecting anatomical knowledge and diagnostic criteria into both phases. Additionally, we incorporate a statistical model representing uncertainty in radiologist diagnoses and train a meta-model to learn from this uncertainty, subsequently integrating it into the ML workflow. Our results indicate that integrating medical knowledge into ML enhances performance, while also offering a more comprehensive understanding of the uncertainty associated with radiologist diagnoses. This work is expected to serve as a foundation for future research aimed at developing expert-based evaluation metrics for ML and fostering collaboration between domain experts and ML specialists. Although significant advancements have been made in diagnosing pneumonia via chest X-rays using deep learning, the field lacks progress in achieving greater fairness and robustness when dealing with atypical COVID-19 lesions. To address this, we introduce a new training strategy called weak-guided learning, which enhances model performance by incorporating weak annotations. This method utilizes a self-supervised contrastive loss to improve the model's invariance to perturbations in lesion areas and a weak binary mask annotation to mitigate the impact of imperfect ground truth. We evaluated the approach using an ensemble of state-of-the-art detectors and segmenters, finding that the integration of weak-guided learning boosted both accuracy and fairness. Specifically, the average AUC increased from 0.880 to 0.891, and the F-score improved from 0.701 to 0.711. Furthermore, fairness metrics saw substantial gains, with the AUC rising from 0.812 to 0.842 and the F-score from 0.621 to 0.681. Finally, we demonstrate the method's robustness on an external dataset. Our open-source code is available at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Weak-guided-learning}. \textbf{Keywords:} Deep learning, fairness, weak-guided learning, binary mask annotation, atypical COVID-19 lesions.

Precise localization of vertebrae within the spine is essential for numerous diagnostic and therapeutic procedures. Spine rectification algorithms are frequently employed to align the complex, curved vertebral column into a linear structure, thereby simplifying subsequent vertebra recognition tasks. However, these algorithms often introduce significant geometric distortions in the vertebral bodies, which can degrade recognition performance. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel enhancement technique that integrates geometric constraints to minimize such distortions. Our approach combines an anatomically informed registration framework with a virtual CT image synthesis method. We present the VPosE 2021 challenge, which comprises a large-scale, diverse dataset of abdominal CT images featuring detailed annotations. Furthermore, we establish a unified evaluation pipeline that incorporates an efficient vertebra positioning metric. The source code for spine rectification, vertebra positioning, and the virtual CT synthesis tool will be made publicly available. This study investigates the dynamical stabilization of electrons in a cavity through vacuum oscillations, focusing on resonant electron scattering within the extremely strong coupling regime. The research employs a theoretical framework combining a scalar relativistic Schrödinger-Newton equation with an electromagnetic vector potential. Numerical simulations reveal that while relativistic effects cause vacuum oscillations to destabilize at moderate laser intensities, these states are stabilized in the extreme regime under near-resonant conditions. Furthermore, relativistic states exhibiting higher angular momentum are stabilized at lower photon energies. These findings align with experimental data from Klein tunneling studies. Additionally, the analysis demonstrates that electron states are stabilized via a combination of repulsive self-interaction and light-matter coupling, with both mechanisms contributing comparably. The report also outlines potential experimental approaches for observing these relativistic vacuum oscillations. Finally, the study explores scenarios involving multiple electrons, offering insights into multielectron relativistic vacuum oscillations and their experimental detectability. Overall, this work establishes a foundation for future research into relativistic quantum electrodynamics in cavities. Key concepts include relativistic quantum electrodynamics, dynamical stabilization, relativistic self-interaction, and relativistic strong-field physics. Keywords: relativistic quantum electrodynamics, dynamical stabilization, relativistic self-interaction, strong field physics, cavity QED. (Published in Phys. Rev. A 104, 063508, 2021) [https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.104.063508] (Last accessed 2024-08-01)

Recent advancements in actuators, controllers, and sensors have accelerated the development of legged robots. Nevertheless, creating robust and reliable walking robots remains difficult. Although the elastic walking dog created by McGeer in 1988 demonstrated that energy conservation is vital for efficient locomotion, this insight has historically hindered progress in designing robots capable of dynamic gaits. This study demonstrates that a feedforward robot controller can successfully design dynamic gaits that conserve energy. We constructed a physics simulator featuring a 4-DOF leg and an elastic body, driven by a full-actuator controller. Our results show that the robot can walk using only actuator counter-torque to maintain energy conservation, even when friction is minimal. Furthermore, a simple neural network was able to generalize across various walking speeds, step lengths, and initial states. These findings indicate that actuator counter-torque is essential for understanding the robot's dynamic behavior. Consequently, this research paves the way for creating energy-efficient gaits in physical robots, offering a significant step toward cost reduction. Additionally, the actuator's ability to sense and regulate power consumption may enhance the robustness of the robot's gait. Finally, the ease with which actuator dynamics can be learned suggests that machine learning techniques can facilitate the design of energy-efficient gaits. Our comprehensive experiments confirm that counter-torque is indispensable for understanding dynamic behavior, and these results offer a crucial foundation for achieving more energy-efficient movements in real-world robots. The actuator's capacity to monitor and manage power usage represents a vital step toward reducing overall costs. Moreover, the fact that actuator dynamics can be easily learned opens new possibilities for applying machine learning to design energy-efficient gaits. We introduce a systematic divisibility issue that arises during the erasure of quantum information via a quantum channel, which can be conceptually framed as a variational problem. Specifically, we establish a sequence of quantum algebras linked by channel-induced division operations and demonstrate its construction through an indeterminate-based method. Furthermore, we prove that this sequence is the maximal such structure that can be generated solely by repeatedly applying a quantum channel. These findings are deeply connected to the concept of tensor powers of quantum channels and hold significant potential for future applications in quantum information theory. Additionally, we suggest an alternative construction method for these quantum algebras rooted in algebraic geometry and highlight the relationship between our work and prior algebraic approaches to quantum divisibility. Finally, we discuss how our findings can be utilized to investigate channel capacity and channel simulation. This manuscript is a significantly expanded and revised version of our arXiv paper [arXiv:2101.01301]. Various enhancements include the development of new methods for constructing quantum algebras, the addition of examples and exercises, and a more comprehensive exploration of the implications of these results within quantum information theory. Mini-scale tearing modes are ubiquitous in collisionless, magnetized plasmas and are recognized for generating magnetic islands on scales significantly smaller than the local mean free path. Despite their prevalence, the internal structure and evolution of these modes remain poorly understood. This study investigates the internal characteristics of mini-scale tearing modes using a collisionless slab model. We demonstrate that the resistive closure scale, which dictates the internal structure in larger modes, is replaced by a tearing-mode-specific scale known as the "reconnection scale." This scale is defined by the ratio of the tearing-mode wavenumber to the local dispersion wavenumber. We show that the internal structure of mini-scale tearing modes is highly sensitive to the local dispersion wavenumber, which is determined by the balance between the magnetic field, background plasma flow, and the tearing-mode wavenumber. Furthermore, we find that the current profile within the internal region is generally asymmetric, and the resulting "hinge" structure of the magnetic field is typically not symmetric about the magnetic X-point. Finally, we derive an analytical expression for the growth rate of mini-scale tearing modes, revealing that their growth rates can be orders of magnitude higher than those of larger-scale tearing modes. These findings are validated through test cases comparing our analytical results with numerical simulations. This work establishes a foundation for understanding mini-scale tearing modes in various astrophysical and laboratory plasma environments. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package, \texttt{MTM}, to facilitate the application of our mini-scale tearing mode formalism. \texttt{MTM} is available at \url{https://github.com/ericjames/MTM}. This research was conducted under the supervision of Dr. Eric N. Lysak. Eric James is currently a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Michigan, where he can be reached at eric.james@umich.edu. His primary research interests include plasma instabilities, space weather, and laboratory plasma physics. He completed his Ph.D. at the University of Michigan in 2021, with his thesis titled "Theoretical and numerical studies of plasma instabilities in space and laboratory plasmas." During his graduate studies, he worked at the University of Michigan's Plasma Physics Center, the Air Force Research Laboratory's High Energy Density Physics Directorate, and the University of Michigan's Institute for Space and Atmospheric Studies. His educational background includes a Bachelor of Science in Physics from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor, and a Master of Science in Physics from the University of Michigan, Ann Arbor.

The growing availability of digital fashion resources has elevated the importance of fashion image retrieval (FR) as a key research area. However, current state-of-the-art methods often fail to retrieve relevant items when domain shifts occur, such as variations in images captured by different cameras or in low-resolution scenarios. To address this, we introduce a novel approach for fashion image retrieval that applies distinct transformations to feature-level representations of images from different domains, thereby eliminating the need for retraining. Specifically, we employ a dual-stream encoder-decoder architecture to extract features from two distinct domains, followed by a dual-variational auto-encoder (VAE) that learns latent representations for both domains. By sampling from this shared latent space, the model generates images in one domain based on inputs from the other. Extensive experiments on the Polyvore dataset demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques in fashion image retrieval, particularly under domain shift conditions. The code is available at \url{https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Domain-Adaptive-Fashion-Image-Search}. Furthermore, we have released a new, larger dataset containing 1.5 million images across 10,000 categories from various domains for fashion FR, which can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/fashion-retrieval-datasets}. We hope this resource will contribute to future advancements in the field. Our paper is scheduled for publication in the IEEE/CVF Conference on Computer Vision and Pattern Learning (CVPR) 2021. Our GitHub repository for the paper is located at \url{https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Domain-Adaptive-Fashion-Image-Search}. Our work is available under the MIT license at \url{https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Domain-Adaptive-Fashion-Image-Search}. Our contributions include: 1) A new dataset for fashion image retrieval featuring multiple domains and over 1.5 million images across 10,000 categories; 2) A new method utilizing a dual-variational auto-encoder to remove domain bias from fashion image features; 3) Empirical evidence showing that our method outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in fashion image retrieval across various datasets. We introduce an iterative method designed for constrained Banach space optimization, specifically targeting problems where the objective function is the gradient of a linear, continuous, real-valued function. This approach serves as a Banach space extension of the projected gradient ascent method commonly used in the economic core allocation problem. We demonstrate that the algorithm converges both weakly and strongly within reflexive Banach spaces. Furthermore, we apply this theoretical framework to the ill-posed $H^1$-minimization of the $L^2$-distance to a given vector, illustrating its practical utility. In this context, the method corresponds to the projected gradient ascent applied to the norm of the Fourier transform. Finally, we compare the algorithm's performance against the previously proposed Tikhonov-Moreau approach for this specific ill-posed constraint. For this comparison, we developed a variant that adapts the algorithm to satisfy the equality constraint $h=0$ in a least-squares sense, where $h$ represents the Fourier transform of the variable. Numerical experiments conducted on test functions confirm that our proposed method outperforms the Tikhonov-Moreau method in both efficiency and precision. Additionally, we examine how varying parameters in both methods influence their behavior. All experiments were executed on a single core of an Intel(R) Xeon(R) CPU E5-1650 v3 @ 3.50GHz. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/fernando-ruiz/Ilk}. Finally, we outline potential applications of the method in solving the Hilbert problem and in regularizing the deconvolution problem. Both applications involve ill-posed equations, though the specific constraints and functional formulations differ between the two cases. Notably, the computational efficiency of our method on test functions is comparable to that of the Tikhonov-Moreau method. Source code for these applications is available at \url{https://github.com/fernando-ruil/Ilk/tree/HilbertProblem}. Finally, we address several open questions regarding the method's applicability to other equations. Source code for these instances can be found at \url{https://github.com/fernando-ruiz/Ilk/tree/OtherInstances}. Finally, we present a comparative analysis of the computational efficiency among the Tikhonov-Moreau method, a Gradient method, and our proposed Iterated Kaczmarz method. We introduce a novel approach to estimating the depth distribution of scenes captured using light field (LF) arrays. By utilizing multiple in-focus sub-aperture images, we identify and account for scene elements that hinder in-focus focusing. We term this distribution the "Occlusion-Responsive Expense Creator" (OREC). Our method relies on the fact that these elements are typically in focus, allowing OREC generation through a straightforward selection process from sub-aperture images. We evaluate OREC's utility in depth estimation by applying it to scene reconstruction. Results demonstrate that incorporating OREC into the reconstruction pipeline significantly enhances image quality. Furthermore, we validate OREC's effectiveness across various depth estimation tasks, including scene reconstruction, depth rendering, and depth-guided deblurring. Finally, we show that the OREC framework is adaptable to real-world conditions by testing it on outdoor, indoor, and macro scenes. All code and OREC datasets will be made publicly available. (Code: https://github.com/ChenYi1995/OREC) (Dataset: https://github.com/ChenYi1995/LF-Depth-Distribution-Dataset)

This paper introduces bilinear representations for the two-component Fokas-Lenells equations using the 2x2 nonlinear Schrödinger Lax pair. Specifically, we establish bilinear formulas, Hirota bilinear forms, and potential functions that yield both components of the Fokas-Lenells system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these representations facilitate the construction of the hierarchy associated with the Fokas-Lenells equation. As an application, we utilize the Hirota bilinear form to analyze the resonance interaction between three optical pulses within a fiber governed by the Fokas-Lenells equations. This approach reveals the internal structure of the resonance solution and enables a comprehensive description of the physical characteristics of the resonance within a fiber. Additionally, we provide a novel method for constructing the eigenfunction matrix for the Fokas-Lenells system, which is essential for applying the generalized Hirota-Matthews method. Finally, we derive the Lax pair for the third nontrivial member of the hierarchy from the Fokas-Lenells equations, a result achieved by employing the generalized Hirota-Matthews method based on the newly constructed Lax pair. This newly developed Lax pair is anticipated to be a valuable tool for further research. Finally, we outline a strategy for constructing the eigenfunction matrix for the Fokas-Lenells system, which is expected to assist future studies. Our findings are expected to significantly advance the understanding and application of the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the Fokas-Lenells hierarchy and its associated Lax pair; Section 3 derives the bilinear form and potential functions for the hierarchy; Section 4 constructs the hierarchy based on the Fokas-Lenells system using the generalized Hirota-Matthews method and a newly defined eigenfunction matrix; and Section 5 presents our conclusions. Additionally, Appendix A details the construction of the eigenfunction matrix for the Fokas-Lenells system. Keywords: Fokas-Lenells hierarchy; bilinear form; potential function; resonance; eigenfunction matrix. MSC(2010): 35Q53; 37K10; 37K25. 35C08; 35C15. 35C60. 35C06. 35C08. 35C15. 35C60. 35

We examine a broad spectrum of non-Riemannian gravitational actions within the Galilean-conformal framework, particularly focusing on those derived from dual field theory connections. Our analysis reveals that these actions are not gauge invariant under Weyl transformations, with the nature and intensity of this non-invariance varying across different cases. Consequently, identifying a corresponding field theory remains challenging. Furthermore, we explore the relationship between these actions and the light-cone formalism. Finally, we investigate the primary gravitational degrees of freedom associated with these non-Riemannian models. Specifically, the actions involving up to three non-Riemannian effects mimic Riemannian holography, suggesting they could be dual to renormalization group flows on the spatial slice. In contrast, for actions involving four or more non-Riemannian effects, only a subset of spacetime is characterized by renormalization group flows, rendering the connection to duality unclear. Additionally, we establish a correspondence between non-Riemannian curvature and the entanglement entropy of the dual theory. We find that when non-Riemannian effects reach their maximum, entanglement entropy vanishes, whereas intermediate effects yield non-zero values. These findings are corroborated by calculations involving both universal and non-universal terms. Finally, we demonstrate that the light-cone action is dual to a theory on the light-cone, where entanglement entropy remains independent of light-cone deformations. However, these results hold exclusively in the deep light-cone limit. The paper concludes with an extensive discussion of these and other related issues. Notably, we show that the light-cone action is equivalent to a Weyl-invariant Galilean-conformal action, implying that specific choices regarding Weyl non-invariance may be arbitrary. We also discuss the correspondence between non-Riemannian curvature and entanglement entropy in this Weyl-invariant formulation. Ultimately, our findings indicate that Weyl non-invariance is unavoidable only in the presence of four or more non-Riemannian effects. The paper is structured into two parts, with Part I covering the topics addressed here and Part II exploring Part II. This work is based on the thesis entitled "Non-Riemannian Gravitational Actions and their Duals" by Shayan S. Jafarzadeh. Additional details regarding the thesis can be found in the accompanying document. Given the extensive scope of this project, we apologize for any errors that may have occurred.

In Home WiFi environments, devices (extending stations) often switch access points (APs) without considering the current load of the destination AP or the capabilities of the extending station. This blind association can cause the extending station to connect to a congested AP, resulting in reduced throughput and increased latency. To address this, a proposed solution employs IEEE 802.11k and IEEE 802.11v standards to have the extending station proactively scan for available APs and assess their loads before associating. Additionally, the extension AP (EP) can instruct its connected extending stations to adjust their transmission power based on local traffic conditions to prevent overloading the backhaul link connecting the EP to the AP. Simulation results demonstrate that this approach significantly improves throughput for both the extending station and non-extending stations sharing the same AP. Furthermore, the method ensures that the extension link's capacity remains proportional to the AP-backhaul link's capacity, thereby preventing the backhaul from becoming a bottleneck. The proposed scheme requires minimal changes to existing 802.11 standards. To validate the feasibility of this mechanism in a real-world setting, a testbed was constructed using three commercial APs, an OpenWRT device as an EP, and 802.11n client stations. The testbed successfully validated the proposed scheme. Finally, the paper outlines the challenges associated with implementing this approach in actual home networks.
